comma_castle.q:
Choose the correct version:
“My brother a talented pianist won the regional contest.”
opts: My brother, a talented pianist, won
My brother a talented pianist, won
My brother, a talented pianist won
comma_castle.why: An appositive (“a talented pianist”) is extra info — it needs a PAIR of commas, one on each side.

comma_castle.q:
Pick the correctly punctuated list:
“She packed apples pears and plums for the hike.”
comma_castle.why: Items in a series take commas between them. The ACT accepts the Oxford comma — and it never hurts.

comma_castle.q:
Which fixes the comma splice?
“The test was long, I still finished early.”
comma_castle.why: Two complete sentences cannot be glued with just a comma. A semicolon, a period, or a comma + FANBOYS fixes it.

comma_castle.q: Which sentence punctuates the city and its country correctly?
opts: We visited Paris, France, in May.
We visited Paris France in May.
We visited Paris, France in May.
We visited, Paris France, in May.
comma_castle.why: City, country needs commas around the country name — it is a paired appositive like any other.

comma_castle.q:
Where does the comma belong?
“After the long drive through the mountains we finally stopped for food.”
comma_castle.why: An introductory element takes one comma at its end — where the introduction stops and the main sentence starts.

comma_castle.q: Which sentence punctuates the “that” clause correctly?
opts: The novel that won the prize is out of print.
The novel, that won the prize is out of print.
The novel that won the prize, is out of print.
The novel, that won the prize, is out of print.
comma_castle.why: A “that” clause is essential — it tells you which novel — so it takes no commas at all.

comma_castle.q: Which sentence contains an illegal comma?
opts: The tall man in the grey coat, waved.
The tall man in the grey coat waved.
The man, who wore grey, waved.
comma_castle.why: Never put a single comma between a subject and its verb. “The tall man … waved” has to stay joined.

comma_castle.q:
Choose the correct joining:
“The engine had failed ___ the crew kept working.”
comma_castle.why: Two complete sentences join with a comma AND a FANBOYS conjunction — both, never one alone.

comma_castle.q: Which sentence punctuates the “because” clause correctly?
opts: We left early because the road was flooded.
We left early because, the road was flooded.
We, left early because the road was flooded.
We left, early because the road was flooded.
comma_castle.why: A “because” clause that trails the main clause normally takes no comma, and a comma never separates “because” from its own clause. Move the clause to the front and it would take one.

comma_castle.q: Which sentence punctuates the pair of adjectives correctly?
opts: It was a cold, damp morning.
It was a cold damp, morning.
It was a, cold damp morning.
It was a cold, damp, morning.
comma_castle.why: Two adjectives that each modify the noun separately take a comma between them — but never between the last adjective and the noun.

comma_castle.q: Which sentence punctuates the date correctly?
comma_castle.why: A full date takes a comma after the day and another after the year when the sentence goes on. The year is set off like any other paired element.

comma_castle.q: Which sentence punctuates the introductory word correctly?
comma_castle.why: “However” opening a sentence is an intro element, so one comma follows it. No comma may split the subject “the vote” from its verb.

comma_castle.q: Only the students who finished early left the room. Which sentence says that?
opts: The students who finished early left the room.
The students, who finished early, left the room.
The students, who finished early left the room.
The students who finished early, left the room.
comma_castle.why: Commas around “who finished early” would make it extra information, and the sentence would then say that all the students left. To pick out some students, the clause must be essential: no commas.

comma_castle.q: One subject does two things here. Which version punctuates the sentence correctly?
opts: The chef tasted the sauce and added more salt.
The chef tasted the sauce, and added more salt.
The chef tasted the sauce and, added more salt.
The chef, tasted the sauce and added more salt.
comma_castle.why: “Added more salt” has no subject of its own, so this is one clause with two verbs. A comma before “and” is only for joining two complete sentences.

comma_castle.q: Which sentence punctuates the adjectives correctly?
opts: They crossed three old stone bridges.
They crossed three, old, stone bridges.
They crossed three old, stone bridges.
They crossed three, old stone bridges.
comma_castle.why: Test with “and”: “three and old and stone bridges” sounds wrong, so these adjectives build on one another rather than each describing the noun separately. Only coordinate adjectives take commas.

comma_castle.q: Which sentence punctuates the name of the person being spoken to correctly?
opts: Thank you, Priya, for the flowers.
Thank you Priya, for the flowers.
Thank you, Priya for the flowers.
Thank you Priya for, the flowers.
comma_castle.why: A name used in direct address is set off like any other interrupter: a comma on each side when it sits mid-sentence. One comma alone leaves the name half-attached, and a comma before “the flowers” does no legal job.

comma_castle.q: Which sentence punctuates the spoken words correctly?
opts: “We leave at dawn,” the captain said.
“We leave at dawn” the captain said.
“We leave at dawn” the captain, said.
“We leave, at dawn” the captain said.
comma_castle.why: A comma separates a quotation from the tag that says who spoke, and it goes inside the closing quotation mark. A comma after “captain” splits a subject from its verb, which no comma may do.

comma_castle.q:
This sentence is missing one comma. Where does it belong?
“The Hadley Bridge, which opened in 1931 carries two lanes of traffic.”
comma_castle.why: The comma after “Bridge” opens a piece of extra information, and extra information takes a pair. The closing comma goes where the extra part ends, after “1931”, so that “The Hadley Bridge … carries” reads straight through.

comma_castle.q: Which of these sentences needs a comma added?
opts: When the whistle blew the players left the field.
The players left the field when the whistle blew.
The players left the field at the final whistle.
The players left the field and went inside.
comma_castle.why: An introductory clause takes a comma where it ends: “When the whistle blew, the players …”. The same clause placed after the main sentence needs none, and one subject with two verbs (“left … and went”) takes no comma either.

comma_castle.q: Leila has one husband, Tomás. Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
opts: Leila’s husband, Tomás, is a pilot.
Leila’s husband Tomás is a pilot.
Leila’s husband Tomás, is a pilot.
Leila’s husband, Tomás is a pilot.
comma_castle.why: Leila has only one husband, so his name is not needed to pick him out: it is extra information and takes a pair of commas. The unpunctuated version reads naturally, which is the trap; it would suit a woman with several husbands, one of them Tomás. The single-comma versions break the pair.

comma_castle.q: Which sentence punctuates the three actions correctly?
opts: She swept the floor, washed the dishes, and fed the cat.
She swept the floor washed the dishes, and fed the cat.
She swept, the floor, washed the dishes and fed the cat.
She swept the floor, washed the dishes, and, fed the cat.
comma_castle.why: A list is one of the legal comma jobs, and it works for actions as well as things: a comma follows each item before the last. A comma between “swept” and its object, or straight after “and”, does no legal job, so it goes.

comma_castle.q: Which sentence sets off of course correctly?
opts: The results, of course, were late.
The results, of course were late.
The results of course, were late.
The, results of course were late.
comma_castle.why: “Of course” is extra information dropped into the middle of the sentence, and extra information takes a pair of commas. With only one, the comma splits “The results” from “were”, and a single comma may never come between a subject and its verb.

comma_castle.q: Which sentence needs a comma before but?
opts: The shop was small but it sold everything.
The shop was small but busy.
The shop sold bread but not cake.
The shop opened early but closed at noon.
comma_castle.why: A comma goes before a FANBOYS word only when it joins two complete sentences. “It sold everything” has its own subject and verb, so the first needs “small, but it”. The others join two describing words, two things, or two verbs sharing the one subject “The shop”, and take no comma.

comma_castle.q:
Which comma should be removed?
“When the lights went out, the audience, waited quietly in their seats.”
comma_castle.why: The comma after “out” ends an introductory clause, which is one of the legal jobs. The comma after “audience” sits alone between the subject and its verb, “waited”, and a single comma may never go there.

comma_castle.q: Which sentence punctuates the contrast correctly?
opts: It was the heat, not the hills, that slowed us down.
It was the heat not the hills, that slowed us down.
It was the heat, not the hills that slowed us down.
It was, the heat not the hills that slowed us down.
comma_castle.why: “Not the hills” is a contrasting aside: lift it out and “It was the heat that slowed us down” still stands. An aside in mid-sentence is extra information, so it takes a pair of commas. The one-comma versions are the trap: each fences the aside on one side only and cuts the sentence in the wrong place.

equation_station.q: If 3x − 7 = 14, what is x?
equation_station.why: Add 7 to both sides (3x = 21), then divide by 3.

equation_station.q: What is the slope of the line through (2, 3) and (6, 11)?
If 2(x + 4) = 18, then x = ?
equation_station.why: Divide by 2 first: x + 4 = 9. Distributing works too, but dividing is faster.

equation_station.q: A gym charges a $20 joining fee plus $15 a month. Mia has paid $110 in total. For how many months has she been a member?
equation_station.why: Write it: 20 + 15m = 110. Undo the one-time fee first (90), then divide by the monthly charge: m = 6.

equation_station.q: Which expression is equivalent to 3(x + 2) − x?
equation_station.why: Distribute first: 3(x + 2) = 3x + 6. Then combine the like terms: 3x − x = 2x, giving 2x + 6. Multiplying only the x by 3 gives 2x + 2.

equation_station.q: If x + y = 6 and x − y = 2, then x =
equation_station.why: Add the two equations and y cancels: 2x = 8.

equation_station.q: Solve for y: 2y − 3x = 12
equation_station.why: Add 3x to both sides, then divide everything by 2 — including the 12.

equation_station.q: If 5 − 2x > 1, then
equation_station.why: Subtract 5, then divide by −2 — and dividing by a negative flips the inequality sign.

equation_station.q: A line has slope 3 and passes through (0, −4). Its equation is:
equation_station.why: Slope-intercept form is y = mx + b, and (0, −4) gives the intercept directly.

equation_station.q: If 3(x − 2) = 2(x + 1), then x =
equation_station.why: Expand both sides: 3x − 6 = 2x + 2. Collect: x = 8.

equation_station.q: If x/3 + 2 = 6, what is x?
equation_station.why: Undo in reverse order: subtract 2 first (x/3 = 4), then multiply by 3. Multiplying before subtracting gives 24.

equation_station.q: A phone plan costs $30 a month plus $0.10 for each text. Which equation gives the monthly cost C for t texts?
equation_station.why: The $30 is paid once however many texts are sent, so it stands alone; only the $0.10 is multiplied by t.

equation_station.q: What is the slope of the line 4x + 2y = 10?
equation_station.why: Get y alone to reach slope-intercept form: 2y = −4x + 10, so y = −2x + 5. The slope is the coefficient of x, sign included.

equation_station.q: For what value of k does the system y = 3x + 2 and y = kx − 5 have no solution?
equation_station.why: Two lines never meet when they are parallel: same slope, different intercepts. The intercepts (2 and −5) already differ, so k must equal the slope 3.

equation_station.q: A taxi fare is C = 2.5m + 4, where m is the number of miles. What does the 2.5 represent?
opts: the total cost of a 1-mile ride
equation_station.why: In y = mx + b the slope is the rate of change: each extra mile adds $2.50. The 4 is the fee charged before any miles.

equation_station.q: The line y = −4x + 9 crosses the y-axis at which point?
equation_station.why: In y = mx + b, b is the y-intercept: the value of y when x = 0. Here b = 9, so the line crosses at (0, 9). The −4 is the slope, not a point on the axis.

equation_station.q: If 7x = 2x + 35, what is x?
equation_station.why: Collect the x terms on one side first: subtract 2x to get 5x = 35, then divide by 5. Dividing 35 by 7 skips moving the 2x, and 35/9 comes from adding 2x instead of subtracting it.

equation_station.q: Adult tickets cost $8 and child tickets cost $5. A family buys 6 tickets for $39. How many adult tickets did they buy?
equation_station.why: Let a be the adult tickets, so 6 − a are child tickets: 8a + 5(6 − a) = 39. Then 3a + 30 = 39, so a = 3. Check: 3 × $8 + 3 × $5 = $39.

equation_station.q: Solve for x: ax + b = cx
equation_station.why: Isolate the variable: move the x terms together, b = cx − ax, then factor out x, b = x(c − a), and divide. Moving ax across without changing its sign gives b/(a − c).

equation_station.q: A plumber charges $45 for a visit plus $30 an hour. A customer can spend at most $180. What is the greatest whole number of hours the plumber can work?
equation_station.why: Write the inequality 45 + 30h ≤ 180, so 30h ≤ 135 and h ≤ 4.5. Only whole hours count, so round down to 4; five hours would cost $195. The 6 comes from forgetting the $45 fee.

equation_station.q: Which ordered pair is a solution of 2x + y = 11?
equation_station.why: A solution is a pair that makes the equation true. Put x = 4 and y = 3 in: 2(4) + 3 = 11. The others give 10, 12 and 9, so each fails.

equation_station.q: A line has slope −2 and crosses the y-axis at (0, 5). What is y on this line when x = 4?
equation_station.why: In y = mx + b the slope is m and the starting value is b, so the line is y = −2x + 5. Then y = −2(4) + 5 = −8 + 5 = −3. Reading the slope as +2 gives 13.

equation_station.q: Solve for x: 0.2x + 1.5 = 3.9
equation_station.why: Undo in reverse order: subtract first, 0.2x = 2.4, then divide, x = 2.4 ÷ 0.2 = 12. Stopping after the subtraction leaves 2.4; adding 1.5 instead of subtracting leads to 27.

equation_station.q: Two numbers add up to 30. One is 6 more than twice the other. What is the larger number?
equation_station.why: Call the smaller n, so the larger is 2n + 6. Then n + 2n + 6 = 30, so 3n = 24 and n = 8. The question asks for the larger number: 2(8) + 6 = 22. Answering 8 solves for the wrong one.

equation_station.q:
How many solutions does this system have?
2x + 3y = 7
4x + 6y = 14
equation_station.why: Put both in y = mx + b form: each becomes y = −(2/3)x + 7/3. Same slope and same intercept means the same line, so every point on it solves both: infinitely many. The second equation is just the first doubled, which is easy to miss when the numbers look different.

vocab_vault.q:
“Her approach was methodical: every trial logged, every variable controlled.”
As used here, methodical most nearly means:
vocab_vault.why: The colon explains the word: logged trials and controlled variables describe organisation. “Slow” is the trap — plausible about a person, unsupported by this sentence.

vocab_vault.q:
“The engineers proposed a novel solution to the bridge problem.”
Novel most nearly means:
vocab_vault.why: A solution cannot be fictional. Substitute each choice back into the sentence and only one survives.

vocab_vault.q:
“Asked about the delays, the director gave a candid response.”
Candid most nearly means:
vocab_vault.why: Candid is frank and unguarded — the opposite of rehearsed or evasive.

vocab_vault.q:
“The critic’s scathing review upset the author for weeks.”
Scathing most nearly means:
vocab_vault.why: It upset the author for weeks, so the review must have been severe.

vocab_vault.q:
“The soil here is poor, but the vines exploit it: their roots drive nine metres down to reach water no weed can find.”
As used here, exploit most nearly means:
vocab_vault.why: The everyday sense of “exploit” is negative, but the sentence admires the vines. Context beats habit.

vocab_vault.q:
“For thirty years the theory was orthodox; the students who questioned it were quietly not renewed.”
Orthodox most nearly means:
vocab_vault.why: The second clause shows the cost of disagreeing with it, which tells you it was the established view.

vocab_vault.q:
“She was frank about the risk, and the crew appreciated it.”
Frank most nearly means:
vocab_vault.why: The crew appreciated it, so the word must be positive — which rules out “severe”.

vocab_vault.q:
“The committee’s report was exhaustive: four hundred pages, six appendices, every objection answered.”
Exhaustive most nearly means:
vocab_vault.why: The colon lists evidence of completeness. “Tiring” borrows from “exhausting”, a different word.

vocab_vault.q:
“His account of the crossing is sober, and duller for it — no storms, no heroics, only distances and dates.”
Sober most nearly means:
vocab_vault.why: The dash defines it: no storms and no heroics. “Accurate” is tempting but the sentence never claims truth, only plainness.

vocab_vault.q:
“The fossil record here is spotty, so any story we tell about the period has to be held loosely.”
Spotty most nearly means:
vocab_vault.why: The consequence — holding the story loosely — points to gaps in the record rather than to poor workmanship.

vocab_vault.q:
“The senator’s plan found little currency among younger voters, who had heard the same promise from her predecessor.”
As used here, currency most nearly means:
vocab_vault.why: Plans do not earn money among voters. “Found little currency” means the idea did not circulate or catch on, and the reason given (they had heard it before) fits that.

vocab_vault.q:
“After the match the coach fielded questions from reporters for nearly an hour.”
As used here, fielded most nearly means:
vocab_vault.why: Substitute each choice: a coach who stays for an hour is responding to the questions, not dodging them. The sports sense of “field” is the trap.

vocab_vault.q:
“The ledger was telling: its entries stopped the same week the manager left.”
As used here, telling most nearly means:
vocab_vault.why: The colon explains the word — the ledger shows something without saying it. A ledger is not an argument, so “persuasive” overshoots.

vocab_vault.q:
“Critics called the chapel austere, but the architect had meant every bare wall and every plain window.”
As used here, austere most nearly means:
vocab_vault.why: “Bare wall” and “plain window” define it. “Cruel” is the sense used of people; “unfinished” contradicts the architect having meant every detail.

vocab_vault.q:
“The ice arrested the ship’s progress for six days.”
Which word could replace arrested without changing the meaning?
vocab_vault.why: The ice stopped the ship moving. “Detained” and “charged” belong to the police sense of arrest, and a ship’s progress cannot be captured.

vocab_vault.q:
“The hikers were famished after eight hours on the trail, and they ate everything in the hut.”
Famished most nearly means:
vocab_vault.why: Eating everything in sight after a long day points to hunger. “Very tired” fits the long day but not the eating, and the eating is the clue the sentence gives. Put “very hungry” back in and the sentence still says the same thing.

vocab_vault.q:
“The instructions were so ambiguous that half the class built the model upside down.”
Ambiguous most nearly means:
vocab_vault.why: Half the class went wrong in the same way, which is what happens when instructions can be read two ways. Swap “unclear” into the sentence and the cause and effect still hold.

vocab_vault.q:
“Rather than argue, the new manager tried to placate the angry customers with free coffee.”
Placate most nearly means:
vocab_vault.why: “Rather than argue” and the free coffee both point toward soothing the customers. Match the tone: a peace offering needs a peaceful word.

vocab_vault.q:
“Though the storm was fierce, the old barn remained intact; not a single board was missing.”
Intact most nearly means:
vocab_vault.why: The sentence explains the word itself: “not a single board was missing.” A barn can stand upright and still lose boards, so “upright” does not match what the sentence says.

vocab_vault.q:
“Before the review ran, the editor asked him to temper the harshest sentences.”
As used here, temper most nearly means:
vocab_vault.why: The familiar “temper” is anger, and harsh sentences make that reading tempting, but the editor wants the sentences changed, not someone provoked. To temper something is to moderate it. “Harden” borrows from tempering steel, which the sentence has no use for, and “shorten” changes length, not force.

vocab_vault.q:
“The recipe calls for a scant cup of sugar, so stop filling just below the rim.”
As used here, scant most nearly means:
vocab_vault.why: The sentence explains the word for you: stop “just below the rim”. Predict “not quite full” and match it. “Heaped” reverses the meaning.

vocab_vault.q:
“The mayor’s speech was a masterpiece of economy: in four minutes she named the problem, the cost and the plan.”
As used here, economy most nearly means:
vocab_vault.why: The familiar money meaning is the trap. The colon tells you what the economy consisted of: a great deal said in four minutes. Economy here is its quieter second meaning, doing much with little.

vocab_vault.q:
“The treaty was a qualified success: trade grew, but the border disputes it was meant to end went on.”
As used here, qualified most nearly means:
vocab_vault.why: Substitute and test: after the colon, one thing worked and one did not, so the success was partial. “Qualified” in its quieter meaning is limited or held back. The familiar meaning, trained or certified, does not fit a treaty.

vocab_vault.q:
“Years of drought had checked the town’s growth; the new reservoir released it.”
As used here, checked most nearly means:
vocab_vault.why: The second half says the reservoir “released” the growth, so the drought must have held it back. That is check’s quieter meaning, the same one as in “check the bleeding”. “Inspected” is the everyday meaning, and a drought does not inspect anything.

vocab_vault.q:
“She kept her own counsel through the long meeting, and only on the train home did she tell us what she thought.”
As used here, kept her own counsel most nearly means:
vocab_vault.why: Use the rest of the sentence: she said what she thought “only on the train home”, so during the meeting she stayed silent. “Followed her own advice” is the tempting literal reading of “counsel”, but nothing in the sentence is about advice.

apostrophe_alley.q: Which sentence uses its correctly?
apostrophe_alley.why: “its” = belonging to the team. “it’s” = “it is”. There is no such word as “its’”.

apostrophe_alley.q: Which is correct for a locker room shared by many players?
apostrophe_alley.why: A plural noun that already ends in s takes just an apostrophe after it.

apostrophe_alley.q:
Fill in:
“___ going to love ___ new coach.”
apostrophe_alley.why: “They’re” = they are; “their” shows possession; “there” is a place.

apostrophe_alley.q: Which sentence gets both the plural and the possessive right?
apostrophe_alley.why: Plain plural “dogs” takes no apostrophe, since the dogs own nothing in that word. The possessive “their” shows the tails belong to them; “they’re” means “they are” and “there” is a place.

apostrophe_alley.q: Which shows one boss owning an office?
apostrophe_alley.why: A singular noun takes ’s even when it already ends in s. “The bosses’ office” would mean several bosses share it.

apostrophe_alley.q: Which sentence writes the decade correctly?
apostrophe_alley.why: A decade is a plain plural, not a possessive. No apostrophe.

apostrophe_alley.q:
Fill in:
“___ coat is on the chair?”
apostrophe_alley.why: “Whose” asks about possession. “Who’s” only ever means “who is” or “who has”.

apostrophe_alley.q: Ana and Ben jointly own one car. Which is correct?
apostrophe_alley.why: Joint ownership marks only the last name. Marking both would mean they own a car each.

apostrophe_alley.q: Which shows the possessive of an irregular plural?
apostrophe_alley.why: “Children” is already plural without an s, so it takes an ordinary ’s.

apostrophe_alley.q:
Fill in:
“___ sure that ___ notes are complete.”
apostrophe_alley.why: “You’re” = you are; “your” shows possession.

apostrophe_alley.q: The Jones family owns one house together. Which phrase is correct?
apostrophe_alley.why: First make the family name plural (one Jones, two Joneses), then make the plural possessive: it already ends in s, so add only an apostrophe.

apostrophe_alley.q: Which sentence shows that the tail belongs to one cat?
apostrophe_alley.why: One owner whose name does not end in s takes ’s. “Cats’” would mean several cats share one tail.

apostrophe_alley.q:
Fill in:
“The museum reopened ___ west wing; ___ been closed since spring.”
apostrophe_alley.why: Expand to test: the wing belongs to the museum, so the first blank is “its”. The second expands to “it has been closed”, so it is “it’s”. Remember that it’s can mean “it has” as well as “it is”.

apostrophe_alley.q:
Fill in:
“After two ___ delay, the ferry finally left.”
apostrophe_alley.why: Time words take possessives, as in “a day’s work”. Two hours is a plural already ending in s, so the apostrophe goes after the s.

apostrophe_alley.q: Ana and Lia each own a bike. Which sentence says so?
opts: Ana’s and Lia’s bikes were stolen.
Ana and Lia’s bikes were stolen.
Anas and Lias bikes were stolen.
Ana and Lias’ bikes were stolen.
apostrophe_alley.why: Separate ownership marks each name. Marking only the last name (“Ana and Lia’s”) is joint ownership, which would mean they share the bikes.

apostrophe_alley.q: Which contraction of “does not” is written correctly?
apostrophe_alley.why: In a contraction the apostrophe stands exactly where letters were dropped. “Does not” loses the o of “not”, so the apostrophe goes between the n and the t.

apostrophe_alley.q:
Fill in:
“The blue bag is mine; the red one is ___.”
apostrophe_alley.why: Possessive pronouns (hers, ours, yours, theirs, its) already show ownership and never take an apostrophe. “Her” needs a noun after it (“her bag”), so it cannot end the sentence.

apostrophe_alley.q:
In the sentence below, which word is a possessive rather than a plural?
“The farmer’s fields flooded after the storms.”
apostrophe_alley.why: An apostrophe plus s marks ownership: the fields belong to the farmer. “Fields” and “storms” are ordinary plurals, made with s and no apostrophe, and “flooded” is the verb.

apostrophe_alley.q:
Fill in:
“___ been borrowing my stapler?”
apostrophe_alley.why: Expand the choice to test it, exactly as with it’s: “who’s” can stand for “who is” or “who has”, and only “who has been borrowing” makes sense here. “Whose” is a possessive and needs a noun after it, and “who is been” is not English.

apostrophe_alley.q:
The Jones family is visiting. Fill in:
“The ___ are coming to dinner on Sunday.”
apostrophe_alley.why: Nothing here belongs to anyone; the sentence only needs the plural. Make a family name plural by adding -es and stop there. Any apostrophe would turn it into a possessive with nothing to possess.

apostrophe_alley.q:
Which word in the sentence is missing an apostrophe?
“Omars bike leans against the school gates.”
apostrophe_alley.why: The bike belongs to one owner, Omar, so his name takes ’s: “Omar’s bike”. “Gates” is an ordinary plural and “leans” is a verb; neither owns anything, so neither takes an apostrophe.

apostrophe_alley.q: A market sign reads “Ripe peach’s, 3 for $2.” How should peach’s be written?
apostrophe_alley.why: The sign means more than one peach and says nothing about ownership, so it needs a plain plural, and a plural takes no apostrophe. A word ending in -ch adds -es: “peaches”.

apostrophe_alley.q:
Fill in:
“We borrowed my ___ car for the weekend.”
apostrophe_alley.why: One person owns the car, so this is a singular possessive, and in a compound noun the ’s goes on the last word of the whole name: “sister-in-law’s”. “Sisters-in-law” is the plural and shows no ownership at all.

apostrophe_alley.q:
Fill in:
“The two ___ head offices are both in Denver.”
apostrophe_alley.why: There are two owners, so make the plural first, “companies” (y becomes ies), and then make it possessive. A plural already ending in s takes only an apostrophe. “Company’s” would give both offices to one company.

apostrophe_alley.q: In which sentence does ’s stand for “is” rather than show ownership?
opts: The storm’s winds died at dawn.
apostrophe_alley.why: Expand to test, exactly as with it’s: “The storm is coming in fast” makes sense, so that ’s is a contraction. In the others the eye, the damage and the winds belong to the storm, and “the storm is eye” is not English. All four look alike, which is the trap; only the expansion test tells them apart.

fragment_forest.q: Which is a COMPLETE sentence?
opts: The storm knocked out the power.
Because the storm knocked out the power.
The storm, knocking out the power.
When the storm hit last night.
fragment_forest.why: It has a subject (storm), a real verb (knocked), and a complete thought.

fragment_forest.q:
Best fix:
“The runners stretched. Before the race began.”
fragment_forest.why: “Before the race began” is a fragment — attach it to the main clause.

fragment_forest.q:
Which fixes the run-on?
“I studied all night I still felt unready.”
fragment_forest.why: Two full sentences need a semicolon, a period, or a comma + FANBOYS.

fragment_forest.q: Which group of words is a fragment because a subordinator opens it?
fragment_forest.why: “Although” turns a complete thought into a dependent clause, which now needs a main clause to finish it.

fragment_forest.q:
Best fix:
“The team practicing all afternoon in the heat.”
opts: The team practiced all afternoon in the heat.
The team, practicing all afternoon in the heat.
Practicing all afternoon in the heat.
fragment_forest.why: “Practicing” on its own is not a verb a sentence can run on. It needs a real one: “practiced”.

fragment_forest.q:
Which fixes the run-on with a conjunction?
“The bell rang no one moved.”
fragment_forest.why: Comma + FANBOYS joins two complete sentences, and the comma goes before the conjunction, not after it.

fragment_forest.q: Which group of words is a fragment because a relative pronoun opens it?
opts: Which was the best part of the trip.
That was the best part of the trip.
The best part was the trip.
fragment_forest.why: A relative clause beginning “which” cannot stand alone — it modifies something in another sentence.

fragment_forest.q: Which sentence is missing a verb?
opts: The long queue outside the theatre in the rain.
The queue stretched outside the theatre.
fragment_forest.why: There is a subject and plenty of description, but nothing the subject actually does.

fragment_forest.q:
Best fix:
“She rewrote the essay, it was much stronger.”
fragment_forest.why: That is a comma splice. Adding a FANBOYS conjunction makes the join legal.

fragment_forest.q: A sentence needs a subject and a verb — though the subject may be understood. Which of these qualifies?
fragment_forest.why: A command has an understood subject (you) and a real verb. One word can be a whole sentence.

fragment_forest.q: Which of these word groups is a complete sentence?
opts: Venice, a city built on canals, floods often.
Venice, a city built on canals and lagoons.
Venice, which is a city built on canals.
Venice, built on canals and often flooding.
fragment_forest.why: The appositive “a city built on canals” renames Venice but is not a verb. Only the first gives Venice a main verb of its own: “floods”.

fragment_forest.q:
Best fix:
“We waited for hours. Hoping the rain would stop.”
opts: hours, hoping the rain would stop.
hours. Hoping, the rain would stop.
hours; hoping the rain would stop.
hours. And hoping the rain would stop.
fragment_forest.why: “Hoping the rain would stop” has no subject or main verb, so attach it to the sentence before with a comma. A semicolon needs a complete sentence on both sides.

fragment_forest.q:
Which fixes the fragment?
“Because the store was closed.”
opts: Because the store was closed, we went home.
fragment_forest.why: “Because” makes the clause dependent. It needs a main clause such as “we went home” to finish the thought.

fragment_forest.q:
Which fixes the error?
“The data looked promising, however, the sample was small.”
fragment_forest.why: A complete sentence stands on each side of “however”, and “however” is not a FANBOYS word, so a comma cannot join them. A semicolon before it can.

fragment_forest.q: Which word group can stand alone as a sentence?
opts: The scientist who first described the virus lived in Lyon.
The scientist who first described the virus in Lyon.
The scientist, having first described the virus in Lyon.
Although the scientist first described the virus in Lyon.
fragment_forest.why: In the other three, the only verbs sit inside a “who” clause, an -ing phrase or an “although” clause. Only the first gives the subject a main verb: “lived”.

fragment_forest.q: Which of these is NOT a complete sentence?
opts: To finish the report by Friday.
She finished the report by Friday.
Nobody finished the report by Friday.
The report was finished by Friday.
fragment_forest.why: A “to” form such as “to finish” is not a main verb, and the group has no subject either, so it cannot stand alone. Each of the others has a subject and a real verb.

fragment_forest.q:
The word group below is not a complete sentence. What does it lack?
“Running along the beach at sunrise.”
opts: a subject and a main verb
fragment_forest.why: An -ing word on its own is not a main verb, and nothing in the group names who is running. It needs both (“She was running …”) before it can stand alone. No punctuation mark can supply a missing subject or verb.

fragment_forest.q:
Which choice fixes the fragment by supplying what it lacks?
“Waited outside the station for an hour.”
opts: We waited outside the station for an hour.
Waited, outside the station for an hour.
Waiting outside the station for an hour.
Waited outside the station, for an hour.
fragment_forest.why: The group has a verb, “waited”, but no subject: nobody is doing the waiting. Adding one (“We”) completes it. Commas do not create a subject, and changing “waited” to “waiting” removes the verb as well.

fragment_forest.q: Which word group is a fragment?
opts: The bridge built by the Romans across the gorge.
The Romans built the bridge across the gorge.
Built by the Romans, the bridge still stands.
The bridge across the gorge was built by Romans.
fragment_forest.why: A past participle such as “built” cannot be a main verb on its own; it needs a helper (“was built”), or it must describe a noun in a sentence that has its own verb. The third choice works because “still stands” is its main verb. The fragment has only “built”, so it never makes a statement.

fragment_forest.q:
What is missing from this word group?
“Although the committee, which met every Tuesday in the old library, had approved the plan that the mayor proposed.”
opts: a main clause to attach to
fragment_forest.why: The group has plenty of verbs (“met”, “had approved”, “proposed”), which is what makes it look complete. But “Although” turns everything up to the full stop into a dependent clause, so a main clause must follow: “…, the council rejected it.” “Had approved” is already the committee’s verb.

fragment_forest.q:
How many complete sentences does this passage contain?
“The bus was late. We walked. Because the rain had stopped.”
fragment_forest.why: “The bus was late” and “We walked” each have a subject, a real verb and a complete thought; two words can make a whole sentence. “Because the rain had stopped” opens with a subordinator, so it cannot stand alone.

fragment_forest.q:
Which word, added to the start of this sentence, would turn it into a fragment?
“The train left on time.”
fragment_forest.why: “Although” is a subordinator: “Although the train left on time.” leaves the reader waiting for a main clause. “Luckily”, “Today” and “Then” only add information to a sentence that is still complete.

fragment_forest.q:
Which choice fixes the error?
“We ate lunch by the lake, then we hiked to the falls.”
fragment_forest.why: “We ate lunch by the lake” and “we hiked to the falls” are both complete sentences, and “then” is not a FANBOYS word, so a comma before it makes a comma splice. Adding “and” gives the legal comma + FANBOYS join.

fragment_forest.q: Which of these is a run-on sentence?
opts: The lights dimmed the play began.
The lights dimmed, and the play began.
When the lights dimmed, the play began.
The lights dimmed; the play began.
fragment_forest.why: The first fuses two complete sentences, “The lights dimmed” and “the play began”, with nothing between them. The others join them legally: comma + FANBOYS, a subordinator that makes the first part dependent, and a semicolon.

fragment_forest.q:
Which choice is best?
“Although the forecast promised sun, we packed umbrellas.”
fragment_forest.why: “Although” makes the first clause dependent, and here it is already attached to a main clause, “we packed umbrellas”, with a comma, which is exactly how a dependent clause should be handled. A period or a semicolon would cut it loose as a fragment. The word “Although” pulls toward a fix the sentence does not need.

dash_dungeon.q:
Choose the correct punctuation:
“Her goal ___ a perfect score ___ drove every session.”
dash_dungeon.why: Dashes setting off extra info must come as a matched pair.

dash_dungeon.q: Which uses a colon correctly?
opts: She had one rule: never quit.
She had: one rule never quit.
She had one: rule never quit.
She had one rule; never quit:
dash_dungeon.why: A colon follows a complete sentence, then introduces the point.

dash_dungeon.q: Pick the correct sentence:
opts: The bus was late; we missed the opening.
The bus was late, we missed the opening.
The bus was late we missed the opening.
The bus was late: we missed—
dash_dungeon.why: A semicolon joins two complete, related sentences.

dash_dungeon.q: Which sentence introduces the list correctly?
opts: I packed rope, a torch, and water.
I packed: rope, a torch, and water.
I packed — rope, a torch, and water.
I packed; rope, a torch, and water.
dash_dungeon.why: A colon needs a complete sentence in front of it. “I packed” is not one — it is still waiting for its object.

dash_dungeon.q: Which is correctly punctuated?
opts: Only one thing stopped her — fear.
Only one thing stopped her, — fear.
Only one thing stopped her — fear —.
Only one thing — stopped her fear.
dash_dungeon.why: A single dash is legal when the extra material runs to the end of the sentence; there it needs no partner.

dash_dungeon.q:
What is wrong with:
“The route — steep, icy, and long, was closed.”
opts: the pair is mismatched: a dash opens it and a comma closes it
a dash may never set off a list of adjectives like this one
the list inside the dashes needs a colon before “steep”
nothing is wrong, since a dash and a comma are interchangeable
dash_dungeon.why: Dashes and commas are both legal fences, but the two ends have to match each other.

dash_dungeon.q:
Choose the correct punctuation:
“The trail was flooded ___ however, we pressed on.”
dash_dungeon.why: “However” joining two sentences needs a semicolon before it; a comma there is a splice.

dash_dungeon.q: Which sentence punctuates the explanation correctly?
opts: The result was clear: the bridge would not hold.
The result was clear, the bridge would not hold.
The result was clear the bridge would not hold.
The result was clear — the bridge would not hold:
dash_dungeon.why: A colon is right when the second half delivers or explains the first. The comma version is a splice.

dash_dungeon.q: Which is punctuated correctly?
opts: We stopped — the engine was smoking — and waited.
We stopped — the engine was smoking and waited.
We stopped, the engine was smoking — and waited.
We stopped — the engine was smoking, — and waited.
dash_dungeon.why: An interruption mid-sentence takes a dash on both sides, and the sentence must still read correctly once the interruption is removed.

dash_dungeon.q: Which list is punctuated correctly?
opts: We visited Lima, Peru; Quito, Ecuador; and Bogotá, Colombia.
We visited Lima, Peru, Quito, Ecuador, and Bogotá, Colombia.
We visited Lima; Peru, Quito; Ecuador, and Bogotá; Colombia.
We visited: Lima, Peru, Quito, Ecuador and Bogotá, Colombia.
dash_dungeon.why: When the items themselves contain commas, semicolons separate the items so the reader can see where each one ends.

dash_dungeon.q:
Choose the correct punctuation:
“The recipe needs three spices ___ cumin, clove, and ginger.”
dash_dungeon.why: A complete sentence announces a list, so a colon introduces it. A semicolon would need a complete sentence after it.

dash_dungeon.q:
Choose the correct version:
“The survey found ___ most residents wanted a park.”
dash_dungeon.why: Nothing separates a verb from the clause it introduces. “Found” needs its object, so any mark there interrupts the sentence where it has no break.

dash_dungeon.q: Which sentence uses parentheses correctly?
opts: The mill (built in 1790) still grinds flour.
The mill, (built in 1790) still grinds flour.
The mill (built in 1790,) still grinds flour.
The mill (built in 1790 still grinds flour.)
dash_dungeon.why: Parentheses are a pair, like two commas or two dashes: they close around the extra fact, and no comma is added beside them. Remove the brackets and the sentence still reads correctly.

dash_dungeon.q:
Which choice would NOT be acceptable in place of the semicolon?
“The storm knocked out the power; the whole street went dark.”
dash_dungeon.why: A period, a comma with “so”, and a dash introducing the result can all join these two sentences. A comma alone cannot: that is a comma splice.

dash_dungeon.q: Which sentence uses its semicolon correctly?
opts: The results were late; the lab blamed the courier.
The results were late; because the courier was delayed.
The results were late; but the lab stayed calm.
The results were late; and they were incomplete.
dash_dungeon.why: Only the first has a complete sentence on each side and no joining word. After “because” the second half cannot stand alone, and with “but” or “and” the right partner is a comma.

dash_dungeon.q: When a semicolon joins two clauses, what must stand on each side of it?
dash_dungeon.why: A semicolon works like a full stop: if a period could go there, a semicolon can. So each side must be able to stand alone as a complete sentence.

dash_dungeon.q: Which version handles the words after “such as” correctly?
opts: The shop sells tools such as hammers, saws, and drills.
The shop sells tools such as: hammers, saws, and drills.
The shop sells tools such as; hammers, saws, and drills.
The shop sells tools such as — hammers, saws, and drills.
dash_dungeon.why: No mark goes after “such as”: the phrase already introduces the examples. A colon would need a complete sentence before it, and “The shop sells tools such as” is not one.

dash_dungeon.q:
Which mark could replace the dash without breaking a rule?
“She ordered only one thing — black coffee.”
dash_dungeon.why: A single dash at the end of a sentence introduces a reveal, which is a colon’s job too, and the words before it form a complete sentence. A semicolon needs a full sentence on both sides, and “black coffee” is not one.

dash_dungeon.q:
Which version is clearest and correctly punctuated?
“The three founders ___ Ada, Ben, and Cy ___ met in 1990.”
dash_dungeon.why: With commas round the names, the reader cannot tell where the list stops and the sentence resumes; it can look like a list of five people. When the extra information already contains commas, a pair of dashes sets it off cleanly. A colon cannot follow “The three founders”, which is not a complete sentence.

dash_dungeon.q:
Choose the correct punctuation:
“The plan ___ however ___ was rejected by the board.”
dash_dungeon.why: “However” here interrupts a single clause (“The plan was rejected”), so it is set off by a pair of commas. A semicolon before “however” belongs only where it joins two complete sentences, and “The plan” is not one.

dash_dungeon.q:
Which pair of marks could fill both blanks?
“The mill ___ the oldest in the county ___ closed in May.”
dash_dungeon.why: Extra information in mid-sentence is fenced by a matching pair: two dashes, two commas or two parentheses. A dash and a comma break the pair, and a colon or semicolon cannot follow “The mill”, which is not a complete sentence.

dash_dungeon.q: Which sentence punctuates the simple list correctly?
opts: We bought bread, milk, and eggs.
We bought bread; milk; and eggs.
We bought: bread, milk, and eggs.
We bought bread — milk — and eggs.
dash_dungeon.why: Semicolons separate list items only when the items already contain commas. These items are single words, so plain commas do the job. A colon cannot follow “We bought”, which is still waiting for its object.

dash_dungeon.q:
The sentence needs a second dash. Where should it go?
“My neighbour — a retired pilot who still flies on weekends taught me to read a map.”
dash_dungeon.why: Dashes around extra information come as a pair, and the closing dash goes where the extra part ends. Lift out “a retired pilot who still flies on weekends” and “My neighbour taught me to read a map” reads straight through.

dash_dungeon.q: Which sentence places the period correctly?
opts: The hall seats 500 (the old one seated 300).
The hall seats 500 (the old one seated 300.)
The hall seats 500. (the old one seated 300)
The hall seats 500, (the old one seated 300).
dash_dungeon.why: The words in parentheses belong to the sentence, so the bracket closes around them first and the sentence’s own period comes after it. Like any pair of parentheses, they take no comma beside them.

dash_dungeon.q:
Which choice is best?
“The kit held three tools; a saw, a drill, and a level.”
dash_dungeon.why: A complete sentence announces a list, and that is a colon’s job. A semicolon needs a complete sentence on both sides, and “a saw, a drill, and a level” is not one. The semicolon looks legal because the words before it do form a sentence; the words after it must too.

verb_valley.q:
Choose the verb:
“The box of old photographs ___ in the attic.”
verb_valley.why: The subject is “box” (singular). Cross out “of old photographs” and the agreement is obvious.

verb_valley.q:
Keep the tense consistent:
“She opened the door and ___ inside.”
verb_valley.why: Past “opened” needs past “stepped”. Verbs joined by “and” share a tense.

verb_valley.q:
Choose the verb:
“Neither of the answers ___ correct.”
verb_valley.why: “Neither” is singular, however plural the phrase after it sounds.

verb_valley.q:
Choose the verb:
“By noon the swimmers had ___ three laps.”
verb_valley.why: After “had”, English needs the past participle. For swim that is “swum”; “swam” is the simple past and takes no helper.

verb_valley.q:
Choose the verb:
“The committee ___ its decision on Friday.”
verb_valley.why: A collective noun acting as one body is singular — and “its” later in the sentence confirms it.

verb_valley.q:
Choose the verb:
“There ___ three reasons to be cautious.”
verb_valley.why: In a “there ___” sentence the real subject comes after the verb. Here it is “reasons”, which is plural.

verb_valley.q:
Choose the verb:
“By the time we arrived, the film ___ already started.”
verb_valley.why: The earlier of two past events takes the past perfect: it had started before we arrived.

verb_valley.q:
Choose the verb:
“The coach, along with two players, ___ the award.”
verb_valley.why: “Along with” does not make a compound subject. The subject is still “the coach”, singular.

verb_valley.q:
Choose the verb:
“The director and the producer ___ on the script.”
verb_valley.why: Two nouns joined by “and” make a genuine plural subject.

verb_valley.q:
Choose the verb:
“Either the manager or the assistants ___ the keys.”
verb_valley.why: With “either … or”, the verb matches whichever subject is nearer. “Assistants” is nearer, and plural.

verb_valley.q:
Keep the tense consistent:
“Every summer we drive to the coast and ___ in a small cabin.”
verb_valley.why: “Drive” is present tense describing a habit, so the second verb stays in the present too.

verb_valley.q:
Choose the verb:
“Tired after the hike, she ___ down on the sofa.”
verb_valley.why: The past of lie (to recline) is “lay”. “Laid” is the past of lay (to put something down), which needs an object; “lied” means told an untruth.

verb_valley.q:
Choose the verb phrase:
“If we had left earlier, we ___ the train.”
verb_valley.why: An unreal past condition takes “would have” + past participle. “Would of” is a mishearing of “would’ve”, and the participle of catch is “caught”.

verb_valley.q:
Choose the verb:
“Everyone on both teams ___ a medal.”
verb_valley.why: “Everyone” is singular. Cross out “on both teams” and “everyone receives” is clear.

verb_valley.q:
Choose the verb:
“On the top shelf ___ two jars of honey.”
verb_valley.why: The sentence is inverted: the subject comes after the verb. Ask what sits there — “two jars”, which is plural. “Shelf” is inside a prepositional phrase and cannot be the subject.

verb_valley.q:
Choose the verb:
“Yesterday the museum ___ its doors at noon.”
verb_valley.why: Keep the tense in step with the timeline: “yesterday” fixes the action in a finished past, so the simple past is right. “Has opened” reaches into the present, which a finished day does not.

verb_valley.q:
Choose the verb:
“The bakers ___ before dawn every morning.”
verb_valley.why: The subject “bakers” is plural and sits right beside the verb, so the verb is plural. “Arriving” is not a main verb, and “arrives” and “has arrived” are singular.

verb_valley.q:
Choose the verb:
“Since 2010, the town ___ three new schools.”
verb_valley.why: “Since” plus a starting point describes something that began in the past and runs up to now, which takes has/have plus a participle. The simple past “built” needs a finished time, such as “in 2010”.

verb_valley.q:
Choose the verb:
“Mathematics ___ her strongest subject this year.”
verb_valley.why: Some nouns end in s but name a single thing: mathematics, news, physics. “Mathematics” is one subject, so it takes the singular verb.

verb_valley.q:
Choose the verb:
“The number of volunteers ___ grown every year since the flood.”
verb_valley.why: The subject is “the number”, which is singular; “of volunteers” sits between subject and verb, so cross it out. (“A number of volunteers”, meaning several, would take “have”.) “Since the flood” also calls for has/have, which rules out “are” and “were”.

verb_valley.q:
Choose the verb:
“Last night the pond ___ over.”
verb_valley.why: “Last night” fixes the action in a finished past, so the simple past is right, and freeze is irregular: freeze, froze, frozen. “Frozen” is the participle and needs a helper (“had frozen”), and “freezed” is not a word.

verb_valley.q: Which sentence keeps its verbs in the same tense?
opts: We packed the car and drove north.
We pack the car and drove north.
We packed the car and drive north.
We will pack the car and drove north.
verb_valley.why: Two actions in one sequence, joined by “and”, share a tense unless the timeline changes. Only the first keeps both in the past.

verb_valley.q:
Choose the verb:
“Running three miles before breakfast ___ her energy for the whole day.”
verb_valley.why: The subject is the whole activity, “Running three miles before breakfast”, and one activity is singular. “Miles” sits inside that subject phrase, so cross it out just as you would a prepositional phrase: running … gives.

verb_valley.q:
Choose the verb phrase:
“If she ___ the map, she would have found the trail.”
verb_valley.why: An unreal past condition has two halves: the “if” half takes had + participle, and the result half takes would have. Putting “would have” in both halves is a common spoken error.

verb_valley.q:
Choose the verb:
“Mia is one of the players who ___ before every match.”
verb_valley.why: The subject of the who-clause is “who”, and “who” stands for the nearest noun, “players”, which is plural: several players stretch, and Mia is one of them. “One” pulls toward the singular, but it belongs to the main clause (“Mia is one”), not to the who-clause.

transition_tower.q: “The plan was expensive. ___, it worked flawlessly.”
transition_tower.why: Expensive set against worked-well is a contrast, so the transition has to turn.

transition_tower.q: “He trained for months. ___, he was ready.”
transition_tower.why: Training leads to readiness — cause and effect, not contrast.

transition_tower.q: “The mayor’s speech was brief. ___, it lasted under two minutes.”
transition_tower.why: The second sentence sharpens the first rather than turning against it or following from it, so the link must intensify: “In fact”.

transition_tower.q: “It was raining hard. ___, the game continued.”
transition_tower.why: Rain would stop a game; the game continuing is the surprise, so the transition concedes.

transition_tower.q: “Several materials resist corrosion. ___, titanium survives years in seawater.”
transition_tower.why: The second sentence is one instance of the general claim in the first.

transition_tower.q: “The engine is quiet. ___, it uses half the fuel.”
transition_tower.why: Both facts point the same way, and the second adds to the first.

transition_tower.q:
Which is best?
“She checked the figures twice. ___ she submitted the report.”
transition_tower.why: These are two steps in sequence. Nothing is being contrasted or illustrated.

transition_tower.q: “The bridge closed for repairs. ___, traffic was rerouted through the valley.”
transition_tower.why: The rerouting is the result of the closure — a consequence, not a concession.

transition_tower.q: The paragraph already says the experiment failed, then explains why. The best transition before the explanation is:
transition_tower.why: An explanation follows the claim it explains. Three of these announce a turn that does not happen.

transition_tower.q:
Which choice is best?
“The soil was poor. However, moreover, the crop failed.”
transition_tower.why: Poor soil and a failed crop already follow one another. Two transitions contradict each other, and neither is needed.

transition_tower.q: “Wolves hunt in packs. ___, wild dogs work together to bring down prey.”
transition_tower.why: Both sentences describe animals hunting as a group, so the link shows likeness: “Similarly”.

transition_tower.q: “___ the tickets were expensive, the show sold out in an hour.”
transition_tower.why: Selling out is the opposite of what expensive tickets would lead you to expect, so the link must concede: “Although”. A transition can be a single word inside the sentence, not only a word after a period.

transition_tower.q: “The study was double-blind. ___, neither the patients nor the doctors knew who received the drug.”
transition_tower.why: The second sentence restates what “double-blind” means. It is not one case of it, a result of it, or a contrast with it.

transition_tower.q: “Wear the helmet at all times. ___, the insurance will not cover you.”
transition_tower.why: The second sentence says what happens if the first is ignored. That relationship is “otherwise”.

transition_tower.q: “The new policy saved the company money. ___, it drove away several of its best engineers.”
transition_tower.why: The policy caused both effects, which is what makes “Consequently” tempting — but losing engineers does not follow from saving money. A cost is set against a benefit, so the link must turn.

transition_tower.q: “First, sift the flour. Next, beat in the eggs. ___, bake for forty minutes.”
transition_tower.why: The sentences are steps in order, and this is the last one. A sequence word (first, next, then, finally) carries the order; the others signal contrast, example and likeness, and none of those relations is there.

transition_tower.q: “The team did not fly to the final. ___, it took an overnight train.”
transition_tower.why: The second sentence names what the team did in place of flying, and “instead” marks a replacement. “In addition” would add the train to a flight that never happened.

transition_tower.q: “The chef plated the main course. ___, in the dining room, the waiter uncorked the wine.”
transition_tower.why: Read both sentences: the two actions happen at the same time in different rooms. “Meanwhile” marks things happening at once. Nothing is caused, opposed or illustrated.

transition_tower.q: “The museum was free on Sundays. Its galleries, ___, were packed every weekend.”
transition_tower.why: A transition in mid-sentence works like one at the start: match it to how the two sentences relate. Free entry explains the crowds, so the link is cause and effect.

transition_tower.q: “The drug lowered blood pressure in mice. ___, it has not yet been tested in humans.”
transition_tower.why: The second sentence limits the first: good results, but only in mice. That is a contrast, and “however” carries it. “On the contrary” is also a contrast, but too strong: it denies the sentence before it, and nothing here says the drug failed.

transition_tower.q: “The hotel was cheap, clean and close to the beach, and the staff were kind. ___, it was the best week of our summer.”
transition_tower.why: The second sentence sums up the first: a list of good points becomes one verdict. That relationship is summary, and “In short” carries it. Nothing turns against the first sentence, illustrates it, or depends on a condition.

transition_tower.q: “The river rose overnight, ___ the ferry did not run.”
transition_tower.why: The rising river is the cause and the cancelled ferry is the effect, so the link must lead from cause to effect: “so”. “For” also joins a cause and an effect, but backwards: it would mean the river rose because the ferry did not run.

transition_tower.q: “The bridge you cross today opened in 1920. ___, a wooden bridge stood on the same spot.”
transition_tower.why: Read both sentences: the wooden bridge came first, so the second sentence steps back in time. A time word has to point the right way; “After that” would put the wooden bridge after 1920. Nothing is caused or illustrated.

transition_tower.q:
“The trip was costly. Nevertheless, it was worth every penny.”
Which choice would NOT be an acceptable replacement for Nevertheless?
transition_tower.why: Costly set against worth it is a contrast, so any replacement must also turn. “Still”, “Even so” and “All the same” all concede in the same way. “Therefore” announces a result, and being costly is no reason for being worth it.

transition_tower.q: “The festival moved indoors this year. ___, the forecast had called for a week of storms.”
transition_tower.why: The second sentence gives the reason for the first: the storms explain the move. “After all” introduces a justification. “As a result” is the trap: the two ideas are linked by cause, but it points the wrong way, making the forecast a result of the move.

fraction_falls.q: A shirt goes from $40 to $50. The percent increase is:
fraction_falls.why: change / original = 10/40 = 25%. The original is the denominator, always.

fraction_falls.q: What is ⅔ of 90?
fraction_falls.why: “Of” means multiply: (2/3) × 90 = 60.

fraction_falls.q: A price rises 20%, then falls 20%. Against the start it is:
fraction_falls.why: 1.20 × 0.80 = 0.96. The second 20% is taken off a bigger number than the first was added to.

fraction_falls.q: Split 40 in the ratio 5 : 3. The larger part is:
fraction_falls.why: 8 parts in total, so each part is 5 — and the larger share is 5 of them.

fraction_falls.q: A value changes from 80 to 72. That is a:
fraction_falls.why: change / original = 8/80 = 10%.

fraction_falls.q: What is 5% of 60?
1/2 written as a percent is:
fraction_falls.why: A percent is hundredths: 1/2 = 50/100.

fraction_falls.q: Simplify: 3/4 ÷ 2/3
fraction_falls.why: Dividing by a fraction means multiplying by its reciprocal: 3/4 × 3/2.

fraction_falls.q: What is 2/5 + 1/3?
fraction_falls.why: Common denominator 15: 6/15 + 5/15. Never add denominators.

fraction_falls.q: 18 is what percent of 24?
fraction_falls.why: part / whole = 18/24 = 0.75. The number after “of” is the whole.

fraction_falls.q: After a 20% discount, a jacket costs $48. What was the original price?
fraction_falls.why: The sale price is 80% of the original: 0.8p = 48, so p = 60. Adding 20% of $48 back on gives $57.60, because the 20% was taken from the larger original price.

fraction_falls.q: A school trip needs 2 adults for every 15 students. How many adults are needed for 60 students?
fraction_falls.why: Ratios scale together: 60 students is 4 times 15, so multiply the adults by 4 as well: 2 × 4 = 8. The 4 is the multiplier, not the answer.

fraction_falls.q: Which is greatest?
fraction_falls.why: Convert to decimals to compare: 0.667, 0.625, 0.6 and 0.583. A larger denominator alone does not make a fraction larger.

fraction_falls.q: A $50 meal has 8% tax added. What is the total?
fraction_falls.why: Adding 8% means multiplying by 1.08: 50 × 1.08 = 54. The $50.40 treats 8% as 0.8%.

fraction_falls.q: The ratio of boys to girls in a club is 3 : 4. There are 12 girls. How many members are there in total?
fraction_falls.why: Four parts are 12 girls, so one part is 3 and there are 3 × 3 = 9 boys. The total is 9 + 12 = 21; 9 alone answers a different question.

fraction_falls.q: What is ¾ × ⅖?
fraction_falls.why: Multiply straight across: (3 × 2)/(4 × 5) = 6/20 = 3/10. Adding tops and bottoms gives 5/9, which is no fraction operation at all, and 15/8 is what dividing would give.

fraction_falls.q: Write 0.35 as a fraction in lowest terms.
fraction_falls.why: 0.35 is 35 hundredths, 35/100, and dividing top and bottom by 5 gives 7/20. 35/10 is 3.5, ten times too big.

fraction_falls.q: A class has 30 students. Three-fifths of them play a sport, and half of those play soccer. How many students play soccer?
fraction_falls.why: A fraction of a fraction is a product: ½ × ⅗ × 30 = 9. The 18 is the sport players before halving, and 15 is half the whole class.

fraction_falls.q: Which pack has the lowest price per bar?
fraction_falls.why: Compare price ÷ number of bars: $0.75, $0.80, $0.80 and $0.90. The cheapest pack to buy ($2.70) is the dearest per bar.

fraction_falls.q: A jar holds red and blue beads in the ratio 2 : 3. After 10 red beads are added, the ratio becomes 1 : 1. How many blue beads are in the jar?
fraction_falls.why: Ratios scale together, so write the parts with one multiplier: 2k red and 3k blue. Adding 10 red makes them equal, so 2k + 10 = 3k and k = 10. Blue is 3k = 30; 20 is the original red count.

fraction_falls.q: A school has 40 teachers, and 15% of them teach math. How many teachers teach math?
fraction_falls.why: “Of” means multiply: 15% of 40 = 0.15 × 40 = 6. The 15 is the percent, not the number of teachers.

fraction_falls.q: In a survey, 45 of 60 students said they walk to school. What fraction of the students do NOT walk?
fraction_falls.why: The students who do not walk number 60 − 45 = 15, and 15/60 simplifies to 1/4. The trap 3/4 is the share who do walk; the trap 1/3 compares non-walkers to walkers (15/45) instead of to the whole class.

fraction_falls.q: A map scale is 1 cm : 5 km. Two towns are 7.5 cm apart on the map. How far apart are they in real life?
fraction_falls.why: A ratio scales together: multiply both parts by the same number. 1 cm becomes 7.5 cm, so 5 km becomes 5 × 7.5 = 37.5 km. Dividing 7.5 by 5 gives 1.5, which runs the scale backwards.

fraction_falls.q: A store raises a price by 25%. By what percent must it then cut the new price to get back to the original price?
fraction_falls.why: Percent change is always measured against the starting value of that step. Take $100: it rises to $125. To fall back by $25 from $125 is 25/125 = 20%. The cut is smaller because it is taken from a larger starting value.

fraction_falls.q: At a shelter the ratio of cats to dogs is 5 : 3, and there are 16 more cats than dogs. How many cats and dogs are there in all?
fraction_falls.why: Give the parts one multiplier: cats 5k, dogs 3k. The difference is 2k = 16, so k = 8. That makes 40 cats and 24 dogs, 64 in all. The traps stop at one part or double the total.

geometry_grotto.q: A circle has diameter 10. Its area is:
geometry_grotto.why: The radius is half the diameter, so r = 5 and area = πr² = 25π.

geometry_grotto.q: A triangle has base 8 and height 5. Its area is:
geometry_grotto.why: Area = ½bh = ½(8)(5).

geometry_grotto.q: Two angles of a triangle are 90° and 40°. The third is:
geometry_grotto.why: The three angles sum to 180°.

geometry_grotto.q: A circle has radius 2. Its circumference is:
geometry_grotto.why: Circumference = 2πr. Area would be 4π too — read which one is asked.

geometry_grotto.q: A rectangle is 12 by 6. Its perimeter is:
geometry_grotto.why: Perimeter = 2(l + w) = 2(18). The 72 is the area.

geometry_grotto.q: A box is 8 × 3 × 6. Its volume is:
geometry_grotto.why: Volume = l · w · h.

geometry_grotto.q: A cylinder has radius 3 and height 10. Its volume is:
geometry_grotto.why: Volume = πr²h = π(9)(10).

geometry_grotto.q: The interior angles of a regular hexagon each measure:
geometry_grotto.why: Interior angles sum to (n − 2)180° = 720°, shared equally among six.

geometry_grotto.q: Two similar triangles have sides in the ratio 2 : 3. Their areas are in the ratio:
geometry_grotto.why: Area scales with the square of the length ratio. 8 : 27 would be volume.

geometry_grotto.q: A square has area 49. Its perimeter is:
geometry_grotto.why: Each side is √49 = 7, and a square has four of them.

geometry_grotto.q: A trapezoid has parallel sides of 6 and 10 and a height of 4. Its area is:
geometry_grotto.why: Area = ½(b₁ + b₂)h = ½(16)(4) = 32. Forgetting the ½ gives 64.

geometry_grotto.q: Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. One of the interior angles measures 65°. What does the other interior angle on the same side of the transversal measure?
geometry_grotto.why: Same-side interior angles are supplementary: 180° − 65° = 115°. Complementary (25°) would need a right angle, which nothing here supplies.

geometry_grotto.q: The volume of a sphere is V = (4/3)πr³. A sphere of radius 3 has volume:
geometry_grotto.why: r³ = 27, and (4/3)(27) = 36. Stopping at r³ gives 27π; multiplying by 4 without dividing by 3 gives 108π.

geometry_grotto.q: A circle is drawn inside a square of side 4 so that it touches all four sides. What is the area inside the square but outside the circle?
geometry_grotto.why: Square minus circle. The circle’s diameter is the side, 4, so its radius is 2 and its area is 4π. Using 4 as the radius gives 16π, which is larger than the square.

geometry_grotto.q: A circle has radius 6. How long is the arc cut off by a 60° central angle?
geometry_grotto.why: The arc is 60/360 = 1/6 of the circumference, and the circumference is 2π(6) = 12π. One-sixth of 12π is 2π.

geometry_grotto.q: Two straight lines cross. One of the four angles they form measures 70°. What does the angle directly opposite it measure?
geometry_grotto.why: Vertical (opposite) angles are equal. The 110° is each neighbouring angle, which makes a straight line with the 70° angle.

geometry_grotto.q: Two angles together form a straight line. One measures 125°. What does the other measure?
geometry_grotto.why: Angles on a straight line add to 180°, so 180° − 125° = 55°. The 235° uses the 360° of a full turn.

geometry_grotto.q: An isosceles triangle has a vertex angle of 40°. What does each base angle measure?
geometry_grotto.why: The base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal, and all three angles add to 180°. That leaves 140° for the two base angles, 70° each. The 140° stops one step early.

geometry_grotto.q: The interior angles of a polygon add up to 1080°. How many sides does it have?
geometry_grotto.why: Use (n − 2) × 180° = 1080°. Then n − 2 = 6, so n = 8. The 6 is n − 2, which is where students stop.

geometry_grotto.q: The radius of a cylinder is doubled and its height is unchanged. Its volume is multiplied by:
geometry_grotto.why: V = πr²h, and the radius is squared: doubling r multiplies r² by 2² = 4. The 8 would be right only if every length doubled, as with similar solids, and the 2 forgets the square.

geometry_grotto.q: A right triangle has legs of 6 and 8. What is its area?
geometry_grotto.why: In a right triangle the two legs meet at the right angle, so one is the base and the other is the height: ½ × 6 × 8 = 24. Forgetting the ½ gives 48; 10 is the hypotenuse.

geometry_grotto.q: A rectangle has an area of 60 and a length of 12. What is its perimeter?
geometry_grotto.why: Area = length × width, so the width is 60 ÷ 12 = 5. The perimeter adds all four sides: 2(12 + 5) = 34. Adding just one length and one width gives 17.

geometry_grotto.q: An exterior angle of a triangle measures 110°. One of the two interior angles not next to it measures 45°. What does the other one measure?
geometry_grotto.why: An exterior angle equals the sum of the two interior angles that are not beside it, so the missing angle is 110° − 45° = 65°. (Check: the interior angle beside the exterior one is 180° − 110° = 70°, and 45° + 65° + 70° = 180°.) The trap 70° is that neighbouring angle.

geometry_grotto.q: A tank with a rectangular base 50 cm long and 20 cm wide holds water 10 cm deep. Then 3,000 cm³ more water is poured in. How deep is the water now?
geometry_grotto.why: Volume = base area × height, so the added height is the added volume ÷ base area: 3,000 ÷ (50 × 20) = 3 cm. The water was already 10 cm deep, so it is now 13 cm. Answering 3 cm gives only the rise.

geometry_grotto.q: Each side of a square is increased by 50%. By what percent does the area of the square increase?
geometry_grotto.why: The new square is similar to the old one, with sides in the ratio 1.5 : 1, so areas are in the ratio 1.5² = 2.25 : 1. The area grows to 225% of the original, an increase of 125%. The trap 225% is the new area, not the increase.

function_foundry.q: If f(x) = 3x − 2, then f(4) =
function_foundry.why: Substitute 4 for every x: 3(4) − 2.

function_foundry.q: If g(x) = x + 2 and f(x) = x², then f(g(3)) =
function_foundry.why: Work from the inside out: g(3) = 5, then f(5) = 25.

function_foundry.q: The graph of y = (x − 4)² is y = x² shifted:
function_foundry.why: A change inside the parentheses shifts horizontally, and it moves opposite the sign.

function_foundry.q: If f(x) = x² − 1, what is f(−3)?
function_foundry.why: (−3)² is 9, not −9. Square first, then subtract.

function_foundry.q: What is the domain of g(x) = √(x + 3) / (x − 1)?
function_foundry.why: Two rules apply at once. Under the square root, x + 3 ≥ 0, so x ≥ −3. The denominator must not be 0, so x ≠ 1. The domain needs both conditions; each of the middle choices keeps only one.

function_foundry.q: If f(x) = (x − 4)/3, what is f⁻¹(5)?
function_foundry.why: An inverse undoes the function: swap x and y and solve. x = (y − 4)/3 gives y = 3x + 4, so f⁻¹(5) = 19. Check: f(19) = 15/3 = 5. The trap 1/3 is f(5), which runs the function forward.

function_foundry.q: The graph of y = x² + 3 is y = x² shifted:
function_foundry.why: A constant added outside the squaring moves the whole curve vertically, in the direction of the sign.

function_foundry.q: If h(x) = 5, what is h(100)?
function_foundry.why: A constant function ignores its input. Every output is 5.

function_foundry.q: For f(x) = x² − 4x, which x makes f(x) = 0?
function_foundry.why: Factor out x: x(x − 4) = 0, so either factor may be zero.

function_foundry.q: The range of f(x) = x² is:
function_foundry.why: A square is never negative, and zero is reachable at x = 0 — so the boundary is included.

function_foundry.q:
x1234
f(x)581114
Which rule fits every column of the table?
function_foundry.why: Each step in x adds 3 to f(x), so the slope is 3, and 3(1) + 2 = 5 fixes the constant. The other rules fit the first column at most.

function_foundry.q: Which set of ordered pairs is NOT a function?
function_foundry.why: A function gives each input exactly one output. The input 1 goes to both 2 and 5. Repeated outputs, as in the second set, are allowed.

function_foundry.q: If f(x) = 4x − 3 and f(a) = 17, what is a?
function_foundry.why: Here the output is given and the input is wanted: 4a − 3 = 17, so a = 5. Plugging 17 in as the input gives 65.

function_foundry.q: The graph of y = −f(x) is the graph of y = f(x):
function_foundry.why: A minus sign outside the function flips every output, so points above the x-axis land below it. A minus inside, f(−x), is the reflection across the y-axis.

function_foundry.q: f(x) = x² when x < 0, and f(x) = 2x + 1 when x ≥ 0. What is f(−2) + f(2)?
function_foundry.why: Each input chooses its own rule: f(−2) = (−2)² = 4 and f(2) = 2(2) + 1 = 5. Using one rule for both inputs gives 2 or 8.

function_foundry.q:
x0123
g(x)4715
What is g(2)?
function_foundry.why: g(2) means the output when the input is 2: find 2 in the x row and read the g(x) value beneath it. The 7 is g(1), read one column early.

function_foundry.q: A graph represents a function when every vertical line crosses it:
function_foundry.why: A function gives each input one output. A vertical line is a single input, so if it meets the graph twice, that input has two outputs.

function_foundry.q: If f(x) = 2x, what is f(a + 1)?
function_foundry.why: Replace every x with the whole input, a + 1: f(a + 1) = 2(a + 1) = 2a + 2. Doubling only the a gives 2a + 1.

function_foundry.q: For which values of x is g(x) = √(2x − 8) a real number?
function_foundry.why: The domain is every allowed input, and a square root needs a quantity that is not negative: 2x − 8 ≥ 0, so x ≥ 4. x = 4 itself is allowed, because √0 = 0. The 8 comes from setting x − 8 ≥ 0 and forgetting the 2.

function_foundry.q:
x1234
f(x)3142
g(x)2341
What is f(g(2))?
function_foundry.why: Work inside-out: g(2) = 3 from the g row, then f(3) = 4 from the f row. Working in the other order gives g(f(2)) = g(1) = 2, and 1 and 3 are the first lookups, f(2) and g(2), left unfinished.

function_foundry.q: If f(x) = x/2 + 3, what is f(10)?
function_foundry.why: Plug in 10 wherever x appears: 10/2 + 3 = 5 + 3 = 8. The 6.5 comes from adding before dividing, which the expression does not say.

function_foundry.q: The point (2, 9) lies on the graph of y = g(x). What is g(2)?
function_foundry.why: A point on a function’s graph is (input, output). The input 2 gives the output 9, so g(2) = 9.

function_foundry.q: If f(x) = 3x and g(x) = x − 4, what is g(f(5))?
function_foundry.why: Work inside-out: f(5) = 15 first, then g(15) = 15 − 4 = 11. Doing g first gives f(g(5)) = f(1) = 3, the reversed order.

function_foundry.q: The graph of y = |x| is moved 2 units left and 5 units down. What is the equation of the new graph?
function_foundry.why: A number added outside moves the graph up or down, so down 5 is −5 at the end. A change inside the bars moves it sideways and opposite the sign, so left 2 is x + 2.

function_foundry.q: If f(x) = 2x² − 3, what is f(x + 1)?
function_foundry.why: Plug in the whole expression x + 1 for x: 2(x + 1)² − 3 = 2(x² + 2x + 1) − 3 = 2x² + 4x − 1. Adding 1 to the output instead gives 2x² − 2, and squaring as x² + 1 loses the middle term.
