trig_trench.why: sin = opposite / hypotenuse = 6/10, reduced.

trig_trench.q: A right triangle has legs 5 and 12. The hypotenuse is:
trig_trench.why: The 5-12-13 triple: √(25 + 144) = 13. Adding the legs gives 17, which is the trap.

trig_trench.q: 180° equals how many radians?
trig_trench.why: A half turn is π radians. A full turn is 2π.

trig_trench.q: Right triangle: opposite 8, adjacent 15, hypotenuse 17. tan θ =
trig_trench.why: tan = opposite / adjacent. The hypotenuse plays no part.

trig_trench.q: θ is acute and cos θ = 3/5. What is sin θ?
trig_trench.why: Draw the triangle: adjacent 3, hypotenuse 5, so the opposite side is 4 (a 3-4-5 triangle). sin θ = opposite/hypotenuse = 4/5.

trig_trench.q: In a right triangle the two non-right angles must:
trig_trench.why: All three sum to 180°, and the right angle already uses 90° of it.

trig_trench.q: A 30-60-90 triangle has short leg 5. Its hypotenuse is:
trig_trench.why: In a 30-60-90 the hypotenuse is always twice the short leg. 5√3 is the long leg.

trig_trench.q: sin 30° =
trig_trench.why: One of the three values worth memorising. cos 30° is the √3/2 one.

trig_trench.q: A ladder leans at 60° to the ground, reaching 12 m up a wall. Which finds its length L?
trig_trench.why: The 12 m is opposite the 60° angle and L is the hypotenuse, so it is a sine relationship.

trig_trench.q: An angle of 2π/3 radians is how many degrees?
In a right triangle, angle θ has an adjacent side of 10 and cos θ = 0.8. How long is the hypotenuse?
trig_trench.why: cos θ = adjacent/hypotenuse, so 0.8 = 10/h and h = 10 ÷ 0.8 = 12.5. Multiplying instead gives 8, which is shorter than a leg — impossible for a hypotenuse.

trig_trench.q: An isosceles right triangle has legs of length 7. Its hypotenuse is:
trig_trench.why: A 45-45-90 triangle has sides in the ratio 1 : 1 : √2. The √3 belongs to the 30-60-90 triangle.

trig_trench.q: For any angle θ, sin²θ + cos²θ equals:
trig_trench.why: On the unit circle, cos θ and sin θ are the legs of a right triangle with hypotenuse 1, so Pythagoras gives 1.

trig_trench.q: If 90° < θ < 180°, which is true?
trig_trench.why: The angle ends in the second quadrant, upper left. On the unit circle sin is the y-coordinate (positive there) and cos is the x-coordinate (negative there).

trig_trench.q: From a point 30 m from the base of a tower, the angle of elevation to the top is 40°. Which expression gives the tower’s height?
trig_trench.why: The height is opposite the 40° angle and the 30 m is adjacent, so tan 40° = h/30 and h = 30 tan 40°. Sine would need the hypotenuse, which is not given.

trig_trench.q: On the unit circle, the point at 180° is (−1, 0). What is cos 180°?
trig_trench.why: On the unit circle, cos is the x-coordinate and sin is the y-coordinate. The x-coordinate here is −1; the 0 is sin 180°.

trig_trench.q: In right triangle ABC the right angle is at C, and sides a, b and c are opposite angles A, B and C. Which ratio is sin A?
trig_trench.why: Sine is opposite over hypotenuse, measured from the angle asked about. The side opposite A is a, and the hypotenuse, opposite the right angle, is c. b/c is cos A, and a/b is tan A.

trig_trench.q: If sin 25° ≈ 0.42, then cos 65° ≈
trig_trench.why: 25° and 65° are the two acute angles of one right triangle, and the side opposite 25° is the side adjacent to 65°. So sin 25° = cos 65°. The 0.58 treats sine and cosine as adding to 1, which only their squares do.

trig_trench.q: θ is in the second quadrant and sin θ = 5/13. What is cos θ?
trig_trench.why: Use sin²θ + cos²θ = 1: cos²θ = 1 − 25/169 = 144/169, so cos θ = ±12/13. In the second quadrant cosine is negative. The positive value is the trap.

trig_trench.q: A triangle has sides of 8 and 10 with an included angle of 30°. What is its area? (Area = ½ab sin C)
trig_trench.why: ½ × 8 × 10 × sin 30° = 40 × ½ = 20. Using cos 30° instead gives 20√3, and dropping the ½ gives 40.

trig_trench.q: In a right triangle, the side opposite angle θ is 4 and the side adjacent to θ is 7. What is tan θ?
trig_trench.why: TOA: tangent is opposite over adjacent, 4/7. The hypotenuse, √65, belongs in sine and cosine, not tangent.

trig_trench.q: cos 60° =
trig_trench.why: On the unit circle, cos is the x-coordinate, and the point at 60° is (1/2, √3/2). So cos 60° = 1/2; √3/2 is sin 60°.

trig_trench.q: What is 45° in radians?
trig_trench.why: 180° is π radians, so 45° is 45/180 of π, which is π/4.

trig_trench.q: θ is acute and sin θ = 0.6. What is tan θ?
trig_trench.why: sin θ = 0.6 = 3/5, so draw a right triangle with opposite 3 and hypotenuse 5. The triples give adjacent 4, and tan θ = opposite/adjacent = 3/4. The trap 4/3 is adjacent over opposite.

trig_trench.q: tan θ = 1 and 180° < θ < 270°. What is θ?
trig_trench.why: tan θ = 1 when the reference angle is 45°. In the third quadrant, sine and cosine are both negative, so their ratio, tangent, is positive. The third-quadrant angle is 180° + 45° = 225°. The trap 45° is right in value but outside the given range.

probability_peaks.q: A fair six-sided die is rolled. P(rolling a 4) =

probability_peaks.q: A fair six-sided die is rolled. P(an even number) =

probability_peaks.q: Two marbles are drawn without replacement from 4 red and 2 blue. P(both red) =
probability_peaks.why: The second draw sees a changed bag: (4/6) × (3/5) = 2/5.

probability_peaks.q: A spinner has 8 equal sectors, 3 of them green. P(not green) =
probability_peaks.why: The complement: 1 − 3/8.

probability_peaks.q: How many different outfits from 4 shirts and 3 trousers?
probability_peaks.why: Independent choices multiply, they do not add.

probability_peaks.why: Thirteen hearts in fifty-two cards.

probability_peaks.q: P(A) = 0.3 and P(B) = 0.5, and the two cannot both happen. P(A or B) =
probability_peaks.why: For mutually exclusive events, OR adds. Nothing is double-counted because there is no overlap.

probability_peaks.q: A card is drawn from a standard 52-card deck. What is the probability it is a king or a heart?
probability_peaks.why: There are 4 kings and 13 hearts, but the king of hearts is in both groups: 4 + 13 − 1 = 16, and 16/52 = 4/13. Adding without subtracting the overlap gives 17/52.

probability_peaks.q: A game pays $10 with probability 0.2 and nothing otherwise. What is the expected payout per play?
probability_peaks.why: Expected value = payout × probability, summed over outcomes: 10(0.2) + 0(0.8) = 2.

probability_peaks.q: In how many ways can first, second and third place be awarded among 5 runners?
probability_peaks.why: Order matters: 5 choices for first, then 4, then 3, so 5 × 4 × 3 = 60. The 10 counts groups of three without order; 125 lets one runner win twice.

probability_peaks.q: A dart lands at a random point on a 10 by 10 board. A red rectangle on the board measures 2 by 5. What is the probability the dart lands on red?
probability_peaks.why: With a random point, probability is a ratio of areas: 10/100 = 1/10.

probability_peaks.q: Which of these can NOT be the probability of an event?
probability_peaks.why: A probability is a share of all outcomes, so it runs from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain). Nothing can happen more often than every time.

probability_peaks.q: A spinner landed on blue 12 times in 40 spins. Based on these results, what is the probability of landing on blue?
probability_peaks.why: Favourable over total: 12/40 = 3/10. Putting 12 over the 28 non-blue spins compares blue with not-blue instead of with every spin.

probability_peaks.q: Three fair coins are flipped. What is the probability of getting exactly two heads?
probability_peaks.why: There are 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 equally likely outcomes, and exactly two heads happens in three of them: HHT, HTH and THH. The 1/4 is the chance of two heads with two coins, and 2/3 treats two heads out of three coins as a probability.

probability_peaks.q: How many different two-person teams can be chosen from 5 people?
probability_peaks.why: There are 5 × 4 = 20 ordered picks, but Ana-and-Ben is the same team as Ben-and-Ana, so divide by the 2 orderings. The 20 counts every team twice.

probability_peaks.q: A player makes 70% of her free throws, and each shot is independent. What is the probability that she misses both of her next two shots?
probability_peaks.why: Find the chance of one miss first, 1 − 0.7 = 0.3, then multiply for two independent misses: 0.3 × 0.3 = 0.09. Adding the misses gives 0.6, and 0.49 is the chance she makes both.

probability_peaks.q: A bag holds 5 green, 3 yellow and 2 white counters. One is drawn at random. What is the probability that it is yellow?
probability_peaks.why: Favorable over total: 3 yellow out of 5 + 3 + 2 = 10 counters, so 3/10. The trap 3/7 compares yellow with the other counters instead of with all of them.

probability_peaks.q: A code is one letter (A, B or C) followed by one digit (0 to 9). How many different codes are possible?
probability_peaks.why: Each of the 3 letters can go with each of the 10 digits, so multiply: 3 × 10 = 30. Adding the choices, 3 + 10 = 13, counts the letters and digits but not the pairings.

probability_peaks.q: You roll a pair of fair dice. What is the chance that the two numbers add up to 7?
probability_peaks.why: There are 6 × 6 = 36 equally likely outcomes. Six of them total 7: (1,6), (2,5), (3,4), (4,3), (5,2), (6,1). So 6/36 = 1/6. The 1/11 treats the 11 possible totals as equally likely, which they are not.

probability_peaks.q: A fair coin is flipped and a fair six-sided die is rolled. What is the probability of getting heads and a number greater than 4?
probability_peaks.why: The two events are independent, so multiply: P(heads) = 1/2 and P(5 or 6) = 2/6 = 1/3, giving 1/2 × 1/3 = 1/6. The 1/3 is the die alone; 1/12 counts only one number above 4.

main_idea_meadow.q:
“Cities were long treated as ecological deserts. Recent surveys have found otherwise: an inner-city churchyard in Berlin holds more bee species than the farmland around it, and abandoned rail sidings across Europe shelter plants now rare in the countryside. The reason is not that cities are kind, but that they are untidy — and untidiness, it turns out, is habitat.”
The main idea of the passage is that:
opts: cities support more wildlife than expected, because they are unmanaged
Berlin churchyards hold more bee species than any other urban habitat
farmland has become hostile to insects because it is so heavily managed
rail sidings should be protected by law because they shelter rare plants
main_idea_meadow.why: The examples all serve one claim, stated in the last sentence. Two of the wrong choices are single details lifted out of the passage.

main_idea_meadow.q:
“The first mechanical clocks did not tell the time. They rang it. Housed in monastery towers, they existed to strike the hours of prayer, and their faces — when they had faces at all — were an afterthought. Only when clocks moved into markets and counting-houses did the dial become the point.”
The passage is primarily concerned with:
opts: how the purpose of early clocks differed from ours
the religious life of medieval monasteries
main_idea_meadow.why: Every sentence contrasts what clocks were for then with what they are for now. The monastery is setting, not subject.

main_idea_meadow.q:
“Translators used to be judged on fidelity to the words. The better test, I think, is fidelity to the effect. A joke that is rendered exactly and lands flat has been mistranslated, whatever the dictionary says.”
The author’s main point is that:
opts: a translation should reproduce a text’s effect rather than its wording
jokes are the hardest kind of writing to carry into another language
dictionaries cannot be trusted to give the meaning of a word in context
older translators were careless about the words of the original text
main_idea_meadow.why: The third sentence is an example supporting the claim in the second. The first sentence is the view being argued against.

main_idea_meadow.q:
“My grandmother kept her accounts in a hardback notebook, one line per day, in a hand that never varied. I have the notebooks still. They record no feeling of any kind — only flour, coal, thread, and the price of each. And yet you can see the year my grandfather fell ill in the widening gaps between entries.”
The passage is mainly about:
opts: how a plain record can reveal what it does not say
how prices of flour and coal changed over one family’s lifetime
the author’s grief at her grandfather’s long illness
why the grandmother’s handwriting never changed over the years
main_idea_meadow.why: The turn comes at “And yet”. The notebooks matter because of what shows through them, not for their contents.

main_idea_meadow.q:
“Every few years someone announces that the essay is dying. The form has been declared dead on the arrival of the newspaper, the radio, the television and the internet, and has outlived each announcement. What actually happens is that the essay moves house.”
The main idea is that the essay:
opts: keeps surviving by adapting to new media
is genuinely in decline at last
is superior to radio and television
main_idea_meadow.why: The last sentence supplies the author’s own answer to the claim reported in the first.

main_idea_meadow.q:
“Coral bleaching is often described as a die-off, but a bleached reef is not yet a dead one. The coral has expelled the algae it lives with, and in cooler water it can take them back. Whether it does depends almost entirely on how long the heat lasts.”
The passage is primarily concerned with:
opts: correcting a common misunderstanding about bleaching
arguing that reefs are not endangered
describing methods of measuring sea temperature
main_idea_meadow.why: It opens by naming a wrong belief and spends the rest of its length qualifying it. It never claims reefs are safe.

main_idea_meadow.q:
“The standard history credits three engineers with the tunnel. The payroll ledgers name eleven hundred people. Most of them appear once, spelled differently each time, and then not again.”
The main idea is that:
opts: the accepted account leaves out most of the people who built the tunnel
the payroll ledgers were kept too carelessly to be trusted as a record
the three engineers did not deserve the credit the history gives them
eleven hundred workers lost their lives during the tunnel’s construction
main_idea_meadow.why: The contrast between three and eleven hundred carries the point. The passage never says the engineers deserved nothing.

main_idea_meadow.q:
“Birdsong is partly learned: a chick raised in silence sings a thin, disordered version of its species’ song. Raised among the wrong species, it learns the wrong song. The template is inherited; the performance is taught.”
The best statement of the main idea is:
opts: song depends on both inheritance and learning
birds cannot sing without hearing other birds
chicks raised in silence never sing
song is entirely a matter of upbringing
main_idea_meadow.why: The final sentence splits the credit between the two. The other three each overstate one half.

main_idea_meadow.q:
“A map is a claim about what matters. The road atlas in my car shows no rivers under fifty metres wide and no hill under a hundred metres high, which is to say it has decided, on my behalf, what a landscape is.”
The passage is mainly about:
opts: how maps encode the priorities of their makers
why road atlases are less accurate than other maps
the author’s frustration with driving through hills
how rivers and hills are measured for printed maps
main_idea_meadow.why: The opening sentence states the claim and the rest of the passage is the single example that supports it.

main_idea_meadow.q:
“Sourdough is not a recipe but a relationship. The starter is a population of yeasts and bacteria that shifts with the flour you feed it, the water you use and the temperature of your kitchen; two bakers following identical instructions will not make the same loaf, and after a month they will not have the same starter either.”
The main idea is that sourdough baking:
opts: depends on living conditions that cannot be standardised
is more difficult than other kinds of home baking
succeeds only when the instructions are followed precisely
tastes best when the kitchen is kept warm and steady
main_idea_meadow.why: The metaphor in the first sentence is cashed out by the second. Nothing here ranks sourdough against other baking.

main_idea_meadow.q:
“Night-shift nurses sleep less than their day colleagues, but the bigger problem is when they sleep. Sleep taken in daylight is shallower and broken more often, even when it lasts as long. Blackout curtains help; so, in one hospital trial, did moving handovers an hour earlier, so that nurses were home before full sunrise.”
Which title best fits the passage?
main_idea_meadow.why: The passage says timing matters more than length and ends with two fixes for daytime sleep. “Never sleep” overstates; the curtains are one detail.

main_idea_meadow.q:
“[1] Libraries once measured success in books lent. [2] Loans have fallen in most branches for a decade. [3] Yet visits have risen, because people come for rooms, computers and help with forms. [4] A library, it turns out, is less a warehouse than a public living room.”
Which sentence states the main idea?
main_idea_meadow.why: Sentences 1–3 build a case, and “it turns out” in Sentence 4 draws the conclusion they support. Sentence 3 is the evidence, not the point.

main_idea_meadow.q:
“The ferry leaves at six, whether or not you are on it. The ticket clerk opens at a quarter to, the café at twenty past, and for fifteen minutes the whole harbour is a queue of people holding coins and looking at the sea.”
The author’s main purpose is to:
opts: capture the routine of an early morning at the harbour
warn travellers about the ferry’s strict timetable
complain about the café’s late opening hours
explain how ferry tickets are priced and sold
main_idea_meadow.why: The details build a picture of one recurring scene. Nothing is argued, warned against or explained.

main_idea_meadow.q:
“For years the town tried to stop the river flooding by building its banks higher. Each wall pushed the water faster downstream, and the next village flooded instead. The new plan does the opposite: it buys the low fields upstream and lets them flood, so the river spreads out and slows before it reaches any houses.”
Which choice best summarises the passage?
opts: The town has turned from holding floodwater back to giving it room upstream.
Higher walls have at last stopped the floods that troubled the town for years.
The village downstream is responsible for the flooding in the town itself.
Farmers who own the fields upstream have refused to sell their land to the town.
main_idea_meadow.why: A summary covers the old approach, why it failed, and its replacement. The second choice reverses the passage; the last two invent claims.

main_idea_meadow.q:
“It is true that the old harbour crane no longer lifts anything; the port closed in 1987. But visitors who come to photograph it learn, from the plaque at its base, how the town earned its living for a century, and the crane has become the one object everyone in town can point to as theirs.”
The main idea is that the crane:
opts: still matters to the town, though it no longer works
should be repaired so that it can lift cargo again
stopped working, which caused the port to close
mainly attracts visitors who come to read its plaque
main_idea_meadow.why: “It is true that … But” sets up a concession and then the real claim. The first sentence is granted, not argued, so a choice built on it misses the point.

main_idea_meadow.q:
“Octopuses are escape artists. Aquarium keepers report them unscrewing jar lids, squeezing through gaps the width of a coin, and climbing out of their tanks at night to raid the tanks next door.”
The main idea of the passage is that octopuses:
opts: are kept badly in most aquariums
can unscrew the lids of jars
main_idea_meadow.why: The first sentence states the point, and every detail after it is an example of escaping. Unscrewing lids is one of those examples, too narrow to be the main idea.

main_idea_meadow.q:
“The bicycle changed more than transport. In the 1890s it gave young women a way to travel alone, loosened the rules about what they could wear, and widened the circle of people a person might meet and marry.”
Which statement best summarises the passage?
opts: The bicycle had social effects beyond getting people around.
Young women in the 1890s were the first to ride bicycles.
Clothing rules in the 1890s were stricter than they are now.
The bicycle was the fastest form of transport in the 1890s.
main_idea_meadow.why: The opening sentence is the thesis (the bicycle changed more than transport), and the rest lists those wider changes. The other choices either shrink to one detail or claim something the passage never says.

main_idea_meadow.q:
“Public benches are vanishing from city centres. Some are removed to discourage loitering; others are never replaced when they break. The result is a city that is harder to rest in, and hardest of all for the old and the ill.”
The main point of the passage is that:
opts: losing benches hurts people who most need to rest
benches are removed mainly to stop loitering
old people should avoid busy city centres
broken benches cost too much to replace
main_idea_meadow.why: The passage names the trend in its first line and its cost in its last: fewer benches, and the old and ill suffer most. Loitering is one cause, a detail; the other two choices are never claimed.

main_idea_meadow.q:
“A beaver dam slows a stream. Behind it a pond spreads; silt settles; willows root along the edges; frogs and ducks arrive. Take the dam away, and within a few years most of that is gone.”
The passage is mainly about how:
opts: a beaver dam creates a habitat that needs it
beavers build dams to slow down streams
ponds attract frogs and ducks to a valley
willows need slow water to take root
main_idea_meadow.why: No single sentence states the point; it is assembled from the shape of the whole. The dam builds a community, and removing the dam unmakes it. Each of the other choices is one link in that chain.

main_idea_meadow.q:
“It is tempting to blame the smartphone for the decline of the personal letter. But the decline began with the telephone, which by 1950 had already halved the number of personal letters sent. The smartphone finished a job that had been under way for decades.”
The main idea is that:
opts: the letter was declining long before smartphones
the smartphone is what killed the personal letter
telephones were in most homes by 1950
letters are more personal than phone calls
main_idea_meadow.why: The passage opens with the tempting view only to correct it. “But” introduces the real point: the decline started with the telephone. The second choice is the view the author sets aside.

main_idea_meadow.q:
“Hedgehogs are in steep decline in Britain, and gardens may be part of the answer. A hedgehog travels up to two kilometres a night looking for food, but fences block its way. Residents who cut a small hole at the base of a fence can link a whole street into one hunting ground.”
Which statement best expresses the main idea?
opts: Small gaps in garden fences can help hedgehogs find food.
Hedgehogs travel up to two kilometres every night.
British gardens are too small to support wildlife.
Fences should be banned in residential streets.
main_idea_meadow.why: The opening line sets up the point (gardens may help) and the last line gives it (a gap links a street). The two kilometres is one supporting detail, too narrow, and nothing suggests banning fences.

main_idea_meadow.q:
“Libraries lend more than books now. Branches in our county lend fishing rods, sewing machines, telescopes and even cake tins, and the telescope waiting list runs to three months. For many families, the library has become the place to try a hobby before paying for it.”
The passage is mostly about:
opts: libraries lending objects that let people try hobbies
the long waiting list for library telescopes
libraries no longer lending any books
hobbies becoming too costly for most families
main_idea_meadow.why: The first and last sentences carry the point: libraries now lend things, and people use them to try hobbies. The telescope list is one example, and the passage never says books have stopped.

main_idea_meadow.q:
“It is true that the concrete harbour wall is ugly, and visitors complain about it every summer. But the wall has kept the town dry through three storm surges since it was built, and a stone replacement would cost twice as much for less protection.”
The author mainly argues that:
opts: the wall should stay despite its looks
a stone wall would look much better
storm surges are growing more common
main_idea_meadow.why: A passage that opens “It is true that … But” puts its real point after the “But”: the wall works and should stay. That visitors dislike it is true, but it is the point being conceded, not the argument.

main_idea_meadow.q:
“When the town clock stopped in 1962, nobody fixed it; the council had other priorities. Over the years people began giving directions by it (‘turn left at the stopped clock’) and meeting under it. When a firm offered to repair it free in 2004, residents voted against. A broken clock had become a landmark.”
The passage is chiefly about:
opts: how a broken clock became a valued landmark
why the council would not pay to fix the clock
how people in the town give directions
a firm’s offer to repair old clocks for free
main_idea_meadow.why: The closing sentence states the point, and every earlier sentence builds toward it. The council, the directions and the repair offer are each one step in that story, so each alone is too narrow.

main_idea_meadow.q:
“Most accounts of the Wright brothers dwell on the first flight at Kitty Hawk. That flight lasted twelve seconds. What made the brothers’ name was the two years that followed, in a cow pasture outside Dayton, where they flew again and again, crashed, rebuilt, and learned to turn. Kitty Hawk proved flight was possible; the pasture made it practical.”
The main idea is that the Wright brothers’ achievement:
opts: owed more to their later practice than to the first flight
began and ended with twelve seconds at Kitty Hawk
was nearly ruined by their many crashes
is best remembered through the Kitty Hawk flight
main_idea_meadow.why: The passage opens with the usual account only to turn away from it (“What made the brothers’ name was …”), and the last line sums up the turn. Choices about Kitty Hawk repeat the view the author is correcting, and the crashes are one detail of the practice years.

detail_desert.q:
“The survey ran for six weeks in the spring of 1974. Of the two hundred nests examined, forty-one held eggs that never hatched; of those, the team attributed twenty-nine to cold and the rest to predation.”
According to the passage, how many unhatched clutches were attributed to predation?
detail_desert.why: 41 unhatched, 29 from cold, so “the rest” is 12. The passage makes you do one subtraction rather than handing you the number.

detail_desert.q:
“Ferns reproduce by spore, not by seed, and a single frond may release millions. Almost none survive. The spore must land on ground that is damp, shaded and already free of competitors — three conditions that rarely coincide.”
The passage states that a spore needs ground that is:
detail_desert.why: Go back and read the list. Two of the wrong choices change exactly one item, which is how detail traps are built.

detail_desert.q:
“Ada Lovelace’s notes on the Analytical Engine run to about three times the length of the paper she was translating. It is in the notes, not the paper, that she describes a machine operating on symbols rather than numbers.”
According to the passage, the description of a symbol-processing machine appears in:
detail_desert.why: The second sentence names the location explicitly, and sets it against the obvious wrong answer in the same breath.

detail_desert.q:
“The lighthouse was automated in 1982. The last keeper, Mairead Quinn, had served eleven years; her predecessor served thirty-four, and the one before him died in post after nine.”
How long did the keeper before Quinn’s predecessor serve?
detail_desert.why: Three keepers are named in reverse order. Reading the chain carefully is the whole task.

detail_desert.q:
“Roman concrete used volcanic ash from the Bay of Naples. Modern analysis shows that seawater reacts with this ash to grow a rare mineral inside the cracks, so that harbour walls two thousand years old are stronger now than when they were poured.”
According to the passage, the mineral forms as a result of:
opts: the weight of the harbour walls
detail_desert.why: The passage gives one cause. The other three are the kind of plausible mechanism a reader supplies from memory.

detail_desert.q:
“Between 1911 and 1913 the museum acquired eleven paintings, of which it had authenticated only four at the time of purchase. Three of the remaining seven were later shown to be copies.”
How many of the eleven paintings remained neither authenticated at purchase nor shown to be copies?
detail_desert.why: 11 − 4 authenticated = 7; 7 − 3 copies = 4. Detail questions on the ACT often hide one subtraction.

detail_desert.q:
“Monarch butterflies do not complete the migration in one lifetime. The generation that leaves Mexico in spring dies in Texas; it is the third or fourth generation that reaches Canada, and a single long-lived autumn generation that flies the whole way back.”
According to the passage, which generation makes the entire southward journey?
detail_desert.why: The last clause answers it. The trap is that several generations are named going north.

detail_desert.q:
“The glacier has retreated 2.4 kilometres since the first survey in 1894. Two-thirds of that loss has occurred since 1980.”
Approximately how far did the glacier retreat between 1894 and 1980?
detail_desert.why: Two-thirds came after 1980, so one-third — about 0.8 km — came before it.

detail_desert.q:
“Tea reached Britain through Portuguese and Dutch traders decades before the East India Company took an interest. Samuel Pepys records drinking it in 1660; the Company did not ship its first direct cargo until 1669.”
According to the passage, Pepys drank tea:
opts: nine years before the Company’s first direct cargo
in the same year as the Company’s first cargo
after the Company began direct trade
detail_desert.why: 1669 − 1660 = 9. The claim that he drank it before tea reached Britain contradicts the passage outright.

detail_desert.q:
“The report lists three causes of the failure and ranks them. Poor drainage is first; the sequence of the concrete pours is second; the choice of aggregate, which the press seized on, is third and least significant.”
The passage indicates that the aggregate was:
opts: the least significant of the three causes
the most significant of the three causes
a cause the report ruled out entirely
the second-ranked of the three causes
detail_desert.why: The passage ranks it explicitly, and flags that the press got the emphasis wrong.

detail_desert.q:
“The mill’s first owners chose the site for three reasons: the river fell sharply there, the road to the market town had just been paved, and a quarry across the valley supplied cheap stone.”
The passage mentions all of the following as reasons for the choice EXCEPT:
opts: a steep fall in the river
detail_desert.why: On an EXCEPT question, check each choice off against the text. Three are in the list; workers are never mentioned, however sensible a reason they would be.

detail_desert.q:
“Most of the island’s birds nest on the cliffs; only the petrels, which feed at night, dig burrows in the turf above.”
According to the passage, the petrels nest:
opts: on the cliffs with the other birds
detail_desert.why: The sentence answers it directly. “At night” describes when petrels feed, not where or when they nest.

detail_desert.q:
“The engineer thought the crack was cosmetic. The inspector, who had seen the same pattern on the older bridge, disagreed, and it was the inspector who ordered the closure.”
According to the passage, who ordered the bridge closed?
opts: the owner of the older bridge
the engineer and the inspector together
detail_desert.why: The last clause names the inspector outright. The engineer thought the crack was harmless, so would have had no reason to close anything.

detail_desert.q:
“The seeds were soaked overnight, then chilled for a month. Only after the chilling were they sown; weeks later, the seedlings that had come up were thinned to one per pot.”
According to the passage, which step came immediately before sowing?
detail_desert.why: Put the steps in order: soak, chill, sow, thin. “Only after the chilling were they sown” places chilling directly before sowing.

detail_desert.q:
“The old telescope gathered light with a mirror 1.5 metres across. Its replacement has a 4-metre mirror and, being newer, a far more sensitive camera.”
According to the passage, the replacement differs from the old telescope in:
opts: mirror size, but not camera sensitivity
camera sensitivity, but not mirror size
neither mirror size nor camera sensitivity
detail_desert.why: The passage names two differences, joined by “and”. Choices that keep only one of them drop half the sentence.

detail_desert.q:
“The town’s first public library opened in 1887, in two rooms above the fire station. It moved into its own building in 1912.”
According to the passage, the library was first housed:
detail_desert.why: The passage says it directly: “in two rooms above the fire station.” The library got its own building only in 1912, and “next to” swaps one word of the text.

detail_desert.q:
“Emperor penguins breed in the depths of the Antarctic winter. The male holds the single egg on his feet for about two months while the female returns to the sea to feed.”
According to the passage, how long does the male hold the egg?
detail_desert.why: Go back to the text: “for about two months.” “The whole winter” stretches what the passage says, and the other figures are not in it at all.

detail_desert.q:
“The bridge is repainted every seven years. The work takes a crew of twelve about fourteen months, and the paint, a grey-green chosen in 1936, has never changed.”
According to the passage, the colour of the paint:
opts: was chosen by the painting crew
detail_desert.why: The last clause answers it: chosen in 1936 and “has never changed”. The wrong choices reuse real numbers from the passage (seven years, fourteen months) attached to the wrong claim.

detail_desert.q:
“Before the canal, barley from the valley reached the coast by cart, a trip of four days. Barges made it in two, and at a sixth of the cost.”
The passage indicates that, compared with carts, barges were:
opts: twice as fast and far cheaper
twice as fast but more costly
four times as fast and cheaper
detail_desert.why: Four days by cart against two by barge is twice as fast, and a sixth of the cost is far cheaper. The stem paraphrases, so translate the numbers back into the passage’s terms before choosing.

detail_desert.q:
“The mill employed forty people in 1850. … By 1870, when a second mill opened across the river, the original mill employed fewer than half its 1850 workforce.”
According to the passage, in 1870 the original mill employed:
detail_desert.why: Two statements must be read together: the 1850 workforce was forty, and in 1870 it was fewer than half that, so fewer than twenty. “Exactly twenty” is half, not fewer than half.

detail_desert.q:
“The ferry leaves the north pier at 7:15 each morning and returns at 6:40 in the evening, except on Sundays, when it makes a single round trip at noon.”
According to the passage, on Sundays the ferry:
opts: makes one round trip at noon
detail_desert.why: Go back to the words after “except on Sundays”: a single round trip at noon. The 7:15 and 6:40 times are the weekday schedule that Sunday is an exception to.

detail_desert.q:
“Of the 40 seedlings planted in March, 12 died in a late frost. Half of the survivors were then eaten by deer, and the rest were moved to the greenhouse.”
According to the passage, how many seedlings were moved to the greenhouse?
detail_desert.why: Reread each step in order: 40 − 12 = 28 survived the frost, half of those (14) were eaten, and the rest, 14, were moved. The 28 stops a step early, and 20 takes half of the original 40.

detail_desert.q:
“The first lighthouse on the point burned whale oil and could be seen for eight miles. Its replacement, built in 1871, burned kerosene and reached fourteen miles. The electric lamp installed in 1932 is visible for twenty-two miles, though the tower itself has not changed since 1871.”
According to the passage, what changed in 1932?
opts: the lamp, but not the tower
both the tower and the lamp
the tower, but not the lamp
the fuel, from oil to kerosene
detail_desert.why: Reread the last sentence: a new electric lamp came in 1932, “though the tower itself has not changed since 1871”. The switch to kerosene belongs to 1871, a near-miss that swaps one date for the other.

detail_desert.q:
“Maria was born two years after the family arrived in Halifax. Her brother Tomas, the eldest, was nine when they arrived; her sister Ana was born the year before Maria.”
How old was Tomas when Ana was born?
detail_desert.why: Put each detail on one timeline. Maria was born two years after arrival, and Ana a year before Maria, so Ana was born one year after arrival. Tomas was nine at arrival, so ten. The 11 is his age when Maria was born.

detail_desert.q:
“The survey counted 120 nests. Two-thirds were in the reed beds, and a quarter of those failed. Every nest outside the reed beds succeeded.”
According to the passage, how many nests succeeded in all?
detail_desert.why: Work through the passage one clause at a time. Reed beds: 2/3 of 120 = 80, of which a quarter (20) failed, leaving 60. Outside: 40, all successful. Total 60 + 40 = 100. The 60 forgets the last sentence, and 90 takes a quarter of all 120.

inference_icefield.q:
“She set down the letter and stared out of the window for a long time.”
It can reasonably be inferred that:
inference_icefield.why: Take the smallest supported step. The other three invent facts the sentence does not carry.

inference_icefield.q:
“The café had been there forty years. The new sign was in a typeface the owner’s daughter had chosen, and the prices had gone up by a third, and the regulars still came, but earlier, and they did not stay.”
It can be inferred that the regulars:
opts: could no longer afford the café
had moved out of the area
inference_icefield.why: They still come, so they can afford it and have not moved. The change in how they come is the evidence.

inference_icefield.q:
“Every reference in the bibliography predates 1961, though the book was published in 1974.”
This most strongly suggests that:
opts: the author did not engage with recent work
the bibliography is incomplete by accident
inference_icefield.why: The gap is the point. Saying the book was written in 1961 goes further than the evidence allows.

inference_icefield.q:
“He wrote to his brother twice a week for eleven years. The letters from the last year are shorter, and in three of them he asks a question he had asked the month before.”
It can reasonably be inferred that in the last year he was:
opts: losing his memory or his grip on the correspondence
no longer interested in his brother’s replies
inference_icefield.why: Repeating a question he recently asked is the specific evidence. Anger and disinterest would not produce that detail.

inference_icefield.q:
“The recipe calls for the dough to rest overnight. My mother never let it. She said the waiting was for people with cold kitchens.”
It can be inferred that the mother believed:
opts: her kitchen was warm enough to make the rest unnecessary
the recipe was wrong about almost every step it described
resting the dough overnight would spoil its final texture
she was a more skilled cook than the author of the recipe
inference_icefield.why: Her reason names the condition the rest is for, and implies her kitchen does not meet it.

inference_icefield.q:
“The company’s annual report devotes eleven pages to its environmental programme and one paragraph to the closure of its two largest plants.”
The proportions most strongly suggest that the report is:
opts: shaped more by presentation than by significance
a complete and balanced account of the company’s year
primarily an environmental document, not a business one
legally required to say little about plant closures
inference_icefield.why: The mismatch between space and importance is the inference. Nothing supports a legal claim.

inference_icefield.q:
“When the interviewer asked about the second trial, the researcher said the data were still being cleaned, and moved on to the third.”
It can reasonably be inferred that the researcher:
opts: preferred not to discuss the second trial
had not conducted a second trial
inference_icefield.why: Answering and immediately changing subject is the evidence. Whether the data really were unclean is beside the point.

inference_icefield.q:
“The island’s only bookshop orders four copies of each new novel. It has never ordered a fifth.”
It can be inferred that:
opts: demand on the island is small and predictable
the island has few readers of any kind
four is the publisher’s minimum order
inference_icefield.why: Consistency across many titles implies the owner knows the market. “Few readers of any kind” overreaches — this is one shop and one genre.

inference_icefield.q:
“He kept the receipts for everything he bought that year, and the following January he wrote out a list of what he wished he had not.”
It can be inferred that he:
opts: was reviewing his own spending habits
had been asked to account for the money
inference_icefield.why: The list is made for himself, after the fact. Returning goods and being audited both require someone else in the picture.

inference_icefield.q:
“The tide table is printed on the wall of the harbour office, and beside it, in a different hand, someone has written: “Add twenty minutes in the channel.””
The added note most strongly suggests that:
opts: the printed table is not quite accurate for local conditions
the printed table was written for a different harbour entirely
the channel is too dangerous to navigate at any state of the tide
the harbour office is poorly run and rarely updates its notices
inference_icefield.why: A local correction implies a local discrepancy. That is a narrower claim than the table being wrong everywhere.

inference_icefield.q:
“Tomas checked the oven twice before he left, then turned back at the corner and checked it again.”
It can reasonably be inferred that Tomas:
opts: was worried he had left the oven on
inference_icefield.why: Checking the same thing three times is the evidence, and it points to worry about the oven. Nothing mentions keys, work or a purchase.

inference_icefield.q:
“The school bought forty tablets in September. By March, the library log showed that thirty-one of them had never been signed out.”
The log most strongly suggests that:
opts: most of the tablets were not being used
most of the tablets had been stolen
students preferred paper books to devices
the library log had been kept carelessly
inference_icefield.why: Thirty-one of forty never leaving the library is the smallest step: they went unused. Theft and preference each need facts the passage does not give.

inference_icefield.q:
“The council has, once again, discovered the problem it was warned about in 2015.”
It can be inferred that the author believes the council:
inference_icefield.why: “Once again” and “discovered” a problem it “was warned about” imply the warning went unheeded. The problem is plainly not new.

inference_icefield.q:
“Boats were inspected for two things only: a working radio and enough life jackets. The Kestrel carried a life jacket for every crew member, yet it failed inspection.”
It can be inferred that the Kestrel:
inference_icefield.why: Two statements combine: only two things were checked, and the life jackets passed. The only thing left to fail is the radio.

inference_icefield.q:
“‘Lovely weather,’ said Mr Adair, shaking the water from his umbrella.”
It can reasonably be inferred that Mr Adair:
opts: is being ironic about the rain
inference_icefield.why: His words and his dripping umbrella point opposite ways. When speech contradicts the scene, the speaker usually means the reverse.

inference_icefield.q:
“Priya put on her coat, then saw the sun come out, took the coat off again and hung it back on its hook.”
It can reasonably be inferred that Priya:
opts: judged it warm enough to go without it
could not find the coat she wanted
changed her mind about going out
disliked the colour of her coat
inference_icefield.why: Take the smallest step past the text: she takes the coat off right after seeing the sun, so the weather changed her mind about the coat. Nothing says she stayed in, and nothing mentions colour.

inference_icefield.q:
“The shelves were empty except for a handwritten sign: ‘More bread tomorrow at seven.’”
It can reasonably be inferred that:
opts: the bread had sold out for the day
the shop was closing down for good
the baker had fallen ill that week
bread is only sold at the weekend
inference_icefield.why: Empty shelves plus a promise of more tomorrow support one small step: today’s bread is gone. “Closing for good” contradicts the sign, and the other two are guesses nothing on the page forces.

inference_icefield.q:
“Every seat in the hall was taken, and people stood two deep along the back wall.”
The sentence most strongly suggests that:
opts: the event drew a large crowd
the hall had been poorly designed
inference_icefield.why: Full seats and a standing crowd support one modest conclusion: many people came. Why they came, fame perhaps, could be true, but nothing on the page supports it.

inference_icefield.q:
“Ivan kept glancing at the clock, and when the bell finally rang he was the first one out of the door.”
It can reasonably be inferred that Ivan:
opts: was eager for the class to end
was late for a different class
inference_icefield.why: Watching the clock and leaving first both point to wanting the lesson over, which is the smallest leap. “Disliked his teacher intensely” goes too far, and the other two have no support.

inference_icefield.q:
“The recipe book belonged to my aunt. Its pages are clean except for one, which is stained, splashed and soft at the corners from turning.”
It can be inferred that the aunt:
opts: made that one recipe far more than any other
rarely cooked anything from the book at all
spilled water on the book on one occasion
disliked most of the recipes in the book
inference_icefield.why: Two details combine: one page is worn from use (“soft at the corners from turning”), and the rest are clean. Together they point to one recipe used again and again. A single spill would not wear the corners soft.

inference_icefield.q:
“Leila checked the bus timetable twice, then ran the last two blocks to the stop, her bag bouncing against her hip.”
It can reasonably be inferred that Leila:
opts: was worried about missing the bus
had never taken this bus before
inference_icefield.why: Take the smallest leap: checking the time twice and then running points to worry about catching the bus. Nothing says where she was going, so “late for school” reaches beyond the page.

inference_icefield.q:
“The sign on the gallery door read: ‘Closed Mondays. Late opening Thursdays until nine.’ Joon arrived on a Monday evening at eight and turned back.”
It can reasonably be inferred that Joon turned back because:
opts: the gallery was closed that day
he arrived an hour too early
inference_icefield.why: Point to the line that forces it: the sign says “Closed Mondays”, and Joon came on a Monday. The late opening is for Thursdays, so the times do not matter here.

inference_icefield.q:
“The museum has only two public entrances, the east door and the west door. On Monday the west door was shut all day for repairs.”
It can reasonably be inferred that Monday’s visitors:
opts: came in through the east door
did not visit the museum at all
came through the west door after repairs
inference_icefield.why: Combine the two statements: there are only two public entrances, and one was shut all day, so visitors used the other. The staff entrance and a reopening are never mentioned.

inference_icefield.q:
“Leaves on the north side of the hedge were still green; those on the south side, which faces the road, had turned brown and curled. The council had salted the road all winter.”
It can reasonably be inferred that:
opts: salt from the road may have harmed the south side of the hedge
the north side of the hedge gets more sunlight
the council plans to replace the whole hedge
road salt is the only thing that turns leaves brown
inference_icefield.why: The two facts sit side by side for a reason: the damaged side faces the salted road. The modest “may have harmed” is the smallest leap. “The only thing” is an extreme that the passage cannot support.

inference_icefield.q:
“The inspector passed every truck that carried a valid permit. Truck 7 was turned back at the border, though its driver insisted his paperwork was in order.”
It can reasonably be inferred that:
opts: the driver of Truck 7 was lying
inference_icefield.why: Every truck with a valid permit was passed, and Truck 7 was not passed, so it cannot have had a valid permit. The driver’s protest pulls toward “the inspector made a mistake”, but that contradicts the first sentence. The driver may simply have been wrong rather than lying, and cargo is never mentioned.

viewpoint_vista.q:
Writer A: Rewilding works because it stops managing. Left alone, the land finds an arrangement more robust than any we design.
Writer B: There is no “alone” left. The soils are altered, the herbivores are gone, and doing nothing simply hands the ground to whatever arrived last.
Both writers would agree that:
opts: human activity has already changed the land
viewpoint_vista.why: A implies past management; B states past alteration outright. The other three are exactly what they disagree about.

viewpoint_vista.q:
Writer A: Standardised tests are the only instrument that treats every applicant identically.
Writer B: Identical treatment is not fair treatment when preparation is purchasable.
Their disagreement is best described as:
opts: whether applicants differ from one another
viewpoint_vista.why: B does not dispute A’s fact; she disputes what it is worth. Locating the hinge is the whole skill.

viewpoint_vista.q:
Writer A: The city should widen the ring road; congestion costs the region millions in lost hours.
Writer B: Every widening in this city’s history has filled within four years.
Writer B responds to Writer A by:
opts: citing evidence that the proposed remedy does not last
denying that congestion costs the region anything at all
proposing that a different road be widened instead
questioning the accuracy of Writer A’s cost figures
viewpoint_vista.why: B never argues with the cost of congestion — only with whether widening fixes it.

viewpoint_vista.q:
Writer A: Museums should return contested objects without waiting for perfect provenance.
Writer B: Return the wrong object to the wrong claimant and you have committed a second theft.
Writer B’s main concern is:
opts: the risk of acting on incomplete information
whether the objects were stolen at all
viewpoint_vista.why: B accepts that theft occurred — that is what “a second theft” concedes — and worries only about error.

viewpoint_vista.q:
Writer A: Remote work has made teams more productive and people happier.
Writer B: It has made experienced people more productive and new hires invisible.
Writer B’s position is best described as:
viewpoint_vista.why: B grants part of A’s claim and restricts it to a group. That is qualification, not contradiction.

viewpoint_vista.q:
Writer A: Any language with fewer than a thousand speakers will be gone within two generations.
Writer B: Hebrew had no native speakers at all and now has nine million.
Writer B’s use of Hebrew serves to:
opts: offer a counterexample to a general rule
change the subject to ancient languages
question the count of a thousand speakers
viewpoint_vista.why: One case that breaks the rule is the classic way to answer a universal claim.

viewpoint_vista.q:
Writer A: The painting is certainly by the master; the underdrawing matches his workshop practice.
Writer B: The underdrawing matches the practice of his workshop — which employed thirty people.
Writer B’s reply works by:
opts: showing the evidence supports a weaker conclusion
disputing that the underdrawing matches the workshop
introducing a rival painter as the true author of it
attacking Writer A’s expertise in reading underdrawings
viewpoint_vista.why: B accepts the evidence exactly as given and shows it cannot carry the weight A puts on it.

viewpoint_vista.q:
Writer A: Nuclear power is the only low-carbon source that runs regardless of weather.
Writer B: It is also the only one that takes fifteen years to build.
The two writers differ mainly in:
opts: which drawback or advantage they treat as decisive
their estimates of how much carbon each source emits
whether nuclear power counts as a low-carbon source
whether the weather affects any other energy sources
viewpoint_vista.why: Neither contradicts the other’s fact. They disagree about which fact should settle the question.

viewpoint_vista.q:
Writer A: Children should learn to write by hand before they type; the motor memory aids recognition.
Writer B: The studies showing that effect all predate touchscreens.
Writer B objects on the grounds that:
opts: the evidence may not apply to current conditions
motor memory plays no real part in learning letters
typing has been shown to be faster than handwriting
the studies were poorly designed from the very start
viewpoint_vista.why: B raises the age of the evidence, not its quality or its conclusion.

viewpoint_vista.q:
Writer A: Subtitles let a film keep its own language.
Writer B: Subtitles let a film keep its own language while the audience looks at the bottom of the frame instead of the actor’s face.
Writer B’s sentence is best described as:
opts: conceding Writer A’s point and naming its cost
restating Writer A’s point in other words
viewpoint_vista.why: B repeats A’s clause word for word and then adds to it. The repetition is the concession.

viewpoint_vista.q:
Writer A: Schools should start later; teenagers’ body clocks run late for biological reasons.
Writer B: Start later and students will simply stay up later. The clock will shift again.
Writer A would most likely respond to Writer B by arguing that:
opts: the late body clock is biological, not a habit that shifts
students should be required to go to bed earlier
a later start would make school days shorter
Writer B has exaggerated how tired students are
viewpoint_vista.why: B treats the late clock as a habit that will adjust. A’s own claim is that it is biological, so A would answer on exactly that point.

viewpoint_vista.q:
Writer A: Zoos should exist only to breed endangered species.
Writer B: Zoos should exist to teach the public about animals.
Both writers would most likely reject the idea that zoos exist mainly to:
viewpoint_vista.why: Each writer gives zoos a serious purpose, and neither is entertainment. The second and third choices are each one writer’s own view.

viewpoint_vista.q:
Writer A: The new stadium will transform the neighbourhood!
Writer B: It may bring visitors. It may also bring traffic. We will see.
Compared with Writer A, Writer B is more:
viewpoint_vista.why: “May … may … we will see” holds judgement back. B is not hostile — the visitors are granted as a possibility.

viewpoint_vista.q:
Writer A: A four-day week must cut output; there are fewer hours to work.
Writer B: Output depends on focus, not hours.
Which finding would most support Writer B?
opts: Firms that moved to four days kept the same weekly output.
Workers on four-day weeks said they felt happier at work.
Output fell at the firms that moved to a four-day week.
Some firms already offer three-day weeks to part-time staff.
viewpoint_vista.why: The dispute is about output. Output holding steady with fewer hours is what B predicts and A says cannot happen. Happiness is beside the point.

viewpoint_vista.q:
Writer A: Ban cars from the old town to protect its buildings.
Writer B: Charge cars to enter, and spend the money on repairs.
Both proposals take for granted that:
opts: cars are damaging the old buildings
a ban is fairer than a charge
repairs cost more than the town has
residents want to keep their cars
viewpoint_vista.why: A ban to protect the buildings and a charge to pay for repairs both start from the same premise: the cars do harm. They differ only on the remedy.

viewpoint_vista.q:
Writer A: Homework in primary school does little for learning.
Writer B: Primary homework builds habits that pay off in later years.
The writers disagree about:
opts: how much homework older pupils need
whether the school day is too long
viewpoint_vista.why: Map each writer first: A says primary homework does little, and B says it builds useful habits. Both are about the value of homework for young children; the other topics are never raised.

viewpoint_vista.q:
Writer A: Parks should close at dusk; empty parks at night are unsafe.
Writer B: Lit parks stay busy after dark, and busy parks are safe.
Both writers are chiefly concerned with:
viewpoint_vista.why: They disagree about the remedy, closing or lighting, but both argue from the same concern: whether parks are safe after dark. Cost is never mentioned.

viewpoint_vista.q:
Writer A: Restore the old library; the town will never build anything so fine again.
Writer B: Knock it down. Restoring it would cost twice as much as a new building.
Which writer is more concerned with cost?
viewpoint_vista.why: Keep the voices separate: only Writer B mentions money (“twice as much”). Writer A argues from beauty and history.

viewpoint_vista.q:
Writer A: Electric scooters clutter the pavements and should be banned.
Writer B: They clutter the pavements only because the city gives them nowhere to park.
Writer B would agree with Writer A that:
opts: scooters should be banned from the city
the city has built enough scooter parking
pavements in the city are too narrow
viewpoint_vista.why: B accepts A’s observation (“they clutter the pavements”) and disputes only the cause and the cure. So they agree about the clutter, not about the ban.

viewpoint_vista.q:
Writer A: Tourism is ruining the island: the beaches are crowded and rents have doubled.
Writer B: Before the tourists came, half the island’s young people left to find work.
Writer B would most likely respond to Writer A by arguing that:
opts: tourism’s costs must be weighed against the jobs it brings
the beaches are not really as crowded as Writer A claims
rents on the island have in fact fallen in recent years
young people would prefer to leave the island anyway
viewpoint_vista.why: B does not dispute A’s facts; B points to what tourism replaced, an island its young people had to leave. That is an argument for weighing costs against benefits, not a denial of the crowds or the rents.

viewpoint_vista.q:
Writer A: A four-day school week saves money and gives families a long weekend together.
Writer B: A four-day week leaves working parents paying for childcare on the fifth day.
Writer B’s main worry about the four-day week is:
opts: the length of the school day
viewpoint_vista.why: Map Writer B in a phrase: childcare costs for parents on the day off. Family time and savings are Writer A’s points, so keep the voices separate.

viewpoint_vista.q:
Writer A: Street murals brighten the city and should be encouraged.
Writer B: Murals painted without permission are vandalism, however skilled.
Writer B objects only to murals that are:
viewpoint_vista.why: Writer B’s complaint has a condition built in: “without permission”. The words “however skilled” show that skill is not the issue, so B’s objection is to permission alone.

viewpoint_vista.q:
Writer A: Electric scooters cut out short car trips and should be allowed on every street.
Writer B: Scooters left lying on pavements trip up blind and elderly walkers. Allow them, but only with proper parking bays.
Writer B’s view is best summed up as:
opts: support for scooters, on a condition
a call to ban cars from streets
viewpoint_vista.why: Writer B opens with a harm, which pulls toward “opposition”, but the second sentence says “Allow them”. Read to the end of each voice before labelling it. The support comes with a condition: parking bays.

viewpoint_vista.q:
Writer A: The river should be dredged; silt is what floods the town.
Writer B: Dredging will help for a year or two. But the forest upstream was cleared, and until it is replanted the silt will keep coming.
Which new evidence would most strengthen Writer B’s argument?
opts: Silt levels jumped after the forest was cleared.
The river was last dredged about thirty years ago.
Flooding in the town has cost millions in repairs.
Dredging machinery has become cheaper to hire.
viewpoint_vista.why: Writer B’s distinctive claim is that the cleared forest is the source of the silt. Evidence linking the silt to the clearing favours B. The flood costs and the cheaper dredging concern the problem or Writer A’s remedy, not B’s cause.

viewpoint_vista.q:
Writer A: Exams should be scrapped; they measure only how well pupils sit exams.
Writer B: Scrap the exams and you are left with teachers’ impressions, which favour the confident and the well-spoken.
Both writers appear to assume that:
opts: exams should stay as they are
viewpoint_vista.why: They disagree about exams, but each objects to a method because it is unfair: A says exams reward exam technique, and B says impressions reward confidence. Fairness is the shared ground. “Exams should stay” is B’s implied side only, and “always biased” goes beyond what B says.

graph_gorge.q: Where two curves on the same axes intersect, the two quantities are:
graph_gorge.why: An intersection is the one place the two y-values agree.

graph_gorge.q: A curve rises steeply, levels off, and stays flat. The flat portion shows that the quantity:
graph_gorge.why: A flat line means no change, not no quantity. Height and slope are different readings.

graph_gorge.q: On a graph of distance against time, a straight line means the speed is:
graph_gorge.why: Slope is speed here, and a straight line has one slope throughout.

graph_gorge.q: A scatterplot shows points scattered with no pattern from lower-left to upper-right or otherwise. This indicates:
opts: little or no relationship between the variables
a strong positive relationship between the variables
a strong negative relationship between the variables
an error in how the measurements were taken
graph_gorge.why: Absence of a trend is a finding. It is not, by itself, evidence that anything went wrong.

graph_gorge.q: A graph’s y-axis runs from 98 to 102. A curve that looks dramatic on this axis:
opts: may represent a very small real change
must represent a large real change
graph_gorge.why: Always read the axis range before judging a shape. A truncated axis magnifies everything.

graph_gorge.q: Two curves both rise, but curve P is always above curve Q. This shows that:
opts: P is greater than Q at every x shown
P rises faster than Q at every x shown
P and Q must intersect somewhere off the graph
Q will eventually rise above P
graph_gorge.why: Being above is about value; rising faster is about slope. Only the first is visible here.

graph_gorge.q: A quantity is plotted on a logarithmic y-axis. Equal vertical distances on that axis represent:
graph_gorge.why: On a log scale a fixed vertical step means multiplying by the same factor (one decade is ×10), not adding the same amount.

graph_gorge.q: Extending a graph’s trend beyond the plotted data to predict a value is:
opts: extrapolation, and less reliable than reading within the data
interpolation, and just as reliable as reading within the data
always invalid, because no graph may be read beyond its axes
the most reliable way to use a graph, since it uses the trend

graph_gorge.q: Two bars on a chart have error bars that overlap widely. The safest conclusion is that:
opts: the difference between them may not be real
the taller bar is definitely the larger value
the measurements were carried out incorrectly
the two values are known to be exactly equal

graph_gorge.q: A graph shows air temperature (y-axis) against altitude in km (x-axis). To find the temperature at 2 km, you should:
opts: find 2 km on the x-axis and read the y-value of the curve there
find 2 on the y-axis and read across to the curve and down
read the value where the curve crosses the y-axis at the left
find the highest point of the curve and read its y-value off
graph_gorge.why: Start on the axis of the quantity you know (altitude, on x), go up to the curve, then across to the axis you want. Starting on the y-axis answers a different question.

graph_gorge.q: On a graph, the y-axis is labelled “Mass (kg)”. A point sits at 2.5 on that axis. The mass it shows is:
graph_gorge.why: The axis label carries the unit: every number on that axis is in kilograms. Read the label before the number.

graph_gorge.q: On a distance–time graph, an object is moving fastest where the line is:
graph_gorge.why: Steepness is rate: the steeper the line, the more distance covered per unit of time. The highest point is only the farthest distance, not the fastest speed.

graph_gorge.q: A bar chart shows the number of birds counted each month. The tallest bar is above July. This means that:
opts: July had the highest count of the year
July was the warmest month of the year
birds were counted only in July
the count rose every month until July

graph_gorge.q: A graph shows temperature on the y-axis against time on the x-axis. The line slopes down from left to right. The temperature is:
graph_gorge.why: Read the axes first. Moving right means later in time, and the line going down means the temperature is lower. So the temperature falls as time passes.

graph_gorge.q: A graph’s x-axis is marked 0, 1, 2, 5 and 10 at equal spacing. A line on this graph looks perfectly straight. The line:

experiment_expanse.q: The variable the researchers deliberately change is the:
experiment_expanse.why: Independent = what is changed on purpose. Dependent = what you then measure.

experiment_expanse.q: The purpose of a control group is to:
opts: give a baseline with no treatment
test a second variable at once
experiment_expanse.why: Without a baseline there is nothing for the treated group to be different from.

experiment_expanse.q: If two variables change between trials, you:
opts: cannot tell which one caused the result
get a stronger and more reliable result
have a better control for the experiment
have shown that both variables matter
experiment_expanse.why: Changing one thing at a time is what makes a cause attributable.

experiment_expanse.q:
Students measured plant growth under three light colours, using the same soil, pot size and watering schedule throughout.
Soil, pot size and watering schedule are:
experiment_expanse.why: They are deliberately held constant so that light colour is the only thing that differs.

experiment_expanse.q:
A trial is repeated five times and the results averaged.
The main reason for repeating is to:
opts: reduce the effect of random variation
experiment_expanse.why: Repetition addresses noise. It cannot fix a design that measures the wrong thing.

experiment_expanse.q:
Experiment 1 heated the sample in air. Experiment 2 repeated it in nitrogen.
The purpose of Experiment 2 was most likely to test whether:
opts: oxygen was involved in the result
experiment_expanse.why: Swapping air for nitrogen removes oxygen and holds nearly everything else. The changed variable names the question.

experiment_expanse.q: A study finds that towns with more libraries have lower unemployment. The strongest objection is that:
opts: a third factor, such as town wealth, may explain both
libraries cannot possibly affect whether people find work
the sample of towns studied was far too large to be useful
unemployment is too hard to define for a fair comparison
experiment_expanse.why: Correlation invites a confounder. Naming a plausible one is the standard move.

experiment_expanse.q:
The thermometer used in all trials read 2 °C high.
This is best described as:
opts: a systematic error affecting every trial the same way
a random error that varies from one trial to the next
a controlled variable held constant across the trials
a reason to discard every result from the experiment
experiment_expanse.why: A constant offset shifts every reading equally, so comparisons between trials survive it.

experiment_expanse.q:
Group A received the drug; Group B received an identical-looking pill with no active ingredient.
Group B is:
experiment_expanse.why: Matching everything except the active ingredient is what makes the comparison clean.

experiment_expanse.q: A result is reported from a single trial on one sample. The most reasonable response is to:
opts: treat it as preliminary until it is repeated
accept it as established, since it was measured
reject it outright, since one trial proves nothing
assume the researcher made an error somewhere
experiment_expanse.why: One trial is a start, not a conclusion — and doubting a result is not the same as disproving it.

experiment_expanse.q:
Students dropped a ball from several different heights and measured how high it bounced each time.
The dependent variable is:
experiment_expanse.why: The dependent variable is what is measured in response. The students chose the drop height; the bounce is what they recorded.

experiment_expanse.q: A student wants to test whether water temperature affects how fast sugar dissolves. Which setup is best?
opts: Equal sugar and water in each cup; only the water temperature differs
Different amounts of sugar in cups of water at the same temperature
Sugar cubes in the hot water and granulated sugar in the cold
One cup of hot water, stirred once and timed a single time
experiment_expanse.why: Only the variable under test should change. The second choice changes the wrong variable, the third changes two at once, and the fourth has nothing to compare against.

experiment_expanse.q: A student times one swing of a pendulum with a stopwatch, then instead times 20 swings and divides by 20. The main benefit is that:
opts: her reaction-time error is spread over 20 swings
the pendulum swings faster when timed longer
the independent variable changes each time
a control group is no longer necessary
experiment_expanse.why: Starting and stopping the watch adds roughly the same error however long the timing lasts. Divided by 20, that error shrinks to a twentieth per swing.

accept the result for all soil types

experiment_expanse.q: A gardener gives fertiliser to the plants in a sunny bed and none to the plants in a shady bed. The fertilised plants grow taller. Why does this not show that the fertiliser worked?
opts: sunlight differs between the groups as well as fertiliser

the plants in the shady bed should have been given water
fertiliser is known to make most plants grow more slowly
experiment_expanse.why: A fair test changes one variable. Here sunlight and fertiliser both differ, so either could explain the extra growth; the two are confounded. More beds would not fix that.

experiment_expanse.q: A lab tests water samples for lead. Its blank, distilled water that should contain no lead, reads 4 parts per billion. What does this mean?
opts: the test itself is contaminated, so every result is in doubt
the distilled water is the most polluted sample tested
the blank can be ignored, since it is not a real sample
lead must be naturally present in all pure water
experiment_expanse.why: A blank is a control with none of the thing being measured. If it reads above zero, the lead is coming from the equipment or reagents, and every sample reading carries that same error.

experiment_expanse.q: A student tests whether the colour of a ball affects how high it bounces. What is the independent variable?
opts: the height it is dropped from
experiment_expanse.why: The independent variable is what the student changes on purpose: the ball’s colour. The bounce height is what is measured (the dependent variable), and the drop height and floor should be held constant.

experiment_expanse.q: A student measures plants with a ruler whose scale starts 1 cm from its end, so every reading is 1 cm too long. This error:
opts: adds 1 cm to every height but leaves differences correct
is random and cancels out when readings are averaged
makes tall plants look shorter than short plants do
