experiment_expanse.why: The error is systematic: the same 1 cm is added every time. Repeating or averaging cannot remove an error that is always the same, but because every plant is off by the same amount, the difference between two plants is still right.

experiment_expanse.q: Researchers testing a new pain pill give a second group an identical-looking sugar pill. Why?
opts: to cancel out the effect of just taking a pill
to save money on the real medicine
to make the sugar group feel worse on purpose
to test whether sugar relieves pain
experiment_expanse.why: This is a control group. People can feel better simply because they took a pill, so the sugar pill (a placebo) gives a baseline with everything the same except the drug. Any extra effect in the drug group is then due to the drug.

experiment_expanse.q: A class measured how fast yeast made gas at 20 °C, 30 °C and 40 °C, using a new batch of yeast for each temperature. The 40 °C trial was fastest. What is the main weakness of this design?
opts: The yeast batch changed with the temperature.
Only three different temperatures were tested.
Gas production is hard to measure.
experiment_expanse.why: Two variables changed between trials: temperature and the batch of yeast. The faster rate at 40 °C might come from a livelier batch. Only one variable should change, so every trial should use yeast from the same batch.

conflict_canyon.q:
Scientist 1: The crater formed by meteorite impact; the quartz at the rim is shocked.
Scientist 2: It is volcanic. Shocked quartz also forms in explosive eruptions.
The two scientists disagree about:
conflict_canyon.why: They agree the quartz is there. They disagree about what it proves — which is where the questions will live.

conflict_canyon.q:
Scientist 1: The decline is caused by the new pesticide.
Scientist 2: The decline began four years before the pesticide was licensed.
Scientist 2’s point works by:
opts: showing the proposed cause came after the effect
denying that any decline in numbers occurred
proposing that a different pesticide is to blame
questioning the method used to measure the decline
conflict_canyon.why: A cause cannot follow its effect. That is the cleanest way to break a causal claim.

conflict_canyon.q:
Scientist 1: Birds navigate by the stars.
Scientist 2: They navigate by the earth’s magnetic field.
Which finding would support Scientist 2 over Scientist 1?
opts: Birds in a windowless room still orient correctly until a magnet is switched on
Birds fly mainly at night, when the stars are the brightest guide available
Birds released under heavy cloud become disoriented and scatter in all directions
Young birds navigate less accurately than adults on their first migration
conflict_canyon.why: It removes the stars and manipulates the magnetic field — testing exactly the difference between the two views.

conflict_canyon.q:
Scientist 1: The mass extinction was rapid, over a few thousand years.
Scientist 2: It took at least half a million years.
Both would most likely agree that:
opts: the timescale can be measured precisely
conflict_canyon.why: The shared ground is whatever neither disputes. They differ only on duration.

conflict_canyon.q:
Student 1: The metal expanded because it was heated.
Student 2: It expanded because it absorbed moisture.
Which result would weaken Student 2?
opts: The same expansion occurs in a sealed dry chamber
The metal expands more on humid days than on dry ones
Heating the sample also increases its measured mass
The metal contracts again when it is cooled and dried
conflict_canyon.why: Removing moisture entirely and still seeing the effect leaves Student 2 with nothing to explain it.

conflict_canyon.q:
Scientist 1: The lake’s algae bloom is driven by farm runoff.
Scientist 2: It is driven by warmer water.
New evidence that blooms occur in cold years after heavy fertiliser use would:
conflict_canyon.why: Cold years remove Scientist 2’s proposed driver while the blooms continue.

conflict_canyon.q:
Scientist 1: Dinosaurs were warm-blooded; their bone growth rings resemble those of mammals.
Scientist 2: Some modern reptiles kept warm by their environment show the same rings.
Scientist 2 is arguing that Scientist 1’s evidence is:
opts: consistent with more than one explanation
measured incorrectly in the original study
irrelevant to the question of dinosaurs
fabricated to support the warm-blooded view
conflict_canyon.why: The evidence stands; what is challenged is its uniqueness as a signal.

conflict_canyon.q:
Scientist 1: Language ability is mostly innate.
Scientist 2: It is mostly learned from exposure.
A finding that children exposed to almost no speech still form grammatical rules would:
conflict_canyon.why: Rules appearing without input is precisely what an innate account predicts and a learning account does not.

conflict_canyon.q:
Scientist 1: The sediment layer was laid down by a flood.
Scientist 2: It was laid down by wind.
Which observation best distinguishes the two?
opts: Whether the grains are rounded and well sorted by size
Whether the layer is thicker than the layers around it
Whether the layer is grey or brown in colour throughout
Whether any fossils are present anywhere in the layer
conflict_canyon.why: Wind sorts grains far more strictly than water does, so grain sorting is the discriminating observation.

conflict_canyon.q: When a conflicting-viewpoints passage gives two theories, a question asking what both scientists accept is answered by:
opts: the facts neither of them disputes
the first sentence of each theory
conflict_canyon.why: Shared ground sits in what both take for granted, not in either conclusion.

conflict_canyon.q:
Scientist 1: Moths fly to lamps because they steer by keeping a light at a fixed angle.
Scientist 2: Moths fly to lamps because warmth attracts them.
Which scientist would predict that moths gather around a cold LED as readily as around a hot bulb of the same brightness?
conflict_canyon.why: Scientist 1’s explanation depends only on light, so equal brightness means equal attraction. Scientist 2 would expect the cold LED to draw fewer moths.

conflict_canyon.q:
Scientist 1: The lake formed when a glacier gouged out the basin.
Scientist 2: The lake formed when a landslide dammed a river.
Which observation is consistent with both views?
opts: The lake is more than ten thousand years old.
Glacial scratches line the rock of the basin.
A buried river channel runs under the debris.
The basin is U-shaped and its outlet is clear.
conflict_canyon.why: Neither scientist commits to an age, so the age fits both. Each of the others is evidence for one mechanism in particular.

conflict_canyon.q:
Scientist 1: The fossil footprints were made by one animal walking at a steady pace, because the prints are evenly spaced.
Scientist 1’s reasoning assumes that:
opts: an animal walking steadily leaves evenly spaced prints
the footprints are older than the rock around them
several animals of one species made the prints
the animal that made the prints was running
conflict_canyon.why: The argument runs from even spacing to steady walking, which only works if steady walking produces even spacing. That unstated link is the assumption.

conflict_canyon.q:
Scientist 1: Yawning cools the brain.
Scientist 2: Yawning is social; it spreads by imitation.
Which observation would Scientist 2 predict but Scientist 1 would not?
opts: people yawn more soon after seeing someone else yawn
people yawn more in warm rooms than in cool ones
a yawn is followed by a small drop in brain temperature
people who are alone never yawn at any time
conflict_canyon.why: Contagion follows from imitation and not from cooling. The next two fit Scientist 1; the last overstates Scientist 2, who never says yawning needs company.

conflict_canyon.q:
Scientist 1: The bridge cracked because of heavy trucks.
Scientist 2: It cracked because of repeated freezing and thawing.
An identical crack appears on a footbridge in the same cold valley that no truck has ever crossed. This observation:
conflict_canyon.why: The crack appears where trucks are absent but the cold is present. That favours Scientist 2; one case supports a view without proving it.

conflict_canyon.q:
Scientist 1: A comet’s tail streams out behind it, like smoke from a moving train.
Scientist 2: The solar wind pushes the tail, so it always points away from the Sun.
Which observation would best support Scientist 2?
opts: the tail points away from the Sun
the tail always trails behind the comet
the tail grows longer far from the Sun
the tail is made mostly of ice and dust
conflict_canyon.why: Find the prediction only one model makes. Scientist 2 predicts a tail pointing away from the Sun even when that means leading the comet; a trailing tail is Scientist 1’s prediction.

conflict_canyon.q:
Scientist 1: The cave paintings are 30,000 years old; charcoal in them has been dated.
Scientist 2: The charcoal may have come from old wood. Their style suggests they are no more than 20,000 years old.
According to Scientist 2, the paintings are:
conflict_canyon.why: Keep each viewpoint separate. The 30,000 figure is Scientist 1’s; Scientist 2 doubts it and gives an upper limit of 20,000 years.

conflict_canyon.q:
Scientist 1: The range is still rising as the two plates collide.
Scientist 2: The range stopped rising millions of years ago; erosion is now wearing it down.
Which scientist would predict that the mountains are not getting taller?
conflict_canyon.why: Scientist 1 says the range is still rising. Scientist 2 says it stopped rising and is being worn down, so only Scientist 2 predicts no growth.

conflict_canyon.q:
Student 1: Heavier objects fall faster than lighter ones.
Student 2: Without air, all objects fall at the same rate.
A feather and a hammer dropped together in a vacuum land at the same moment. This result supports:
conflict_canyon.why: Match the result to each claim. Landing together in a vacuum is exactly Student 2’s prediction, and it contradicts Student 1’s.

conflict_canyon.q:
Scientist 1: Dogs were first domesticated in Asia about 15,000 years ago.
Scientist 2: Dogs were domesticated earlier, in Europe: a dog-like skull from Belgium is 30,000 years old.
Which reply would best defend Scientist 1 against Scientist 2’s evidence?
opts: It may come from a wolf line that left no living descendants.
Skulls this old cannot be dated with any real accuracy.
Dogs and wolves have entirely different skull shapes.
Belgium is too far from Asia for dogs to have spread.
conflict_canyon.why: Scientist 1 must explain the skull without giving up the claim. If it belonged to an early wolf line that died out, it can be old and dog-like without being an ancestor of today’s dogs. Denying all dating would sink Scientist 1’s own 15,000-year date too.

conflict_canyon.q:
Scientist 1: The fish in the lake died because a factory upstream released warm water.
Scientist 2: The fish died because an algae bloom used up the oxygen in the water.
Both scientists accept that:
opts: the fish in the lake died
the water’s oxygen level was normal
conflict_canyon.why: Summarise each view: warm water versus an algae bloom. They disagree on the cause but agree it happened. The factory and the algae each belong to one scientist only.

conflict_canyon.q:
Scientist 1: Dinosaur X walked on two legs; its front limbs were too short to bear its weight.
Scientist 2: Dinosaur X walked on four legs; fossil trackways show four prints in each set.
What evidence does Scientist 2 rely on?
opts: the length of the front limbs
conflict_canyon.why: One line per scientist: Scientist 2 cites trackways with four prints. The front limbs are Scientist 1’s evidence, and neither mentions the skull or teeth.

conflict_canyon.q:
Scientist 1: Island lizards have longer legs than mainland lizards because, over many generations, long legs helped their ancestors run on the island’s broad tree trunks.
Scientist 2: The longer legs are not inherited. Each lizard grows them during its life by running on broad trunks.
Which result would favour Scientist 2?
opts: Island-born lizards raised on the mainland grow short legs.
Island lizards have had long legs for many generations.
Long-legged lizards outrun short-legged ones on trunks.
Mainland lizards mostly climb thin, narrow branches.
conflict_canyon.why: Ask what each view predicts. If legs are inherited (Scientist 1), island-born lizards keep long legs wherever they grow up. If legs grow with use (Scientist 2), those raised on the mainland should grow short ones. That result tells the views apart. Faster running on trunks fits both views.

conflict_canyon.q:
Scientist 1: The amino acids in the meteorite formed in space, before it fell to Earth.
Scientist 2: They are contamination: soil bacteria got into the rock after it landed.
Which finding would most weaken Scientist 2?
opts: The core holds as many amino acids as the surface.
The meteorite landed in a damp, grassy field.
Amino acids are found in all living things.
The meteorite was found a week after it fell.
conflict_canyon.why: Contamination from soil enters from the outside, so Scientist 2 predicts more amino acids near the surface than at the core. An even spread cuts against that. The damp field and the week’s delay make contamination more likely, so they help Scientist 2.

conflict_canyon.q:
Scientist 1: Many songbirds migrate at night because the air is cooler and they lose less water.
Scientist 2: They migrate at night so they can steer by the stars.
Which observation would count against Scientist 2 but not against Scientist 1?
opts: Night migrants fly the right way even under thick cloud.
Birds lose less water when they fly in cool air.
Night migrants fly lower on warm nights than cold ones.
Birds under a planetarium sky follow its fake stars.
conflict_canyon.why: Look for an observation one view needs to be false. If birds steer correctly with the stars hidden, stars are not needed to steer, which hurts Scientist 2. Scientist 1’s water-saving reason is untouched. The planetarium result supports Scientist 2, and the water-loss fact supports Scientist 1, so neither counts against Scientist 2 alone.

outside_outpost.q: A solution with pH 3 is:
outside_outpost.why: Below 7 is acidic, above 7 is basic, 7 is neutral.

outside_outpost.q: Photosynthesis takes in carbon dioxide and light and releases:
outside_outpost.why: Plants release O₂ as a by-product.

outside_outpost.q: Pure water at sea level boils at:
outside_outpost.why: 100 °C — the 212 is the same temperature in Fahrenheit, which is the trap.

outside_outpost.q: In an atom, the particle with no charge is the:
outside_outpost.why: Protons are positive, electrons negative, neutrons neutral.

outside_outpost.q: Which of these is a chemical change rather than a physical one?
outside_outpost.why: A chemical change produces a new substance. The other three can be reversed without one.

outside_outpost.q: DNA is copied during which process?
outside_outpost.why: Replication copies DNA; translation builds protein from RNA.

outside_outpost.q: An object in motion stays in motion unless acted on by an external force. This is:
opts: the law of conservation of mass
outside_outpost.why: The first law is the law of inertia.

outside_outpost.q: The density of pure water is closest to:
outside_outpost.why: 1 gram per millilitre — worth knowing, because Science passages assume it without saying so.

outside_outpost.q: In a food chain, organisms that break down dead material are:
outside_outpost.why: Producers make their own food; decomposers return nutrients from dead matter.

outside_outpost.q: The organelle in which aerobic cellular respiration releases most of the energy from food is the:
outside_outpost.why: Mitochondria carry out aerobic respiration. Chloroplasts capture light energy in photosynthesis; ribosomes build proteins; the nucleus holds DNA.

outside_outpost.q: Which of these is a mixture rather than a pure substance?
outside_outpost.why: Salt water is two substances that can be separated by evaporation. The others are each a single element or compound.

outside_outpost.q: A pea plant with genotype Tt is crossed with a tt plant. What fraction of the offspring are expected to be tt?
outside_outpost.why: Draw the Punnett square: T or t from the first parent, t from the second. Two of the four boxes are Tt and two are tt.

outside_outpost.q: In a thunderstorm you see the lightning before you hear the thunder because:
opts: light travels much faster than sound
sound slows down when it rains
outside_outpost.why: Both are produced at the same moment. Light arrives almost instantly; sound covers only about a third of a kilometre each second.

outside_outpost.q: Which layer of Earth is liquid?
outside_outpost.why: The outer core is molten iron and nickel. The inner core is solid under enormous pressure, and the mantle is solid rock that flows only very slowly.

outside_outpost.q: A gas is heated inside a sealed, rigid container. Its pressure:
outside_outpost.why: Hotter particles move faster and hit the walls harder and more often. The container cannot expand, so the pressure rises.

outside_outpost.q: Which of these is an element?
outside_outpost.why: An element is made of one kind of atom. Water and table salt are compounds (elements bonded together), and air is a mixture of gases.

outside_outpost.q: A block has a mass of 30 g and a volume of 40 cm³. Water has a density of 1 g/cm³. Placed in water, the block will:
opts: float, because it is less dense than water
sink, because its mass is more than its volume
sink, because it is denser than the water
float, because its mass is under 40 grams
outside_outpost.why: Density is mass ÷ volume: 30 ÷ 40 = 0.75 g/cm³, less than water’s 1 g/cm³, so it floats. Comparing mass with volume directly skips the division.

outside_outpost.q: A student dissolves salt in water, and the solution boils at 103 °C instead of 100 °C. The student should conclude that:
opts: the data stand: dissolved salt raises the boiling point
the thermometer must be faulty, since water boils at 100 °C
the air pressure in the room must have been unusually low
the salt must have evaporated before the water could boil
outside_outpost.why: Outside knowledge settles it: dissolving a solute raises the boiling point, so 103 °C is expected. Low pressure would lower the boiling point, the wrong direction, and blaming the thermometer throws out good data.

outside_outpost.q: In pea plants, tall (T) is dominant over short (t). Two Tt plants are crossed. What fraction of the offspring are expected to be tall?
outside_outpost.why: A Tt × Tt cross gives TT, Tt, Tt and tt in a 1 : 2 : 1 ratio. Every plant with at least one T is tall, so 3 of 4. The 1/2 counts only the Tt plants and forgets TT.

outside_outpost.q: A sealed flask with its contents has a mass of 250.0 g. A reaction inside produces a gas. Nothing enters or leaves the flask. Afterwards, the total mass is:
outside_outpost.why: Conservation of mass: in a closed system, a reaction rearranges atoms but never creates or destroys them. The gas stays in the sealed flask, so the mass cannot change.

outside_outpost.q: Which gas makes up most of Earth’s atmosphere?
outside_outpost.why: Dry air is about 78% nitrogen and 21% oxygen, with carbon dioxide well under 1%. Oxygen is the gas we need, which is why it feels like the obvious answer, but nitrogen is far more plentiful.

outside_outpost.q: Dew forms on grass on a cool, clear morning. Which process makes the dew?
outside_outpost.why: Water vapour in the air cools on the cold grass and turns back into liquid: gas to liquid is condensation. Evaporation is the reverse, liquid to gas, which is what later dries the dew.

outside_outpost.q: Adding a catalyst to a chemical reaction:
opts: speeds it up without being used up
increases the amount of product made
is used up as the reaction goes on
outside_outpost.why: A catalyst speeds a reaction up by giving it an easier path, and it comes out unchanged at the end. It makes the same product faster; it does not make more of it.

outside_outpost.q: A ball is thrown straight up. At the very top of its path its speed is zero for an instant. What is its acceleration at that moment?
opts: it depends on the ball’s mass
outside_outpost.why: Gravity pulls the ball down the whole time, so its acceleration is always about 9.8 m/s² downward, even at the top. Zero speed does not mean zero acceleration: the velocity is changing from upward to downward at that very moment.

outside_outpost.q: An animal cell is placed in very salty water. Which way does water move?
opts: out of the cell, so it shrinks
into the cell, so it swells
neither way, so it stays the same
salt moves in, but no water moves
outside_outpost.why: In osmosis, water moves across a membrane toward the side with more dissolved substance. The salty water outside has more, so water leaves the cell and it shrinks. The pull is to think the salt draws water in, but it draws water out.

exponent_expanse.why: Multiplying powers of the same base adds the exponents: 3 + 4.
A power of a power multiplies the exponents: 2 × 3.
A negative exponent means reciprocal, not a negative number: 1/2².
Dividing powers of the same base subtracts the exponents.
Any non-zero base raised to the zero power is 1.
A square root is the ½ power, so the exponent halves: 6 × ½.
The outside exponent hits every factor inside, the 2 included: 2⁴ = 16.
Pull out the largest perfect square: 50 = 25 × 2.
The denominator is the root and the numerator is the power: (∛8)² = 2².
Add the exponents: 5 + (−5) = 0, and anything to the zero power is 1.
Write 32 as a power of 2: 2⁵. Equal bases mean equal exponents, so x + 1 = 5. The 5 is the exponent, not x.
Multiply the front numbers (3 × 2 = 6) and add the exponents of 10 (4 + 5 = 9). Multiplying the exponents gives 10²⁰.
Simplify each root first: √18 = 3√2 and √8 = 2√2. Now they are like terms, and 3√2 + 2√2 = 5√2. Roots do not add under one sign.
Multiply top and bottom by √3: 6√3/3 = 2√3. Stopping before dividing by 3 gives 6√3.

exponent_expanse.q: Which is equal to x^(−1/2) for x > 0?
exponent_expanse.why: Two rules at once: the negative exponent means reciprocal, and the ½ means square root. Neither one makes anything negative.
Scientific notation puts one non-zero digit before the decimal point, then counts the places moved: four. 45 × 10³ has the right value but not the form, and 4.5 × 10³ is only 4,500.
Equal exponents on different bases combine: aⁿ · bⁿ = (ab)ⁿ, so 2³ · 5³ = 10³ = 1000. Adding the exponents (10⁶) works only when the bases match.
Roots are powers of ½, so they multiply under one sign: √3 · √12 = √36 = 6. √15 adds the numbers instead of multiplying them, and 2√3 is only √12 simplified.

exponent_expanse.q: A calculator that follows the order of operations is given −3² with no brackets. What does it display?
exponent_expanse.why: The exponent applies before the minus sign unless brackets say otherwise: −3² = −(3²) = −9. Only (−3)² equals 9, and −6 treats the power as multiplying by 2.
Rewrite both sides with the same base: 9ˣ = 3²ˣ and 27 = 3³, so 2x = 3 and x = 3/2. The 3 comes from writing 27 as 3³ but forgetting that 9 is 3².
A power of ten with a negative exponent moves the decimal point left. Three places left from 3.2 gives 0.0032. A positive power would move it right, giving 3,200.
The brackets put the negative sign inside the power: (−2)(−2)(−2)(−2). An even number of negative factors multiplies to a positive, so the answer is 16. Without brackets, −2⁴ would be −16.
Divide by subtracting exponents, one base at a time: a⁴ ÷ a¹ = a³, and b² ÷ b⁵ = b⁻³ = 1/b³. The lone a still has exponent 1, which the trap a⁴/b³ ignores.
81 = 3⁴, so x = 4 and 3^(4 − 2) = 3² = 9. Or divide: 3^(x − 2) = 3ˣ ÷ 3² = 81 ÷ 9 = 9. Subtracting 2 from 81 treats the exponent like an ordinary term.

A square root is the power ½, so this is x^(1/2) · x^(3/2). Multiplying adds the exponents: ½ + 3/2 = 2. Multiplying the exponents gives x^(3/4), which is the rule for a power of a power, not a product.

quadratic_quarry.q: Factor x² + 7x + 12:
quadratic_quarry.why: Find two numbers that multiply to 12 and add to 7.
Zero-product rule: set each factor to zero. The signs flip.

quadratic_quarry.q: How many real solutions does x² = 16 have?
quadratic_quarry.why: Both 4 and −4 square to 16. Taking only the positive root loses one.

quadratic_quarry.q: Factor x² − 9:
quadratic_quarry.why: A difference of two squares always factors into a sum times a difference.

quadratic_quarry.q: Solve x² + 2x − 8 = 0:
quadratic_quarry.why: Factors to (x − 2)(x + 4) = 0. Check by expanding if the signs feel slippery.

quadratic_quarry.q: The vertex of y = (x − 3)² + 5 is:
quadratic_quarry.why: In vertex form y = (x − h)² + k the vertex is (h, k), and h takes the opposite sign to the one written.

quadratic_quarry.q: In the quadratic formula, the discriminant is:
quadratic_quarry.why: It is the part under the root, and its sign tells you how many real solutions there are.

quadratic_quarry.q: If b² − 4ac < 0, the quadratic has:
quadratic_quarry.why: A negative under a square root leaves the real number line.

quadratic_quarry.q: Factor 2x² + 6x:
quadratic_quarry.why: Always take out the greatest common factor first — here 2x.

quadratic_quarry.q: The parabola y = −x² + 4 opens:
quadratic_quarry.why: A negative leading coefficient opens the curve downward; the +4 lifts the vertex.

quadratic_quarry.q: Which equation has solutions x = 3 and x = −5?
quadratic_quarry.why: Run the zero-product rule backwards: x = 3 comes from the factor (x − 3), and x = −5 from (x + 5). Each factor carries the opposite sign to its solution.

quadratic_quarry.q: What is the x-coordinate of the vertex of y = x² − 6x + 2?
quadratic_quarry.why: For y = ax² + bx + c the vertex sits at x = −b/(2a) = 6/2 = 3. Forgetting the minus sign in the formula gives −3.

quadratic_quarry.q: Solve 2x² − 5x − 3 = 0.
quadratic_quarry.why: Factor: (2x + 1)(x − 3) = 0. The factor 2x + 1 = 0 gives x = −1/2, not −1: the 2 in front has to be divided out.

quadratic_quarry.q: At how many points does the graph of y = x² − 4x + 4 touch the x-axis?
quadratic_quarry.why: The graph meets the x-axis at the real solutions. Here b² − 4ac = 16 − 16 = 0, so there is exactly one: the curve is (x − 2)² and just touches at x = 2.

quadratic_quarry.q: Expand (x + 5)².
quadratic_quarry.why: (x + 5)² means (x + 5)(x + 5). The middle term comes from both cross products, 5x + 5x = 10x. Squaring each term alone loses it.

quadratic_quarry.q: In the equation 3x² − 5x + 2 = 0, what is the value of b in the quadratic formula?
quadratic_quarry.why: Match the equation to ax² + bx + c = 0, sign included: a = 3, b = −5 and c = 2. Dropping the minus sign is the most common formula error.

quadratic_quarry.q: Where does the graph of y = x² + 4x − 5 cross the y-axis?
quadratic_quarry.why: The y-axis is where x = 0, so y = 0 + 0 − 5 = −5. In y = ax² + bx + c the y-intercept is always c. (−5, 0) and (1, 0) are where it crosses the x-axis.

quadratic_quarry.q: Solve (x − 2)² = 9.
quadratic_quarry.why: Take the square root of both sides, keeping both signs: x − 2 = 3 or x − 2 = −3, so x = 5 or x = −1. Keeping only the positive root loses a solution, and ±3 forgets the − 2.

quadratic_quarry.q: x = 3 is a solution of x² + kx − 12 = 0. What is k?
quadratic_quarry.why: Substitute the known root: 9 + 3k − 12 = 0, so 3k = 3 and k = 1. A sign slip when moving the −3 gives −1. (The equation is then (x + 4)(x − 3) = 0, whose other root is −4.)

quadratic_quarry.q: For what value of c does x² + 6x + c = 0 have exactly one solution?
quadratic_quarry.why: One solution means the discriminant is zero: 6² − 4c = 0, so c = 9, and the equation is (x + 3)² = 0. Setting c = 36 forgets the 4 in b² − 4ac.

quadratic_quarry.q: What are the solutions of x(x − 6) = 0?
quadratic_quarry.why: By the zero-product rule, one of the factors must be 0: either x = 0 or x − 6 = 0. So x = 0 and x = 6. The lone x is a factor too, which is why “x = 6 only” is wrong.

quadratic_quarry.q: Write x² − 10x + 25 as a product of factors.
quadratic_quarry.why: Find two numbers that multiply to 25 and add to −10: −5 and −5. So the expression factors as (x − 5)(x − 5) = (x − 5)². (x − 5)(x + 5) would give x² − 25 with no middle term.

quadratic_quarry.q: A ball’s height in metres after t seconds is h = −5t² + 20t. At what time, other than t = 0, is the ball at ground level?
quadratic_quarry.why: Ground level means h = 0. Factor: −5t(t − 4) = 0, and by the zero-product rule t = 0 or t = 4. The ball lands at 4 seconds; t = 2 is when it is highest.

quadratic_quarry.q: What is the minimum value of y = (x + 1)² − 7?
quadratic_quarry.why: In vertex form y = a(x − h)² + k the vertex is (h, k). Here it is (−1, −7), and since a > 0 the parabola opens up, so the vertex is the lowest point. The minimum value is its y, −7. The −1 is where the minimum happens, not the value.

quadratic_quarry.q: The solutions of x² + bx + c = 0 are 2 and 5. What is c?
quadratic_quarry.why: Build the equation from its roots: (x − 2)(x − 5) = x² − 7x + 10, so c = 10. The −7 is b, the coefficient of x.

statistics_summit.why: Sum is 30, and there are five values.

statistics_summit.q: Median of 4, 1, 9, 2, 7:
statistics_summit.why: Sort first — 1, 2, 4, 7, 9 — then take the middle. Skipping the sort is the usual mistake.
5 appears three times, more than anything else.

statistics_summit.q: Median of 2, 6, 9, 15:
statistics_summit.why: With an even count there is no single middle, so average the two middle values.

statistics_summit.q: Adding the value 100 to the set 2, 3, 4 changes the mean and the median:
opts: mean a lot, median a little
median a lot, mean a little
statistics_summit.why: An outlier drags the mean toward itself but only nudges the median one position.

statistics_summit.q: Range of 12, 4, 19, 7:
statistics_summit.why: Largest minus smallest: 19 − 4.

statistics_summit.q: A set of 5 numbers has mean 8. Their sum is:
statistics_summit.why: Mean × count = sum. Reading the mean formula backwards is a standard ACT move.

statistics_summit.q: Four tests average 82. What is needed on a fifth to average 84 over all five?
statistics_summit.why: Five tests at 84 need 420 points; four at 82 have given 328.

statistics_summit.q: Which is least affected by one extreme outlier?
statistics_summit.why: The median depends only on position, not on how far out a value sits.

statistics_summit.q: A data set is 6, 6, 6, 6. Its standard deviation is:
statistics_summit.why: Nothing varies from the mean, so the spread is zero.

statistics_summit.q: A class of 20 students averaged 70 on a test, and a class of 30 averaged 80. What is the average of all 50 students?
statistics_summit.why: Averages of different-sized groups cannot be averaged directly. Turn them into totals: 1400 + 2400 = 3800, and 3800 ÷ 50 = 76. The larger class pulls the result toward 80.

statistics_summit.q:

What is the median of the data?
statistics_summit.why: There are 3 + 5 + 2 + 1 = 11 values, so the median is the 6th in order. The first three are 1s and the next five are 2s, so the 6th is 2. The 5 is a frequency, not a value.

statistics_summit.q: Every value in a data set is increased by 5. What happens to the standard deviation?
statistics_summit.why: Standard deviation measures how far values sit from their mean. Adding 5 to everything moves the mean by 5 too, so every distance is unchanged.

statistics_summit.q: Set A is 10, 10, 10, 10. Set B is 1, 5, 15, 19. Which statement is true?
opts: Same mean; B is more spread out.
Same mean; A is more spread out.
statistics_summit.why: Both sets total 40 over four values, so both means are 10. A does not vary at all; B ranges from 1 to 19.

statistics_summit.q: A student’s score is at the 80th percentile. This means the score is:
opts: at or above about 80% of all scores
statistics_summit.why: A percentile is a rank, not a mark: it tells you what share of the group scored at or below you. A student at the 80th percentile may have answered only half the questions correctly.

statistics_summit.q:

What is the mode shoe size?
statistics_summit.why: The mode is the most frequent value. Size 7 appears 9 times, more than any other. The 9 is the count, not the size.

statistics_summit.q: A data set has a range of 12, and its smallest value is 5. What is its largest value?
statistics_summit.why: Range = largest − smallest, so the largest is 5 + 12 = 17. Subtracting gives 7, which cannot be right: it is barely above the smallest value.

statistics_summit.q: The numbers 4, 6, 8 and 10 have a mean of 7. Which number could be added to the set without changing the mean?
statistics_summit.why: Think in totals: the sum is 28 for 4 values. Adding the mean itself keeps the balance, (28 + 7) ÷ 5 = 7. Any other value pulls the mean toward itself.

statistics_summit.q: In a data set, the first quartile is 20, the median is 30 and the third quartile is 50. About what percent of the values lie between 20 and 50?
statistics_summit.why: Quartiles cut the sorted data into four equal quarters. From the first quartile to the third covers two of them, the middle half, however far apart the numbers are.

statistics_summit.q: In the data set 2, 4, 4, 5, 10, the 10 is changed to 20. Which statistics change?
statistics_summit.why: The total rises by 10, so the mean goes up, and the largest value moves, so the range does too. The median and mode (both 4) depend only on the middle and the most common values, which stay put. Forgetting the range is the usual slip.

statistics_summit.q:
DayMonTueWedThuFri
Visitors121591519
What is the median number of visitors?
statistics_summit.why: Sort first: 9, 12, 15, 15, 19. The middle of the five is 15. Taking Wednesday’s 9 because it sits in the middle column skips the sorting; 14 is the mean.

statistics_summit.q: The mode of 4, 7, x, 9, 7, 4 is 4. What is x?
statistics_summit.why: Without x, 4 and 7 each appear twice. For 4 alone to be the mode it must appear most often, so x must be 4, making three 4s. If x were 7, the mode would be 7.

statistics_summit.q: Scores in a class have a mean of 70 and a standard deviation of 5. Maya scored 80. How many standard deviations above the mean is her score?
statistics_summit.why: Standard deviation measures distance from the mean. Maya is 80 − 70 = 10 points above it, and each standard deviation is 5 points, so she is 10 ÷ 5 = 2 standard deviations above. The 10 is the distance in points.

statistics_summit.q: A box of 10 apples has a mean mass of 150 g. Two apples of 120 g each are taken out. What is the mean mass of the apples left?
statistics_summit.why: Work with sums: the box totals 10 × 150 = 1,500 g. Removing 240 g leaves 1,260 g for 8 apples, a mean of 1,260 ÷ 8 = 157.5 g. Removing lighter-than-average apples raises the mean, so it cannot stay at 150.

statistics_summit.q: The mean of x, 2x and 3x is 16. What is the median of the three numbers?
statistics_summit.why: The sum is the mean × count: x + 2x + 3x = 48, so 6x = 48 and x = 8. The three numbers are 8, 16 and 24, and the middle one is 16. Stopping at x = 8 answers a different question.

coordinate_cove.q: Distance between (0, 0) and (6, 8):
coordinate_cove.why: √(36 + 64) = √100. It is Pythagoras wearing coordinates.

coordinate_cove.q: Midpoint of (2, 3) and (8, 7):
coordinate_cove.why: Average the x values and average the y values.

coordinate_cove.q: A line falling as you move right has a slope that is:
coordinate_cove.why: Downhill left-to-right means rise is negative while run is positive.

coordinate_cove.q: A vertical line has a slope that is:
coordinate_cove.why: The run is zero, and division by zero is undefined. A horizontal line is the one with slope zero.

coordinate_cove.q: Which line is parallel to y = 2x + 1?
coordinate_cove.why: Parallel lines share a slope; only the intercept may differ.

coordinate_cove.q: Which line is perpendicular to y = 2x + 1?
coordinate_cove.why: Perpendicular slopes are negative reciprocals: the opposite sign and the flipped fraction.

coordinate_cove.q: The point (−3, 5) lies in which quadrant?
coordinate_cove.why: Negative x with positive y is the upper-left quadrant.

coordinate_cove.q: Where does y = 3x − 6 cross the x-axis?
coordinate_cove.why: The x-axis is where y = 0. Setting y = 0 gives x = 2; (0, −6) is the y-intercept.

coordinate_cove.q: The circle (x − 1)² + (y + 2)² = 9 has centre and radius:
coordinate_cove.why: The centre takes the opposite signs to those written, and the right-hand side is r², not r.

coordinate_cove.q: Translating (4, −1) three units left and two units up gives:
coordinate_cove.why: Left subtracts from x; up adds to y.

coordinate_cove.q: M(4, 1) is the midpoint of segment AB, and A is (1, −3). What are the coordinates of B?
coordinate_cove.why: The midpoint is halfway, so B is as far past M as A is before it: x goes 1 → 4 → 7 and y goes −3 → 1 → 5. Averaging A and M gives (2.5, −1), a point between them; adding them gives (5, −2).

coordinate_cove.q: The point (3, −2) is reflected across the y-axis. Where does it land?
coordinate_cove.why: Reflecting across the y-axis flips left and right, so only x changes sign. Changing y would be a reflection across the x-axis.

coordinate_cove.q: Where do the lines y = x + 1 and y = −x + 5 intersect?
coordinate_cove.why: At the intersection both equations give the same y: x + 1 = −x + 5, so x = 2 and y = 3. Each wrong point lies on at most one of the lines.

coordinate_cove.q: What is the equation of the line through (2, 7) and (−5, 7)?
coordinate_cove.why: Both points have y = 7, so the line is horizontal and every point on it has y = 7. An equation of the form x = … is a vertical line.

coordinate_cove.q: A triangle has vertices (0, 0), (6, 0) and (0, 4). What is its area?
coordinate_cove.why: The legs lie along the axes, so the base is 6 and the height is 4: ½ × 6 × 4 = 12. Leaving out the ½ gives 24.

coordinate_cove.q: Which point lies on the line y = 2x − 1?
coordinate_cove.why: A point is on a line if its coordinates make the equation true: 2(3) − 1 = 5. (5, 3) swaps x and y, and (0, 1) has the sign of the intercept wrong.

coordinate_cove.q: How far apart are the points (−2, 5) and (7, 5)?
coordinate_cove.why: Both points have y = 5, so they sit on one horizontal line and the distance is the difference in x: 7 − (−2) = 9. The 5 subtracts 2 without its sign, and 81 forgets the square root.

coordinate_cove.q: A line passes through (1, 2) and (3, 8). What is the slope of a line perpendicular to it?
coordinate_cove.why: The first line’s slope is (8 − 2)/(3 − 1) = 3. Perpendicular slopes are negative reciprocals: flip it and change the sign. −3 changes only the sign, and 1/3 only flips it.

coordinate_cove.q: Which equation describes the circle with centre (−3, 2) that passes through the point (1, 5)?
coordinate_cove.why: The radius is the distance from the centre to the point: √(4² + 3²) = 5. The equation needs r² = 25, and the signs inside flip: centre (−3, 2) gives (x + 3) and (y − 2). Using the point as the centre is the other trap.

coordinate_cove.q: Which line is the perpendicular bisector of the segment from (0, 0) to (4, 2)?
coordinate_cove.why: It must pass through the midpoint, (2, 1), and be perpendicular to the segment, whose slope is ½. The negative reciprocal is −2, so y − 1 = −2(x − 2), or y = −2x + 5. y = 2x − 3 passes through the midpoint but is not perpendicular, and y = −2x + 1 has the right slope but misses the midpoint.

coordinate_cove.q: The point A is at (−4, 3). How far is A from the x-axis?
coordinate_cove.why: The x-axis is the line y = 0, and the y-coordinate tells how far above or below it a point sits. A is 3 units above it. The 4 is the distance from the y-axis, and 5 is the distance from the origin.

coordinate_cove.q: The point (5, 2) is reflected across the line y = x. Where does it land?
coordinate_cove.why: Reflecting across y = x swaps the two coordinates, so (5, 2) becomes (2, 5). Reflecting across the y-axis would give (−5, 2), and across the x-axis (5, −2).

coordinate_cove.q: A line has slope 3/4 and passes through (0, 1). Which of these points is also on the line?
coordinate_cove.why: The line is y = (3/4)x + 1, and a point lies on it if its coordinates make the equation true. At x = 4, y = 3 + 1 = 4. Slope 3/4 means up 3 for every 4 across, so (3, 5) mixes up rise and run.

coordinate_cove.q: The points (1, 2), (4, 6) and (k, 10) all lie on one line. What is k?
coordinate_cove.why: The slope from (1, 2) to (4, 6) is 4/3: up 4 for every 3 across. From (4, 6), going up another 4 to y = 10 means going 3 more across, to x = 7. The trap 8 adds 4 to the x-value, confusing rise with run.

coordinate_cove.q: The segment from (−2, 1) to (6, 7) is a diameter of a circle. What is the radius of the circle?
coordinate_cove.why: Distance is Pythagoras: the endpoints are 8 across and 6 up, so the diameter is √(64 + 36) = 10. The radius is half of that, 5. The trap 10 stops at the diameter, and 4 halves only the horizontal gap.

units_uplands.q: 3 kilograms equals how many grams?
units_uplands.why: Kilo means a thousand, so multiply.

units_uplands.q: Which is largest?
units_uplands.why: Convert everything to one unit first: 1000 mm, 500 mm, 900 mm, 500 mm.

units_uplands.q: The same quantity expressed in a larger unit gives a number that is:
units_uplands.why: Bigger unit, fewer of them. It is the one check that catches a flipped conversion.

units_uplands.q: 250 millilitres is how many litres?
units_uplands.why: A thousand millilitres make a litre, so divide.

units_uplands.q: A rate given in grams per second is converted to grams per minute by:
units_uplands.why: More seconds in the window means more grams, so the number goes up.

units_uplands.q: Which unit measures a volume?
units_uplands.why: Three dimensions multiplied gives a cubic unit. cm² is area.

units_uplands.q: A table lists concentration in µg/L and a question asks for mg/L. 4000 µg/L equals:
units_uplands.why: A milligram is a thousand micrograms, so divide by 1000.

units_uplands.q: Two data columns are headed “Mass (kg)” and “Mass (g)”. Comparing the numbers directly would:
opts: be meaningless until one column is converted
be valid because both columns report masses
require a graph before any comparison is made
require the density of each sample first
units_uplands.why: Reading the unit in the column heading is the first thing to do, and the most commonly skipped.

units_uplands.q: A speed of 72 km/h in metres per second is:
units_uplands.why: 72 km is 72 000 m and an hour is 3600 s, so 72 000 ÷ 3600 = 20.

units_uplands.q: Temperature is recorded in kelvin. A reading of 273 K is approximately:
units_uplands.why: Kelvin and Celsius are offset by 273, so 273 K is water’s freezing point.

units_uplands.q: One square metre is how many square centimetres?
units_uplands.why: A square metre is 100 cm by 100 cm, so it holds 100 × 100 = 10 000 cm². Area units convert by the square of the length factor.

units_uplands.q: A quantity measured in g/cm³ is a:
units_uplands.why: Mass divided by volume is density. Reading the unit tells you which quantity it is before any number is involved.

units_uplands.q: Pressure is force divided by area. If force is in newtons (N) and area in square metres (m²), pressure has units of:
units_uplands.why: Units follow the same operation as the numbers: dividing force by area divides N by m².

units_uplands.why: Convert A before comparing: 0.5 kg = 500 g. Then 520 g is the largest. The small number 0.5 hides the largest unit.

units_uplands.q: A process takes 0.2 hours. How long is that?
units_uplands.why: An hour is 60 minutes, so 0.2 × 60 = 12. Reading the decimal as “20 minutes” treats an hour as if it had 100 minutes.

units_uplands.why: The unit is in the column heading, so the 43 in Leaf B’s row is 43 mm. Always carry the heading’s unit along with the number.

units_uplands.q: A rectangular plot measures 3 m by 4 m. What is its area?
units_uplands.why: Multiplying metres by metres gives square metres. 12 m is a length, 12 m³ a volume, and 7 m² comes from adding the sides.

units_uplands.q:

What is the mass of Sample A in grams?
units_uplands.why: The table is in milligrams, not grams. There are 1,000 mg in a gram, so divide: 2,500 ÷ 1,000 = 2.5 g. The 2,500 g answer forgets to convert.

units_uplands.q: Aluminium has a density of 2.7 g/cm³. What is this in kg/m³?
units_uplands.why: Convert top and bottom separately. 2.7 g = 0.0027 kg, and 1 cm³ = 0.000001 m³, because a volume scales by the cube of the length factor (100³). So 0.0027 ÷ 0.000001 = 2,700. Converting only the grams gives 0.0027.

units_uplands.q: A pump moves 120 mL of water per second. What is this rate in litres per minute?
units_uplands.why: Two conversions: × 60 for seconds to minutes (7,200 mL/min), then ÷ 1,000 for mL to L (7.2 L/min). Stopping after one step gives 7,200 or 0.12.

units_uplands.q: How many centimetres are in 2.5 metres?
units_uplands.why: 1 m = 100 cm, so multiply: 2.5 × 100 = 250. The smaller unit gives the bigger number.

units_uplands.q: Which of these lengths is the shortest?
units_uplands.why: All four say “1”, so the unit decides. A millimetre is a thousandth of a metre, smaller than a centimetre (a hundredth), which is smaller than a metre and a kilometre.

units_uplands.q: A snail crawls 30 cm per minute. How many metres does it cover in one hour?
units_uplands.why: Convert both units. In an hour it crawls 30 × 60 = 1,800 cm, and 1,800 cm ÷ 100 = 18 m. The 1,800 forgets to change centimetres to metres.

units_uplands.q:

C450 cm³
Which sample has the largest volume?
units_uplands.why: Put every value into one unit first. 0.4 L = 400 mL, and 1 cm³ is exactly 1 mL, so C is 450 mL. Order: C (450) > A (400) > B (350). A’s 0.4 looks smallest only because litres are the bigger unit.

units_uplands.q: A car goes 20 km on each litre of fuel. How many metres does it go on each millilitre?
units_uplands.why: Convert the top and the bottom. 20 km = 20,000 m, and 1 L = 1,000 mL, so 20,000 m ÷ 1,000 mL = 20 m per mL. Converting only the kilometres gives 20,000, and converting only the litres gives 0.02.

rates_ridge.q: A car travels 150 km in 3 hours. Its average speed is:
rates_ridge.why: Rate = amount ÷ time. Dividing, not multiplying, is the whole of it.

rates_ridge.q: A tap fills 12 litres in 4 minutes. How long to fill 30 litres at the same rate?
rates_ridge.why: The rate is 3 L/min, so 30 ÷ 3 = 10.

rates_ridge.q: A reaction produces 6 g of gas in 30 seconds. Its rate is:
rates_ridge.why: 6 ÷ 30 = 0.2. If the answer looks large, check which number you divided by.

rates_ridge.q: Two pumps each move 8 L/min. Working together they move:
rates_ridge.why: Rates working in parallel add.

rates_ridge.q: A population doubles every 3 years. After 9 years it has multiplied by:
rates_ridge.why: Three doublings: 2 × 2 × 2. Doubling periods multiply, they do not add.

rates_ridge.q: A runner covers the first 5 km at 10 km/h and the next 5 km at 5 km/h. Her average speed is:
rates_ridge.why: She spends twice as long on the slow half, so the slow speed carries more weight than the fast one.

rates_ridge.q: A tank loses 2 % of its contents each hour. After two hours it holds:
opts: slightly more than 96 % of the original
slightly less than 96 % of the original
rates_ridge.why: The second 2 % is taken from a smaller amount, so the loss is slightly under 4 % in total.

rates_ridge.q: A printer prints 18 pages per minute. In 40 seconds it prints about:
rates_ridge.why: 40 seconds is two-thirds of a minute, so two-thirds of 18.

rates_ridge.q: Fuel use is 7 litres per 100 km. A 250 km journey uses about:
rates_ridge.why: 250 km is 2.5 hundreds, so 2.5 × 7.

rates_ridge.q: If a rate is constant, a graph of total amount against time is:
rates_ridge.why: Constant rate means constant slope. A flattening curve would mean a falling rate.

rates_ridge.why: Add rates, not times: 1/6 + 1/3 = 1/2 of the pond per hour, so 2 hours. Together they must beat the faster pump alone, which rules out 3 or more.

rates_ridge.q: A heart beats 18 times in 15 seconds. What is the heart rate in beats per minute?
rates_ridge.why: A minute is four lots of 15 seconds, so 18 × 4 = 72. The 270 comes from multiplying 18 by 15.

rates_ridge.q: A shower uses 6 litres of water per minute. How much water does a 5-minute shower use?
rates_ridge.why: Amount = rate × time: 6 L/min × 5 min = 30 L. Adding gives 11, and dividing gives 1.2.

rates_ridge.q: Two cyclists ride in the same direction on the same road. The one in front rides at 15 km/h; the one 10 km behind rides at 20 km/h. How long until the second catches the first?
rates_ridge.why: Moving the same way, the gap closes at the difference of the speeds: 20 − 15 = 5 km/h. Then 10 ÷ 5 = 2 hours. Adding the speeds (35 km/h) gives about 17 minutes, the answer for riders heading toward each other.

rates_ridge.q: Four workers take 6 hours to paint a fence. At the same rate each, how long would three workers take?
rates_ridge.why: The job is 4 × 6 = 24 worker-hours. Fewer workers take longer: 24 ÷ 3 = 8 hours. The 4.5 treats time as if it shrinks with fewer workers.

rates_ridge.q: A cyclist rides at 18 km/h for 2 hours. How far does she go?
rates_ridge.why: Predict by multiplying the rate by the time: 18 km/h × 2 h = 36 km. Dividing gives 9, which would be the speed if 18 km were the distance.

rates_ridge.q: A candle 15 cm tall burns down 2 cm every 30 minutes. How long will it take to burn away completely?
rates_ridge.why: First make the rate per hour: 2 cm per 30 min is 4 cm per hour. Then 15 ÷ 4 = 3.75 hours, which is 3 hours 45 minutes. The 7.5 is 15 ÷ 2, a count of half-hour blocks, and reading it as hours gives 7 hours 30 minutes.

rates_ridge.q: A walker covers 6 km in 1 hour 30 minutes. What is her average speed?
rates_ridge.why: Write the time in hours before dividing: 1 hour 30 minutes is 1.5 hours, not 1.3. Then 6 ÷ 1.5 = 4 km/h. Using 1.3 gives about 4.6, and multiplying gives 9.
