pronoun_pass.q: “The coach gave the trophy to Sam and ___.”
pronoun_pass.why: It is the object of “to”. Drop “Sam and” and your ear does the rest.

pronoun_pass.q: “Each of the robots ___ charged at ___ own station.”
pronoun_pass.why: “Each” is the subject, not “robots”, so the verb is singular — and a robot is a thing, so the pronoun is “its”.

pronoun_pass.q: “The student ___ won the prize is here.”
pronoun_pass.why: It is the subject of “won”, and “who” is the subject form. “Which” never refers to a person.

pronoun_pass.q: “The scientist ___ the committee praised has published again.”
pronoun_pass.why: Here the committee did the praising, so the pronoun is the object — “whom”.

pronoun_pass.q: Which sentence has a clear pronoun reference?
opts: When Maya met Priya, Maya was nervous.
When Maya met Priya, she was nervous.
Maya met Priya, and she was nervous.
She was nervous when Maya met Priya.
pronoun_pass.why: Three of these leave “she” pointing at either woman. Repeating the name is clumsy but correct, and the ACT prefers correct.

pronoun_pass.q: “The company announced that ___ would expand.”
pronoun_pass.why: A company is one thing. Keep it singular all the way through the sentence.

pronoun_pass.q: “My sister runs faster than ___.”
pronoun_pass.why: The sentence is short for “faster than I run”, so the subject form is right.

pronoun_pass.q: Which sentence uses the right pronoun in the compound subject?
opts: The manager and I reviewed the budget.
The manager and myself reviewed the budget.
The manager and me reviewed the budget.
Myself and the manager reviewed the budget.
pronoun_pass.why: Remove the other person to test: “I reviewed the budget”, not “me reviewed” or “myself reviewed”. The pronoun is part of the subject, so it takes the subject form. “Myself” is only for reflecting back on a subject already named.

pronoun_pass.q:
What is wrong with:
“The road was flooded and the bridge was out, which delayed us.”
opts: “which” has no single noun to refer to
pronoun_pass.why: “Which” should point at one noun. Here it points at a whole situation (the flood and the closed bridge), which the ACT treats as vague. Name the thing instead: “…, and the two problems delayed us.”

pronoun_pass.q: “Every one of the laptops shipped with ___ charger.”
pronoun_pass.why: “Every one” is the singular subject and names a thing, so the possessive is “its”. “Their” agrees with “laptops”, the wrong word; “it’s” means “it is”.

pronoun_pass.q: “When one travels abroad, ___ should carry a copy of one’s passport.”
pronoun_pass.why: The sentence has already chosen “one”. Switching to “you”, “they” or “we” midway is a shift in person; stay with the pronoun the sentence set up.

pronoun_pass.q: “The principal thanked ___ students for cleaning the park.”
pronoun_pass.why: Drop the noun to test: “thanked us”, not “thanked we”. The pronoun is the object of “thanked”, so it takes the object form.

pronoun_pass.q: “Either Tom or Raj left ___ jacket on the bus.”
pronoun_pass.why: With “or”, only one of them left the jacket, so the pronoun is singular. “Their” would suit “Tom and Raj”.

pronoun_pass.q: “After weeks of practice, she taught ___ to juggle.”
pronoun_pass.why: When the object is the same person as the subject, the pronoun is reflexive: “she taught herself”.

pronoun_pass.q: Which sentence avoids a vague pronoun?
opts: At the clinic, the nurses explained the new rules.
At the clinic, they explained the new rules.
At the clinic, it explained the new rules to us.
At the clinic, you were told the rules by them.
pronoun_pass.why: “They” and “them” need a noun to point at, and no people have been named. Naming the nurses fixes it.

pronoun_pass.q: “The twins packed ___ own lunches before school.”
pronoun_pass.why: The only noun the pronoun can point to is “the twins”, which is plural, so the possessive is plural. “There” is a place word that sounds the same.

pronoun_pass.q: “The hive lost half of ___ bees over the winter.”
pronoun_pass.why: “The hive” is one thing, so its pronoun is singular. “Their” would need a plural noun, and “it’s” means “it is”.

pronoun_pass.q: “When visitors enter the cave, ___ must switch off their phones.”
pronoun_pass.why: The sentence starts with “visitors” and ends with “their”, so the pronoun stays in the third person plural. Switching to “you” or “one” changes person midway.

pronoun_pass.q: Which sentence uses “myself” correctly?
opts: The coach picked Lena and myself.
Please send the forms to myself.
pronoun_pass.why: “Myself” is correct only when “I” is already the subject of the sentence, as here, where it adds emphasis. Elsewhere use the ordinary case: “picked Lena and me”, “Lena and I were chosen”, “send the forms to me”.

pronoun_pass.q: “Give the spare key to ___ arrives first.”
pronoun_pass.why: A pronoun takes its case from its job in its own clause. The whole clause “___ arrives first” is the object of “to”, but inside that clause the pronoun is the subject of “arrives”. “Whomever” is tempting only because it follows “to”.

pronoun_pass.q:
Which pronoun could replace the words in bold?
“Maria and Leo painted the fence.”
pronoun_pass.why: “Maria and Leo” are two people doing the painting, so the pronoun must be plural and in the subject case: “They painted”. “Them” is the object form, and “their” shows possession.

pronoun_pass.q: “To ___ should I address the letter?”
pronoun_pass.why: The pronoun is the object of “to”, and whom is the object form. Turn the question into a statement to test it: “I should address it to him”, and him matches whom.

pronoun_pass.q: “Neither the coach nor the players remembered ___ water bottles.”
pronoun_pass.why: With “neither … nor”, a pronoun agrees with the nearer noun, just as a verb does. “The players” is nearer and plural, so the pronoun is “their”.

pronoun_pass.q: “___ volunteers painted the whole hall in a single day.”
pronoun_pass.why: Drop the noun to test: “We painted the whole hall”, not “Us painted”. The pronoun is part of the subject, so it takes the subject form even with “volunteers” after it.

pronoun_pass.q:
The writer means that the coach trusts Mia more than the coach trusts the writer. Which word completes the sentence?
“The coach trusts Mia more than ___.”
pronoun_pass.why: Finish the comparison to find the case: “more than she trusts me”, so the pronoun is an object. “Than I” is the trap: it sounds formal, but it means “more than I trust Mia”, which is not what the writer means.

modifier_marsh.q:
Fix the dangler:
“Walking home, the rain started.”
opts: Walking home, I felt the rain start.
Walking home, the rain fell hard.
modifier_marsh.why: The subject right after the comma has to be the one doing the walking.

modifier_marsh.q: The umbrella belongs to the woman. Which sentence says so without ambiguity?
opts: The woman with the red umbrella hailed a cab.
The woman hailed a cab with the red umbrella.
With the red umbrella, a cab was hailed by the woman.
A cab, with the red umbrella, was hailed by the woman.
modifier_marsh.why: A modifier belongs next to the word it describes. In “the woman with the red umbrella” the phrase sits on “woman”; elsewhere it attaches to the cab or to the hailing.

modifier_marsh.q: Which has NO dangling modifier?
opts: Tired from practice, Jordan went to bed.
Tired from practice, bed sounded great.
Tired from practice, the game ended.
Tired from practice, it got late.
modifier_marsh.why: Jordan is the one who is tired. A bed, a game and “it” cannot be.

modifier_marsh.q:
Where should “only” go?
“She ___ ate ___ the salad ___.” (she ate nothing else)
modifier_marsh.why: “Only” modifies whatever follows it. Put it before “the salad” and the salad is the sole thing eaten.

modifier_marsh.q: Which sentence gives the opening phrase something it can sensibly describe?
opts: Covered in dust, the hikers reached the hut.
Covered in dust, the hut appeared.
Covered in dust, it was a long walk.
The hut appeared covered in dust, exhausted.
modifier_marsh.why: The hikers are the ones covered in dust, so they must be the subject that follows.

modifier_marsh.q:
What is wrong with:
“We saw a deer driving through the park.”
opts: it reads as though the deer was driving
it needs a comma after “deer” to be clear
nothing is wrong; the meaning is obvious
modifier_marsh.why: A participial phrase attaches to the nearest noun. Move it: “Driving through the park, we saw a deer.”

modifier_marsh.q: Which is clearest?
opts: She walked nearly the whole route.
She nearly walked the whole route.
Nearly she walked the whole route.
She walked the whole nearly route.
modifier_marsh.why: Placing “nearly” before “walked” says she almost did not walk at all. Before “the whole route” it says she covered most of it.

modifier_marsh.q: Which sentence avoids a dangling participle?
opts: Hoping for a better view, we climbed the ridge.
Hoping for a better view, the ridge was climbed.
Hoping for a better view, the view improved.
The ridge, hoping for a better view, was climbed.
modifier_marsh.why: A passive main clause is the classic dangler trap — the ridge cannot hope for anything.

modifier_marsh.q:
Fix the misplaced phrase:
“The letter was mailed by the lawyer in a blue envelope.”
opts: The lawyer mailed the letter in a blue envelope.
In a blue envelope the lawyer was mailed the letter.
The letter in a blue envelope was mailed by the lawyer in it.
modifier_marsh.why: As written, the lawyer is in the envelope. Move the phrase next to “letter”.

modifier_marsh.q: Which sentence is correct?
opts: After studying all week, she felt ready.
After studying all week, the exam felt easier.
After studying all week, it went well.
After studying all week, the results arrived.
modifier_marsh.why: She is the one who studied. Exams, results and “it” cannot study.

modifier_marsh.q:
Fix the dangling phrase:
“To pass the exam, careful revision is needed.”
opts: To pass the exam, you need careful revision.
To pass the exam, revision needs to be careful.
To pass the exam, careful revision is what is needed.
Careful revision is needed, to pass the exam.
modifier_marsh.why: An opening “to” phrase names a goal, and the subject after the comma must be the one with the goal. Revision does not want to pass an exam; “you” does.

modifier_marsh.q: Which sentence places the describing clause correctly?
opts: I gave the dog that barked all night to my neighbour.
I gave the dog to my neighbour that barked all night.
That barked all night, I gave the dog to my neighbour.
I gave to my neighbour that barked all night the dog.
modifier_marsh.why: A “that” clause attaches to the noun just before it. Placed after “neighbour”, it says the neighbour barked all night.

modifier_marsh.q: Which sentence is written correctly?
opts: A talented chef, Ana was hired by the new restaurant.
A talented chef, the new restaurant hired Ana.
A talented chef, the restaurant was lucky to get Ana.
A talented chef, Ana’s job was at the new restaurant.
modifier_marsh.why: An opening noun phrase renames whatever comes right after the comma. Ana is the chef, so “Ana” must be the subject — not the restaurant, and not Ana’s job.

modifier_marsh.q: The sentence “Students who revise often score higher” is ambiguous. Which rewrite says that frequent revision leads to higher scores?
opts: Students who often revise score higher.
Students who revise score often higher.
Often, students who revise score higher.
Students who revise score higher often.
modifier_marsh.why: “Often” between two verbs could belong to either. Put it directly before “revise” and it can only describe the revising. Moving it to the front makes it describe the scoring.

modifier_marsh.q:
What is wrong with:
“Arriving late, Maria’s seat had been given away.”
opts: the seat, not Maria, is what arrives late
nothing is wrong, since Maria is named
modifier_marsh.why: The opening phrase attaches to the subject, and the subject is “seat”. A possessive such as “Maria’s” cannot be the doer. Fix: “Arriving late, Maria found her seat had been given away.”

modifier_marsh.q: Which sentence contains a misplaced modifier?
opts: We bought a puppy for my sister called Biscuit.
We bought my sister a puppy called Biscuit.
My sister has a puppy called Biscuit.
Biscuit is the puppy we bought for my sister.
modifier_marsh.why: “Called Biscuit” sits next to “my sister”, so the sentence says the sister is called Biscuit. A describer belongs beside the noun it describes, as in the second choice, where it follows “puppy”.

modifier_marsh.q:
Fill in the blank so that the opening phrase describes the right thing:
“Having crossed the finish line, ___ collapsed onto the grass.”
modifier_marsh.why: Whatever comes straight after the comma is the thing that crossed the finish line. Only the runner did that.

modifier_marsh.q:
As written, what does this sentence say was hanging on the wall?
“Hanging on the wall, Mia admired the painting.”
modifier_marsh.why: An opening phrase describes the first noun after the comma, and that noun is “Mia”. The writer means the painting, which is exactly why the sentence needs rewriting: “Mia admired the painting hanging on the wall.”

modifier_marsh.q:
Which choice fixes the dangling modifier by changing the opening phrase?
“While driving to work, the radio played an old song.”
opts: While I was driving to work, the radio played an old song.
While driving to work, the radio was playing an old song.
While driving to work the radio played an old song.
While driving to work, an old song played on the radio.
modifier_marsh.why: As written, the radio is driving. One fix changes the subject after the comma; the other gives the opening phrase a subject of its own: “While I was driving”. Commas and tense changes leave the radio behind the wheel, and so does swapping in “an old song”.

modifier_marsh.q:
Which phrase is misplaced?
“Soaked from the storm, the hikers hung their jackets by the fire that were dripping.”
modifier_marsh.why: “Soaked from the storm” correctly describes “the hikers”, the noun right after it, so it is fine. “That were dripping” is stuck to “the fire”, but its plural verb shows it means the jackets; it belongs right after “jackets”.

modifier_marsh.q:
In the sentence below, which word does the phrase in the blue hat describe?
“The girl in the blue hat waved from the bus.”
modifier_marsh.why: A describing phrase attaches to the word right beside it. “In the blue hat” follows “girl”, so it tells you which girl; it says nothing about the waving or the bus.

modifier_marsh.q: Which sentence contains a dangling modifier?
opts: Opening the door, the cold air rushed in.
Opening the door, I felt the cold air rush in.
When I opened the door, the cold air rushed in.
The cold air rushed in when I opened the door.
modifier_marsh.why: An opening phrase describes the subject right after the comma. In the first, that subject is “the cold air”, and air cannot open a door. The others either put the person doing the opening after the comma or give the phrase a subject of its own.

modifier_marsh.q:
Which choice corrects the sentence?
“At the age of six, my family moved to Lima.”
opts: When I was six, my family moved to Lima.
At the age of six, my family’s move was to Lima.
My family, at the age of six, moved to Lima.
modifier_marsh.why: As written, the family is six years old, because the opening phrase describes the first noun after the comma. The fix gives the phrase its own subject: “When I was six”. Moving the phrase next to “family” leaves the same problem.

modifier_marsh.q:
Which opening phrase fits the sentence?
“___, the old bridge finally collapsed.”
opts: Having warned the town for years
modifier_marsh.why: Whatever opens the sentence describes “the old bridge”, the subject after the comma. A bridge can be weakened by floods, but it cannot drive, warn a town or watch from a bank.

modifier_marsh.q:
Which choice fixes the sentence?
“Having been painted the day before, the children were warned not to touch the fence.”
opts: The children were warned not to touch the fence, which had been painted the day before.
Having been painted the day before, the children were warned not to touch it.
The children, having been painted the day before, were warned not to touch the fence.
Having been painted, the day before the children were warned not to touch the fence.
modifier_marsh.why: The opening phrase describes the subject after the comma, “the children”, so the sentence says the children were painted. The fence is what was painted, so the describer must sit beside “fence”: “the fence, which had been painted”. Moving commas or swapping in a pronoun leaves the children covered in paint.

parallel_pier.q: Choose the parallel version:
opts: She likes reading, writing, and drawing.
She likes reading, to write, and drawing.
She likes to read, writing, and draws.
parallel_pier.why: All three items are -ing forms. A list has to keep one shape throughout.

parallel_pier.q: “The job requires focus, patience, and ___.”
parallel_pier.why: The first two items are nouns, so the third has to be a noun too.

parallel_pier.q:
Parallel comparison:
“Driving is safer than ___.”
parallel_pier.why: Compare like with like: “driving” to “flying”.

parallel_pier.q: “The report was thorough, current, and ___.”
parallel_pier.why: Three adjectives describing the report. The other choices change grammatical shape mid-list.

parallel_pier.q:
Which is parallel?
“He came not only to watch but also ___.”
parallel_pier.why: “Not only … but also” has to bracket two identical structures. “To watch” demands “to compete”.

parallel_pier.q: “She would rather train early than ___ late.”
parallel_pier.why: “Rather … than” joins two bare verbs. “Train” demands “finish”.

parallel_pier.q: Which sentence keeps the three infinitives parallel?
opts: The course teaches students to plan, to draft, and to revise.
The course teaches students to plan, drafting, and to revise.
The course teaches students planning, to draft, and revision.
The course teaches students to plan, draft, and revising.
parallel_pier.why: Repeating “to” before each verb is one valid pattern; dropping it before all of them is another. Mixing the two is not.

parallel_pier.q: “The candidate promised both lower taxes and ___.”
parallel_pier.why: “Both … and” must bracket matching structures. A noun phrase demands a noun phrase.

parallel_pier.q: “Tickets are sold at the box office, on the website, and ___.”
opts: using the mobile app is possible
parallel_pier.why: The list is built from prepositional phrases (“at …”, “on …”), so the third item must be one too.

parallel_pier.q: “Her method is more efficient than ___.”
parallel_pier.why: The comparison is between two methods, so the possessive “his” — short for “his method” — is what balances it.

parallel_pier.q: “On Saturdays she cleans, cooks, and ___.”
parallel_pier.why: The first two items are present-tense verbs, so the third must be one too.

parallel_pier.q: “You can either pay online or ___.”
parallel_pier.why: “Either” sits before the verb “pay”, so “or” must be followed by a verb phrase of the same shape.

parallel_pier.q: “The choice was between staying home and ___.”
parallel_pier.why: “Between … and” joins two matching forms. “Staying” is an -ing form, so the second must be “going”.

parallel_pier.q: “The study found that sleep improves memory, that exercise lifts mood, and ___.”
opts: the effect of diet on focus
parallel_pier.why: The list repeats “that” + a full clause. The third item has to follow the same pattern for the list to stay parallel.

parallel_pier.q: “The population of Lagos is larger than ___.”
parallel_pier.why: Compare population with population. “Larger than Cairo” sets a population against a city; “that of” restores the match.

parallel_pier.q: Which sentence is NOT parallel?
opts: He enjoys hiking, to swim, and cycling.
He enjoys hiking, swimming, and cycling.
He likes to hike, to swim, and to cycle.
He likes to hike, swim, and cycle.
parallel_pier.why: Every item in a list must match the first. “Hiking” and “cycling” are -ing forms, so “to swim” breaks the pattern. The other three keep one form throughout.

parallel_pier.q: “The hotel was neither clean nor ___.”
parallel_pier.why: Neither … nor must join matching parts. “Clean” is an adjective, so the second slot needs an adjective too.

parallel_pier.q: “The manager explained what had gone wrong and ___.”
parallel_pier.why: “What had gone wrong” is a clause, so the item joined to it by “and” should be a clause of the same kind. A noun phrase, an infinitive or an -ing phrase breaks the pairing.

parallel_pier.q: “The team won not because of its stars but ___.”
parallel_pier.why: Not … but needs the same structure on both sides. The first side is “because of its stars”, so the second repeats the pattern.

parallel_pier.q: “The new policy aims to cut costs, to shorten, where possible, waiting times, and ___ staff turnover.”
parallel_pier.why: The list is “to cut … to shorten … ___”, so the third item is another “to” verb. The interruption “where possible” makes the pattern easy to lose, which is what the other choices bet on.

parallel_pier.q:
Which item breaks the pattern of the list?
“The coach told us to warm up, to stretch, and running two laps.”
parallel_pier.why: Every item must match the first. The list is built from “to” verbs, “to warm up” and “to stretch”, so the third should be “to run two laps”; “running” changes the shape.

parallel_pier.q: “She spoke clearly, slowly, and ___.”
parallel_pier.why: The first two items are -ly adverbs describing how she spoke, so the third must be an adverb of the same kind: “calmly”.

parallel_pier.q: Which version keeps the list parallel?
opts: The ad promised fast delivery, low prices, and free returns.
The ad promised fast delivery, low prices, and that returns would be free.
The ad promised fast delivery, low prices, and returning items for free.
The ad promised fast delivery, prices that were low, and free returns.
parallel_pier.why: The list is built from noun phrases (“fast delivery”, “low prices”), so the third item must be one too. A “that” clause, an -ing phrase or a clause in the middle of the list each breaks the shape.

parallel_pier.q: “The question is whether to repair the roof or ___.”
parallel_pier.why: “Whether … or” is a correlative pair, like “either … or”, and needs matching parts on each side. The first side is a “to” verb, “to repair the roof”, so the second is “to replace it”.

parallel_pier.q:
Which choice makes the sentence parallel?
“She not only won the race but also the medal for sportsmanship.”
opts: She won not only the race but also the medal for sportsmanship.
She not only won the race but also won for sportsmanship the medal.
Not only she won the race but also the medal for sportsmanship.
parallel_pier.why: The parts after “not only” and “but also” must match. As written, a verb phrase (“won the race”) is paired with a noun phrase (“the medal”). Moving “not only” after “won” pairs two nouns, “the race” and “the medal”. The original sounds natural, which is why it slips past.

structure_span.q:
“For two centuries the disease was thought to travel in bad air. Then, in 1854, a physician mapped the deaths around a single water pump. The map did not persuade everyone at once, but the argument had changed shape: it was now about water, and it has stayed there.”
The passage is organised as:
opts: a long-held belief, a turning point, and its consequence
a claim followed by three examples that support it
a comparison of two cities and how each fought disease
a definition of a disease followed by its exceptions
structure_span.why: Watch the time markers: “For two centuries”, “Then, in 1854”, “has stayed there”. They are the skeleton.

structure_span.q:
“Consider the cost first. Then consider what the cost buys. Then consider what is lost when the thing is not bought at all, which is the calculation nobody makes.”
The paragraph is structured as:
opts: a sequence of three framings, ending with the author’s own
a list of objections to spending, each with a reply
a chronological narrative of a single purchase
a general rule about costs followed by its exceptions
structure_span.why: Three parallel imperatives, and the last one carries the relative clause that gives the author away.

structure_span.q:
“The bird is small, brown and unremarkable. Its song is small, brown and unremarkable. And yet it can navigate from Finland to Mozambique using, we now believe, a protein in its eye that responds to the earth’s magnetic field.”
The passage moves from:
structure_span.why: The pivot is “And yet”. Everything before it is deliberately flat so the turn can land.

structure_span.q:
“There are three objections. The first — that it is expensive — is true and unimportant. The second, that it is unpopular, is true and temporary. The third is that it will not work, and that one deserves a serious answer.”
The structure of this paragraph is best described as:
opts: an enumeration in which the items are ranked by seriousness
a comparison of two positions on whether it will work
a narrative of how the objections arose, in order
a definition of the proposal supported by examples
structure_span.why: It numbers three objections and dismisses the first two in a clause each to clear room for the third.

structure_span.q:
“Begin with a lemon. Its skin is a store of oil; its flesh is a store of acid; the two are used for opposite purposes and are almost never used together. Most of what follows in this book is an argument with that “almost”.”
The final sentence functions to:
opts: state the book’s subject by turning on a word in the previous sentence
summarise the chemical properties of lemon skin and flesh
explain why lemon skin and flesh are almost never used in the same dish
conclude the discussion of citrus before a new topic begins
structure_span.why: The quotation marks around “almost” do the work — the author has planted the word in order to pick it up.

structure_span.q:
“The engine failed at 04:10. The backup engaged at 04:11 and failed at 04:26. The crew had, by their own later account, believed until 04:31 that the backup was running.”
The paragraph is organised by:
opts: time, with the last sentence revealing a gap in what was known
cause and effect, with the cause of the failure stated last
a comparison between the main engine and the backup engine
a general rule about failures followed by a specific case
structure_span.why: Three timestamps in order, and the fourth lands outside the sequence to show what the crew did not know.

structure_span.q:
“What is a weed? A plant in the wrong place. What is the wrong place? Wherever someone has other plans. The category, in other words, is not botanical at all.”
The passage proceeds by:
opts: a chain of questions and answers ending in a conclusion
a narrative of how weeds spread from garden to garden
a contrast between two kinds of plant and their uses
a list of examples of plants growing in the wrong places
structure_span.why: Two question-and-answer pairs, then “in other words” signals the conclusion drawn from both.

structure_span.q:
“Everyone knows the story: an apple, a head, a law. It is almost certainly embroidered, and the embroidering was probably his own. But the story has done a job no equation could, which is to give the law a place to live in people who will never read it.”
The passage is structured as:
opts: a familiar claim, a doubt about it, and a defence of it on other grounds
a claim about the law supported by three examples from his life
a chronological account of how the law was first discovered
a comparison of two scientists and the different stories told about each of them
structure_span.why: Note “It is almost certainly” and then “But”. The author concedes the story is false and then argues it is useful anyway.

structure_span.q:
“The first paragraph of this report tells you what was found. The second tells you how. The third tells you what it cost, and it is the third that will be read.”
The final clause serves mainly to:
opts: comment wryly on the reader’s priorities
summarise what the report’s findings were
explain the method the report used
justify the length of the third paragraph
structure_span.why: Having laid out a neutral structure, the author adds a judgement about which part matters to people.

structure_span.q:
“Salt was money, then salt was cheap. The change took about eighty years and almost no one recorded it happening, because nothing that becomes ordinary is written down while it is becoming so.”
The second sentence relates to the first by:
opts: explaining why the change left little trace
giving an example of the change
restating the first sentence more precisely
structure_span.why: The first states the change; the second explains the absence of a record of it, with a general principle attached.

structure_span.q:
“Some inventions arrive before anyone needs them. The laser, built in 1960, was called ‘a solution looking for a problem’; it now reads barcodes, cuts steel and carries most of the world’s phone calls.”
The laser is mentioned mainly to:
opts: illustrate the claim in the first sentence
contradict the claim in the first sentence
introduce a new topic about telephones
explain in detail how lasers are built
structure_span.why: A general claim followed by one case of it: the laser is the example. Telephones are one of its later uses, not a new subject.

structure_span.q:
“Online reviews are easy to fake. Still, a restaurant with three thousand of them is hard to fake entirely, and the pattern across many reviews tells you more than any single one.”
The first sentence functions as:
opts: a concession that the author then limits
the main claim of the whole passage
evidence for the claim in the second sentence
a summary of the passage’s conclusion
structure_span.why: “Still” marks the turn. The author grants the first sentence and then narrows how far it matters, which is what a concession does.

structure_span.q:
“For most of the year the marsh is silent. The reeds stand; the water barely moves. Then, in the second week of April, the frogs arrive, and for a month nobody within a mile sleeps well.”
Which word or phrase marks the passage’s main shift?
structure_span.why: Everything before “Then” describes stillness; everything after it is the change. Time words are often the hinge of a passage.

structure_span.q:
“Why do cities keep building roads they know will fill? Partly because congestion is visible and its cure looks obvious; partly because the alternatives take longer than an election.”
The opening question mainly serves to:
opts: introduce the issue the rest of the passage explains
challenge the reader to propose a better alternative
show that the author opposes all road building
suggest that the question cannot be answered
structure_span.why: The question is answered at once, twice over (“Partly … partly …”). It sets up the explanation rather than leaving the reader to supply one.

structure_span.q:
“Early aviators navigated by landmarks: rivers, railway lines, the church spire in each town. Cloud made this impossible, and so the first instrument pilots learned to trust dials over their own senses, which in cloud will tell a pilot that a steady turn is level flight.”
How does the second sentence develop the first?
opts: It names the limit that forced a new method.
It gives more examples of flying by landmarks.
It disputes a claim made in the first sentence.
It restates the first sentence in simpler terms.
structure_span.why: “Made this impossible, and so” is a cause leading to a change: landmark navigation failed in cloud, and instruments replaced it. Nothing in the first sentence is disputed.

structure_span.q:
“Heavy rain washed soil from the hillside. The soil clogged the stream, and the fish that had spawned there for centuries moved elsewhere.”
The passage is organised as:
opts: a chain of causes and effects
a list of examples of one idea
structure_span.why: Each event causes the next: the rain moves the soil, the soil clogs the stream, the fish leave. Nothing is compared, listed or solved.

structure_span.q:
“When I was seven, I tried to dig to the other side of the world with a spoon. Geologists have been digging in the same spirit ever since, and have got about as far: the deepest hole ever drilled reaches twelve kilometres, about a third of the way through the continental crust.”
The first sentence mainly serves to:
opts: introduce the topic through a personal story
prove that geologists are digging wrongly
describe the author’s career in geology
explain how deep holes are really drilled
structure_span.why: Ask the sentence’s job: a childhood memory opens the subject, digging deep, before the passage turns to real drilling. It introduces; it does not prove or explain.

structure_span.q:
“The survey counted cars, bikes and pedestrians at the junction for a week. Cars: 4,100. Bikes: 2,900. Pedestrians: 6,300. The junction, in other words, is used mostly by people on foot, and it is designed almost entirely for cars.”
The last sentence:
opts: draws a conclusion from the counts
adds a fourth count to the survey
questions how the survey was done
structure_span.why: “In other words” flags a restatement: the final sentence turns the three numbers into a point. It adds no new figure and doubts nothing.

structure_span.q:
“[1] Most footbridges are designed to stay perfectly still. [2] One London footbridge was designed to stay still too, and on its opening day it swayed so badly under crowds of walkers that it was closed within days.”
Sentence 2 relates to Sentence 1 by:
opts: giving a case where that design goal failed
offering a solution to a problem in it
comparing the costs of two footbridges
structure_span.why: Sentence 1 states the usual aim; Sentence 2 gives a bridge that shared the aim and missed it. That is a counter-case, not a restatement or a solution.

structure_span.q:
“Receipts from the sugar tax fell in its second year. That might look like failure. It is the opposite: the tax was designed to shrink its own base, and falling receipts mean people are buying less sugar.”
The second sentence functions as:
opts: a reading the author sets up to reject
the author’s own conclusion about the tax
evidence that the tax has worked well
a summary of the first sentence’s data
structure_span.why: The trap is to take “That might look like failure” as the verdict. The next sentence reverses it (“It is the opposite”), so the author voices the obvious reading only to knock it down.

structure_span.q:
“First, the clay is dug and left outside all winter so frost can break it down. In spring it is soaked, sieved and dried to a paste. Only then is it shaped, and the shaped pieces wait another month before firing.”
Which pattern organises the passage?
structure_span.why: Follow the transitions: “First”, “In spring”, “Only then”, “another month”. Each marks a turn in time, so the passage is chronological: a process described step by step.

structure_span.q:
“Why do cats land on their feet? Within a fraction of a second of falling, a cat twists its front half, then its back half, so that its paws face the ground before it lands.”
What follows the opening question?
opts: a list of unrelated facts about cats
a story about one particular cat
structure_span.why: A question the author asks and then answers sets up an explanation. The second sentence describes the twist that answers “why”.

structure_span.q:
“Critics called the new bridge an eyesore when it opened. Ten years later, it is on the city’s postcards.”
How does the second sentence change the picture given by the first?
opts: It shows that opinion of the bridge later reversed.
It gives the reason the critics disliked the bridge.
It adds a second criticism of the bridge.
It explains how the bridge was built.
structure_span.why: The time marker “Ten years later” signals a turn, and the postcards show the bridge is now admired. The second sentence overturns the first rather than supporting it.

structure_span.q:
“Most pond snails are harmless. The one exception in this region, a small cone-shaped species, carries a parasite that can infect cattle. Farmers who find it in a drinking trough should drain the trough.”
The second sentence mainly serves to:
opts: introduce an exception to the first claim
give an example that supports the first claim
describe the life cycle of pond snails
offer a solution to a problem
structure_span.why: Ask what job the sentence does. The first sentence says most snails are harmless; the second names the one that is not. “The one exception” says it outright. The solution comes in the third sentence.

structure_span.q:
“Pale lichen on the old stones suggests clean air. Yet this churchyard sits beside the busiest road in the county. The explanation is the wall: two metres of brick that keeps the exhaust at the level of the traffic.”
What role does the last sentence play?
opts: It resolves the puzzle the first two sentences raise.
It adds a second sign that the air is clean.
It contradicts the claim about the lichen.
It starts a new topic, the history of the wall.
structure_span.why: “Yet” sets clean-air lichen against a busy road, creating a puzzle, and “The explanation is” announces the answer. The wall is mentioned only to explain the puzzle, not to open a new topic, and the lichen claim is confirmed rather than contradicted.

tone_tundra.q:
“The committee’s solution, arrived at after fourteen months, was to form a second committee.”
The tone of this sentence is best described as:
tone_tundra.why: The humour lives in “fourteen months” set against the outcome. “Furious” overshoots — the ACT’s tone answers stay moderate.

tone_tundra.q:
“She has read everything on the subject, and it shows in the worst way: the book cannot move an inch without stopping to cite someone.”
The author’s attitude toward the book is:
opts: critical while acknowledging the author’s diligence
wholly admiring of its thoroughness and scholarship
indifferent to whether the book succeeds or not
hostile toward scholarship and citation in general
tone_tundra.why: The first clause grants a virtue and the second names the fault it produced. A one-sided answer misses half the sentence.

tone_tundra.q:
“It works. It is not elegant, it will not scale, and I would not defend it in a review. But at four in the morning, with the deadline gone, it works.”
The tone is best described as:
tone_tundra.why: Three concessions then a plain claim, repeated. The repetition is satisfaction; the concessions keep it grudging.

tone_tundra.q: A word like meddlesome signals a tone that is:
tone_tundra.why: Connotation does the work: the word carries disapproval before the sentence around it says anything.

tone_tundra.q:
“The restoration has been careful, and the chapel is now exactly as it never was.”
The tone is best described as:
tone_tundra.why: “Exactly as it never was” undercuts the praise in the first clause without raising its voice.

tone_tundra.q:
“I have been asked to describe the conditions in the camp. I will describe the water supply, and the reader may work outwards from there.”
The tone is best described as:
opts: restrained in the face of something serious
detached and uninterested in the camp
openly outraged at the conditions described
tone_tundra.why: The restraint is deliberate and is itself the signal. Outrage would be stated; here it is left to the reader.

tone_tundra.q:
“There is no shortage of advice about sleep. There is, as far as I can establish, one piece of it that survives contact with evidence, and it is: go to bed at the same time.”
The author’s attitude toward sleep advice generally is:
tone_tundra.why: Almost all of it is dismissed and one item survives. That is scepticism, not alarm.

tone_tundra.q:
“He was, by every account including his own, a difficult man to work for, and the six people who stayed twenty years each said they would do it again.”
The tone is best described as:
tone_tundra.why: The sentence refuses to resolve the tension it sets up, which is the point.

tone_tundra.q:
“The new timetable is an improvement in the sense that it is different.”
The tone is:
tone_tundra.why: “In the sense that” withdraws the compliment the sentence just paid.

tone_tundra.q:
“I do not think the method is right. I think it is the best wrong method available, and I would use it tomorrow.”
The author’s attitude is best described as:
tone_tundra.why: The reservation is stated and then set aside for practical reasons. “Undecided” misses that he would act.

tone_tundra.q:
“The shop is a phone store now. For thirty years it sold sweets from glass jars, and on the walk home from school it was where the day turned good.”
The tone of the passage is best described as:
tone_tundra.why: The past is remembered warmly and the present is stated flatly, without complaint. That gentle longing is wistfulness; nothing is blamed.

tone_tundra.q:
“She built the boat alone, over nine winters, from a design she had drawn herself, and it has never leaked.”
The author’s attitude toward the builder is:
tone_tundra.why: Every detail stacks up the achievement — alone, nine winters, her own design, never leaked. The facts are chosen to impress.

tone_tundra.q:
“At first the plan looked sensible. Then the costs doubled, the deadline slipped twice, and the consultants were rehired to explain why.”
The tone shifts from:
tone_tundra.why: The first sentence is plain report. The last clause — paying the same consultants to explain their own failure — is where the mockery enters. Grief overshoots.

tone_tundra.q:
“The council has generously agreed to repair the streetlight it knocked down.”
Which word most clearly signals the author’s irony?
tone_tundra.why: Fixing damage you caused is not generosity. The word praises what the rest of the sentence shows to be an obligation.

tone_tundra.q:
“The sample was small, and the authors say so. Their result is interesting; it is not yet a finding.”
The tone is best described as:
tone_tundra.why: The author credits the authors’ honesty and the result’s interest, then limits the claim. Balanced and careful is measured, not hostile.

tone_tundra.q:
“What a triumph the new park is: wide lawns, shady paths, and a pond the children adore.”
The tone of the sentence is best described as:
tone_tundra.why: “What a triumph” and “adore” are loaded with approval. The sentence is openly delighted, and “enthusiastic” says so without exaggerating.

tone_tundra.q:
“The report is riddled with errors and padded with repetition.”
The author’s attitude toward the report is:
tone_tundra.why: “Riddled” and “padded” are both loaded against the report, and there is no praise anywhere to balance them.

tone_tundra.q:
“The museum opens at ten on weekdays and at nine on Saturdays. Entry is free for children under twelve.”
The tone of the passage is best described as:
tone_tundra.why: Look for loaded words and there are none, only times and prices. Not every passage takes an attitude; a plain factual one is neutral.

tone_tundra.q:
“Sadly, the old theatre will close next month after ninety years.”
The tone is best described as:
tone_tundra.why: “Sadly” is the one loaded word, and it sets the tone: regret at a loss. “Furious” overstates it; the ACT’s tones are usually mild.

tone_tundra.q:
“Each May I wait for the first swifts screaming over the rooftops; the summer does not properly begin until they arrive.”
The author’s attitude toward the swifts is:
tone_tundra.why: “Screaming” sounds harsh, but it is simply how swifts sound. The attitude is carried by the rest of the sentence: waiting for them every year, and summer not beginning without them. Judge the whole sentence, not its loudest word.

tone_tundra.q:
“The new bus timetable is a small miracle: buses every ten minutes, clean seats, and drivers who actually wait for you.”
Which word best describes the writer’s tone?
tone_tundra.why: Loaded words give it away: “a small miracle”, “clean”, and drivers who “actually wait”. The tone is positive, and mild enough that “pleased” fits better than anything stronger.

tone_tundra.q:
“Grandpa’s garden was his pride: he knew every rose by name and talked to the tomatoes.”
The writer describes Grandpa with:
tone_tundra.why: Word choice shows the attitude: “his pride”, roses known “by name”, talking to the tomatoes. These are fond, gently amused details, and nothing in them is negative.

tone_tundra.q:
“The report runs to three hundred pages and says, in the end, that more study is needed.”
The writer’s view of the report is most likely:
tone_tundra.why: The sentence sets the length (“three hundred pages”) against the thin result (“in the end … more study is needed”). That contrast is a quiet criticism. It is mild, so “unimpressed” fits, not anything angrier.

tone_tundra.q:
“For the first hour the walk was a pleasure: larks overhead, the sea glittering below. Then the fog came in, the path narrowed to a ledge, and every step became a negotiation.”
How does the mood of the passage change?
tone_tundra.why: Check the start and the end: “a pleasure”, larks and glittering sea give way to fog, a ledge and steps that must be negotiated. “Then” marks the shift, from easy to anxious.

tone_tundra.q:
“The hotel was, I suppose, adequate. The bed was a bed. The view was of a wall.”
Which description best fits the writer’s tone?
tone_tundra.why: “Adequate” sounds neutral, which is the pull toward “calm and satisfied”. But “I suppose”, a bed that was only “a bed” and a view “of a wall” undercut it. The praise is faint on purpose. Judge the whole passage, and keep the tone mild: dry, not furious.

evidence_estuary.q:
“The bridge was closed for three weeks. Shops on the north bank reported takings down by half; two did not reopen. The council’s own survey found that most north-bank customers had come on foot across the bridge.”
Which detail best supports the claim that the closure caused the losses?
opts: most north-bank customers had crossed the bridge on foot
the bridge was closed to all traffic for three whole weeks
shops on the north bank reported takings down by half
two of the north-bank shops did not reopen afterwards
evidence_estuary.why: The other three establish that there was damage. Only the survey links the damage to the bridge.

evidence_estuary.q:
“Sea otters eat urchins; urchins eat kelp. Where otters were hunted out, kelp forests collapsed within a decade. Where otters have been reintroduced, kelp has returned.”
Which sentence provides the strongest evidence that otters protect kelp?
opts: kelp has returned where otters were reintroduced
otters eat the urchins that would otherwise graze
urchins feed on kelp wherever they are found
otters were hunted out of many coastal areas
evidence_estuary.why: The first two describe a mechanism; the reintroduction result tests it in both directions.

evidence_estuary.q:
“The manuscript is dated 1631 in a later hand. The paper carries a watermark used by a Dutch mill between 1648 and 1659.”
The watermark is significant because it:
opts: shows the manuscript is a forgery
evidence_estuary.why: Paper made after 1648 cannot carry writing from 1631. It does not follow that anyone meant to deceive.

evidence_estuary.q:
“Students who ate breakfast scored higher. They also, on average, lived closer to the school, slept longer, and were less likely to hold an evening job.”
The second sentence mainly serves to:
opts: weaken the case that breakfast caused the difference
strengthen the case that breakfast raised the scores
explain how the study of breakfast and scores was funded
describe the test that the students were given to take
evidence_estuary.why: It supplies alternative explanations, which is how a correlation gets undercut.

evidence_estuary.q:
“No fossil of the animal has ever been found north of the river. Sediments of the right age are exposed on both banks and have been surveyed equally.”
The second sentence matters because it:
opts: makes the absence of fossils meaningful rather than accidental
proves that the animal never crossed the river at all
dates the sediments precisely to a single century
identifies which species the missing fossils would belong to
evidence_estuary.why: Absence of evidence counts only when you have looked equally hard in both places. That is exactly what it establishes.

evidence_estuary.q:
“The defence argued that the letter was written under duress. The letter is nine pages long, in an unhurried hand, and contains two corrections made with the same pen.”
The description of the letter functions as:
opts: a neutral description with no bearing
a summary of the letter’s contents
evidence_estuary.why: Length, unhurried hand and careful corrections are all hard to reconcile with duress.

evidence_estuary.q:
“Every published trial of the drug reported a positive result. A registry shows that of thirty-one trials begun, eleven were never published.”
The registry finding is important because it:
opts: suggests the published record is incomplete in a systematic direction
shows that the drug does not work for most of the patients
proves that the eleven unpublished trials were fraudulent
confirms the positive results reported in the published trials
evidence_estuary.why: Missing trials skew the record. That they showed nothing useful is likely, not proven — and fraud is a further leap.

evidence_estuary.q:
“He claims to have been in Lisbon that week. His bank shows a withdrawal in Lisbon on the Tuesday and a second in Porto on the Thursday.”
The bank records:
opts: partly support and partly complicate his account
fully confirm his account of where he was that week
fully contradict his account of the week
have no bearing on his account either way
evidence_estuary.why: Tuesday supports him; Thursday puts him elsewhere. Answers that pick only one half of the evidence are the trap.

evidence_estuary.q:
“The survey found that 78% of respondents supported the proposal. It was distributed through the campaign’s own mailing list.”
The second sentence primarily:
opts: casts doubt on how representative the result is
confirms that the sample was large enough to trust
explains how the survey question was worded
shows that the survey was expensive to run
evidence_estuary.why: Who was asked determines what the number means. Sampling is the first thing to check.

evidence_estuary.q:
“If the theory is right, the deposits should thin toward the east. Four cores were taken along an east-west line. All four show the same thickness.”
The cores:
opts: fail to support the theory’s prediction
show the deposits thin toward the west
evidence_estuary.why: The theory predicted a change and the data show none. That is a failed prediction, not a reversed one.

evidence_estuary.q:
“[1] The orchard was planted in 1920. [2] Its apples won first prize at every county fair for a decade. [3] The farmer’s daughter kept the ribbons in a biscuit tin. [4] After 1935 the orchard stopped entering.”
Which sentence best supports the claim that the orchard’s fruit was once highly regarded?
evidence_estuary.why: Ten years of first prizes is direct evidence of reputation. Sentence 3 shows only that ribbons were kept, not what they were for.

evidence_estuary.q:
“The new crossing made the street safer: accidents fell from twelve to four in the year after it opened.”
Which fact would most weaken this claim?
opts: That year a bypass opened and traffic on the street fell by two-thirds.
Accidents rose on a nearby street that has no crossing of its own.
Residents said they felt much safer after the crossing was built.
The crossing cost the council less to build than it had expected.
evidence_estuary.why: A second cause arriving at the same time can explain the fall without the crossing. The cost is irrelevant, and feelings of safety are not accident figures.

evidence_estuary.q:
Claim: people who work from home are lonelier. Evidence: a writer’s essay describing her own isolation after two years of remote work.
The main weakness of this evidence is that it:
opts: was written too recently to count
evidence_estuary.why: A general claim about people needs more than one case. The essay is about loneliness; its problem is scope, not relevance.

evidence_estuary.q:
Claim: the herons abandoned the colony because of the new footpath beside it.
Which finding would most strengthen the claim?
opts: The herons returned in the year the path was closed for repairs.
Herons in other parks nest close to busy footpaths without trouble.
Heron numbers fell across the whole region in the same year.
The footpath was built in the spring, during the nesting season.
evidence_estuary.why: Remove the cause and the effect reverses: that is the strongest support a single finding can give. A region-wide fall points to a different cause.

evidence_estuary.q:
“Towns with more cafés have more young residents.”
Which fact would best suggest that cafés follow young people rather than attract them?
opts: The cafés opened only after the young people had moved in.
The cafés charge less than cafés in neighbouring towns do.
Older residents visit the cafés as often as young ones do.
Young people say in surveys that they enjoy visiting cafés.
evidence_estuary.why: The order of events decides the direction of cause. If the young people came first, the cafés cannot have drawn them.

evidence_estuary.q:
Claim: regular watering makes tomato plants produce more fruit.
Which evidence supports the claim most directly?
opts: Watered plants fruited twice as much as dry ones in one bed.
Tomatoes are made up of more than ninety percent water.
Many gardeners water their tomato plants once every day.
Tomato plants need several hours of sunlight a day to grow.
evidence_estuary.why: Evidence supports a claim only if it makes the claim more likely. A side-by-side test in one bed, differing only in watering, bears on it directly. The other facts are about tomatoes and water, but being on the same topic is not support.

evidence_estuary.q:
Claim: the bakery’s new oven has cut waiting times.
Which finding would most weaken the claim?
opts: Queues have been as long since the oven arrived as before.
The new oven cost more than the old one did.
Customers say bread from the new oven tastes better.
The bakery has also started selling coffee.
evidence_estuary.why: The claim is about waiting times, so the evidence that bears on it is about waiting times. Unchanged queues contradict it. Price and taste are about the oven, not about the claim.

evidence_estuary.q:
Claim: the town’s new library is well used.
Which detail is on the same topic but does NOT support the claim?
opts: The building was designed by a local architect.
Loans have tripled since the building opened.
Its study rooms are booked every day of the week.
More than a thousand people visit each week.
evidence_estuary.why: Name the claim first: the library is well used. Loans, bookings and visits all measure use. Who designed the building is about the library, but it says nothing about how much anyone uses it.

evidence_estuary.q:
Claim: exercise improves sleep.
Finding: people who exercised in the morning slept better, but people who exercised late at night slept worse.
The finding:
opts: fits the claim only for some times of day
fully supports the claim as it is stated
has no bearing on the claim at all
shows that exercise always harms sleep
evidence_estuary.why: The finding complicates the claim: it fits part of it (morning exercise) but not all of it (late exercise). It neither confirms the claim as stated nor overturns it.

evidence_estuary.q:
Claim: drinking coffee in the evening causes poor sleep.
Which finding would most weaken the claim?
opts: People who drank no coffee slept just as badly.
Many people drink coffee in the evening.
Coffee contains caffeine, which is a stimulant.
Poor sleepers often feel tired the next day.
evidence_estuary.why: Evidence weakens a causal claim when it shows the effect without the cause. If people who had no coffee slept just as badly, the coffee cannot be what is doing it. The other facts are merely on the same topic.

evidence_estuary.q:
Claim: most teenagers in the country prefer cycling to school over any other way of getting there. Evidence: a survey of the members of one cycling club.
What is the main problem with this evidence?
opts: the people surveyed are likely to favour cycling
the survey asked too many questions
cycling clubs are rare in most towns
evidence_estuary.why: Check who was counted. Members of a cycling club are not a fair sample of all teenagers, so their answers cannot settle a claim about the whole country.

evidence_estuary.q:
Claim: the new pedestrian crossing has made the road safer for children.
Which fact best supports the claim?
opts: Accidents involving children on the road fell by half after it opened.
The crossing was painted bright yellow and white.
Many parents walk their children to school.
evidence_estuary.why: Name the claim first: the crossing made the road safer for children. Only the drop in accidents makes that more likely. The paint, the parents and the cost are about the same topic but change nothing.

evidence_estuary.q:
Claim: a bakery’s sales rose last year because it launched a website.
Which fact casts the most doubt on the claim?
opts: Bakeries without websites saw the same rise.
The website has a page showing every cake.
The owner designed the website herself.
Sales rose by a fifth over the year.
evidence_estuary.why: Evidence weakens a cause when the effect appears without it. If bakeries without a website grew just as much, something else, such as a busier town, probably drove the rise. The other facts either describe the website or restate the rise.

evidence_estuary.q:
Claim: the cold snap in January killed off most of the town’s wasps. Evidence: wasp numbers in July were a tenth of last year’s.
Which further finding would make the claim most convincing?
opts: Towns nearby with no cold snap had normal wasp numbers.
Wasps build their nests out of chewed wood.
Last summer was unusually hot and dry.
Residents said they were glad to see fewer wasps.
evidence_estuary.why: A claim about a cause is strongest when places without the cause lack the effect. Normal numbers in towns that missed the cold snap point to the cold. A hot summer last year, on the other hand, suggests another reason last year’s count was high.

evidence_estuary.q:
Claim: reading on screens at bedtime harms children’s sleep. Evidence: children who read on tablets before bed slept less than those who read paper books.
Which fact would most complicate the claim?
opts: The tablet readers also had more TVs in their bedrooms.
Both groups read for about the same length of time.
Tablets can be set to dim their screens at night.
Most children in the study were aged eight to ten.
evidence_estuary.why: A fact complicates a cause when it points to another one. If the tablet group also had more TVs in their rooms, the TVs might explain the lost sleep. “Same reading time” actually removes a rival explanation, so it helps the claim, which makes it the tempting wrong choice.

figurative_falls.q:
“By March the committee had become a fog: you could walk into it, but you could not find anything in it, and you came out damp.”
The comparison of the committee to a fog emphasises its:
figurative_falls.why: Unpack the three things the fog does. None of them is about secrecy — you can walk right in.

figurative_falls.q:
“His argument is a rope bridge: it holds if you keep moving and do not look at any one plank too long.”
The metaphor suggests that the argument is:
opts: persuasive at speed but weak under scrutiny
dangerous to everyone who relies on it
old-fashioned and no longer taken seriously
figurative_falls.why: The condition attached to the metaphor — keep moving, do not look closely — is where the meaning sits.

figurative_falls.q:
“The coastline here has been chewed.”
The word chewed primarily conveys:
figurative_falls.why: Chewing is slow, repeated and leaves an irregular edge. A single event would be “bitten”.

figurative_falls.q:
“Her prose is furniture: you do not notice it, and you could not sit down without it.”
The comparison suggests that her prose is:
figurative_falls.why: Two clauses, two properties: invisible and load-bearing. Choices that pick only a negative miss the second.

figurative_falls.q:
“The town had one industry, and when it went, the town did not so much decline as exhale.”
The word exhale suggests that the decline was:
opts: quiet and complete, like a long release
violent and sudden, like a collapse
celebrated by everyone who lived there
figurative_falls.why: An exhalation is gradual, quiet and final — the point of choosing it over “collapse”.

figurative_falls.q:
“Grief is not a room you leave. It is a room that keeps being where you turn.”
The figure emphasises that grief:
opts: is a private experience others cannot see
can be escaped with enough effort
figurative_falls.why: The second sentence corrects the first. The point is recurrence; “becomes smaller with time” is exactly what the image denies.

figurative_falls.q:
“The new rules landed on the department like weather — not aimed at anyone, and not avoidable either.”
The comparison to weather emphasises that the rules were:
figurative_falls.why: The dash spells out both halves: not aimed, not avoidable.

figurative_falls.q:
“He read the letter twice, folded it into quarters, and put it where the light could not reach it.”
The last clause chiefly suggests that he:
opts: wanted to put the letter out of mind
was protecting the paper from fading
figurative_falls.why: Read literally, the clause is about protecting the paper; read as a figure, it is about putting the letter out of mind. The double reading and the careful folding point to the figure.

figurative_falls.q:
“The orchestra tuned, and for a moment the hall sounded like a wasps’ nest being carried across a garden.”
The simile conveys:
figurative_falls.why: Carried, not disturbed — the image is of many unresolved sounds moving together.

figurative_falls.q:
“Every map of the estuary is a rumour. The channel moves each winter, and the chart in your hand describes a river that has already gone somewhere else.”
Calling the maps rumours emphasises that they are:
opts: passed on by word of mouth only
unpopular with the sailors who use them
figurative_falls.why: The second sentence explains the metaphor: the maps are outdated, not dishonest.

figurative_falls.q:
“The old house held its breath as the removers carried the piano down the stairs.”
The phrase held its breath suggests:
figurative_falls.why: A house cannot breathe; the personification lends it a person’s suspense as the heavy piano goes down the stairs.

figurative_falls.q:
“I have told you a million times to shut the gate.”
The phrase a million times is used to:
opts: exaggerate how often the reminder has been given
report the exact number of reminders given
suggest that the speaker has a poor memory
show that the gate has been broken for years
figurative_falls.why: Hyperbole: the number is impossible on purpose, to stress frustration at repeating the same reminder.

figurative_falls.q:
“The first draft is the quarry; the second is where you find out what the stone can be; everything after that is polishing.”
The extended metaphor suggests that writing:
opts: moves from gathering rough material to refining it
is physically exhausting, like working in a quarry
goes best when the first draft is thrown away
requires the writer to know something about geology
figurative_falls.why: Follow the image through its stages: quarry (raw material), shaping (discovery), polishing (finish). The metaphor maps a process, not the effort involved.

figurative_falls.q:
“The news rippled through the village.”
The word rippled suggests that the news:
opts: spread outward gradually from one point
arrived everywhere at the same moment
figurative_falls.why: A ripple starts in one place and widens in rings. “Everywhere at once” is the opposite of that picture.

figurative_falls.q:
“After the storm tore off half the roof, Grandpa allowed that the house was ‘a bit draughty.’”
The phrase a bit draughty is best described as:
figurative_falls.why: Losing half a roof is far worse than a draught. Saying much less than the truth, for dry humour, is understatement — the reverse of exaggeration.

figurative_falls.q:
“The lake was as smooth as glass — not a ripple anywhere.”
The simile describes the lake as:
figurative_falls.why: The next words gloss the image: “not a ripple anywhere.” Glass stands for smoothness here, not for cold or for transparency.

figurative_falls.q:
“The wind whispered through the pines.”
The word whispered suggests:
figurative_falls.why: Personification gives the wind a human action, and whispering is quiet. The wind is not literally talking, and nothing is violent or silent.

figurative_falls.q:
“My brother is a night owl; he does his best work after midnight.”
Night owl means someone who:
opts: is most active late at night
figurative_falls.why: The second half of the sentence explains the metaphor: he works best after midnight. Read what the owl stands for, being awake at night, not the bird itself.

figurative_falls.q:
“Her letter was a warm blanket after a long, cold week.”
The metaphor suggests that the letter was:
figurative_falls.why: A warm blanket after the cold is comfort, and the warmth of the image signals a positive meaning. The “cold week” is a mood, not weather to take literally.

figurative_falls.q:
“The deadline was a wall we kept driving toward, and every week the brakes felt a little softer.”
The image suggests a growing sense that:
opts: they could not stop or slow down in time
the deadline had been moved further off
their car was no longer safe to drive
they were eager to reach the deadline
figurative_falls.why: The metaphor is extended: the deadline is a wall, the project is the car, and softening brakes mean less and less control. The fear is of not being able to stop; a literal car is the picture, not the meaning.

figurative_falls.q:
“After the exam my head was a sieve; every date I had learned ran straight out of it.”
The metaphor suggests that the writer:
opts: could not keep hold of facts
figurative_falls.why: Read what the image stands for: a sieve lets things run through, and the rest of the sentence says the dates “ran straight out”. Her memory was not holding the facts.

figurative_falls.q:
“The old mill towns were left to rust in the rain while the money moved south.”
The phrase left to rust primarily conveys:
figurative_falls.why: Towns do not literally rust. Set against “the money moved south”, the image means the towns were abandoned and allowed to decay. A dark image implies a negative idea.

figurative_falls.q:
“The wind worried at the tent all night, tugging at every rope and rattling every pole.”
The writer presents the wind as:
opts: a sign that spring had come
a danger to the whole valley
figurative_falls.why: This is personification: the wind “worried at” and “tugged”, the way a dog worries at a bone. The picture is of something persistent and nagging. The sentence stays with the tent, so a danger to the whole valley overstates it.

figurative_falls.q:
“Her silence at the dinner table was a door closing, quietly, on the whole argument.”
The image of a door closing suggests that she:
opts: ended the discussion without saying so
was about to leave the room
was too shy to join in
agreed with everyone at the table
figurative_falls.why: Pick the meaning, not the picture: the door closes “on the whole argument”, not on the room. Her silence shut the argument down. Leaving the room is the literal reading, and shyness does not fit a deliberate closing.

figurative_falls.q:
“The new policy was a bandage on a broken leg.”
The comparison suggests that the policy:
opts: is too small a fix for a serious problem
will heal the problem slowly but surely
will make the problem much worse
figurative_falls.why: A bandage is a real treatment, which is the pull toward “will heal”, but it is the wrong scale for a broken leg. The comparison says the response is far too slight for the problem, not that it harms or cures.

hypothesis_hollow.q: A hypothesis is best described as:
opts: a guess that cannot be checked
hypothesis_hollow.why: Testability is the whole point. A claim no result could contradict is not a hypothesis.

hypothesis_hollow.q:
Hypothesis: fertiliser increases yield. Result: treated plots yielded no more than untreated plots.
The result:
hypothesis_hollow.why: Failing to support is not the same as showing harm. Stay exactly as far as the data go.

hypothesis_hollow.q: A model predicts the reaction will stop after 40 seconds. The reaction stops after 41. This:
hypothesis_hollow.why: Close agreement supports a model without proving it. Neither of the extreme readings is warranted.

hypothesis_hollow.q: Which statement could NOT be tested by experiment?
opts: Sunsets over the harbour are more beautiful than those inland
Adding salt lowers the freezing point of water on roads
This fertiliser increases the yield of spring wheat
Bats locate flying insects at night by listening for echoes
hypothesis_hollow.why: No measurement decides a question of taste. The other three name something observable.

hypothesis_hollow.q:
A researcher predicts that if temperature causes the colour change, warming the sample in the dark will still change it.
This prediction is useful because it:
opts: separates temperature from light as a cause
increases the sample size of the experiment
shortens the time the experiment takes
confirms the hypothesis before any test
hypothesis_hollow.why: A good prediction is one where the two rival explanations give different answers.

hypothesis_hollow.q: A hypothesis survives ten experiments. It is now:
opts: well supported but still open to revision
proven true beyond any further doubt
a law that no experiment can overturn
hypothesis_hollow.why: Support accumulates; proof, in this sense, does not arrive.

hypothesis_hollow.q: Two models predict identical results for every experiment anyone can perform. Choosing between them:
opts: cannot be settled by those experiments
is settled by whichever is older
is settled by whichever is simpler to state
hypothesis_hollow.why: If the predictions never differ, no result discriminates. That is a limit of the experiments, not of knowledge for ever.

hypothesis_hollow.q:
Hypothesis: the lake’s fish are declining because of rising temperature.
Which finding would most weaken it?
opts: Fish also declined in nearby lakes whose temperature did not rise
The lake warmed by 2 °C over the period of the fish decline
Fish numbers in the lake fell by 40 % over the same period
Warm water holds less dissolved oxygen than cold water
hypothesis_hollow.why: The decline happening without the proposed cause is what breaks the link. The others are consistent with the hypothesis.

hypothesis_hollow.q: An experiment is designed so that no possible result would count against the hypothesis. The design is:
opts: flawed, because the hypothesis cannot be tested
ideal, because the hypothesis will be confirmed
acceptable if the sample is large
hypothesis_hollow.why: A test that cannot fail is not a test. Repetition and sample size do not fix it.

hypothesis_hollow.q: A prediction derived from a model is confirmed. This shows that the model is:
opts: useful so far, not necessarily true
hypothesis_hollow.why: A wrong model can still make some right predictions. One success narrows the field without closing it.

hypothesis_hollow.q: Which is the best hypothesis for an experiment on bean plants and fertiliser?
opts: Beans given fertiliser grow taller than beans without
Fertiliser is probably good for most kinds of plants
Bean plants are the most interesting plants to grow
Plants may or may not respond to fertiliser at all
hypothesis_hollow.why: A usable hypothesis names what changes and what will be measured, and it could turn out false. “May or may not” can never fail, and “good for plants” measures nothing.

hypothesis_hollow.q: Hypothesis: seeds need light to germinate. If the hypothesis is correct, which result is expected?
opts: Seeds kept in the dark fail to germinate
Seeds kept in the dark germinate faster
Seeds in light and dark germinate equally
Seeds kept in the light grow heavier
hypothesis_hollow.why: Turn the hypothesis into a prediction about the test: remove light, and germination should not happen.

hypothesis_hollow.why: Germination rises from 10 to 30 °C and then falls at 40 °C. A hypothesis can fit part of a range and fail beyond it.

hypothesis_hollow.q: To test the hypothesis “adding salt raises the boiling point of water”, which should the experimenter vary on purpose?
hypothesis_hollow.why: The hypothesis names the cause (salt) and the effect (boiling point). Vary the cause and measure the effect; hold the pot and stove constant.

hypothesis_hollow.q: Ice-cream sales and swimming accidents rise and fall together over a year. Which hypothesis best explains this?
hypothesis_hollow.why: When two things move together, look for a third that drives both. Summer heat brings both ice cream and swimming.

hypothesis_hollow.q: A student grows plants under blue and red light. Which statement is a hypothesis rather than an observation?
opts: Blue light makes plants grow taller than red light.
The plant under blue light grew 12 cm in two weeks.
The leaves of the red-light plant turned pale yellow.
Both plants were given 50 mL of water each morning.
hypothesis_hollow.why: A hypothesis is a testable prediction about cause and effect; an observation records what happened. Only the first statement makes a general claim that an experiment could test.

hypothesis_hollow.why: Check the direction the hypothesis predicts: every extra hour of sleep comes with a higher score, so the data support it.

hypothesis_hollow.q: Hypothesis: dissolving salt in water lowers its freezing point. Which result would contradict it?
opts: Salt water froze at a higher temperature than fresh water.
Salt water froze at a lower temperature than fresh water.
Salt water and fresh water both froze within an hour.
Salt water took longer to freeze than fresh water did.
hypothesis_hollow.why: A result contradicts a hypothesis when it goes the opposite way from the prediction. The prediction is a lower freezing point, so freezing at a higher temperature contradicts it.

hypothesis_hollow.q: A gardener spreads lawn feed over the whole lawn, and a week later the grass is greener. She concludes the feed worked. The main weakness is that:
opts: nothing shows untreated grass would not have greened too
the lawn was not large enough to give a reliable result
a week is too long to wait before judging the results
the feed should have been spread more thickly in places
hypothesis_hollow.why: Without an untreated patch to compare against, the change could be rain, warmth or the season. A hypothesis needs a comparison that differs in only the factor being tested.

hypothesis_hollow.q: Bees visited blue flowers more often than yellow ones. The blue flowers also held more nectar. A student concludes that bees prefer the colour blue. The study:
opts: cannot separate colour from nectar as the cause
proves bees can see blue better than yellow
shows that nectar has no effect on bee visits
supports the conclusion without any doubt
hypothesis_hollow.why: Colour and nectar changed together, so either could explain the visits. To test colour, the nectar must be the same in both kinds of flower.

hypothesis_hollow.q: A student predicts: “If a ramp is made steeper, a toy car will reach the bottom sooner.” What will the student need to measure?
opts: the time the car takes to reach the bottom
the colour of the toy car
the number of cars in the class
hypothesis_hollow.why: A testable hypothesis names what will change (the steepness) and what will be measured (how soon the car arrives). So the student times the run for each steepness.

hypothesis_hollow.q: Hypothesis: earthworms move away from light. In a tray that is half lit and half dark, most of the worms gather in the dark half. The result:
opts: proves the hypothesis for every animal
shows the hypothesis cannot be tested
hypothesis_hollow.why: Compare the data with the prediction: worms that move away from light should end up in the dark, and they did. That is support. One tray of worms says nothing about every animal.

hypothesis_hollow.q: Towns with more fire stations report more fires each year. Which hypothesis best explains this pattern?
opts: Bigger towns have both more fire stations and more fires.
Fire stations cause fires in the streets around them.
Fires are only reported when a station is nearby.
Towns build stations once their fires have stopped.
hypothesis_hollow.why: When two things rise together, look for a third factor driving both. Size does that here: a larger town has more buildings to catch fire and needs more stations. Nothing suggests the stations cause fires.

hypothesis_hollow.q: A model says a bridge cable stretches 2 mm for every 1,000 kg of load. At 6,000 kg the cable stretches 12 mm; at 8,000 kg it stretches 22 mm. What should the scientists conclude?
opts: the model holds up to about 6,000 kg only
the model is wrong at every load
the model is right at every load
the 8,000 kg reading must be an error
hypothesis_hollow.why: At 6,000 kg the model predicts 12 mm, a match. At 8,000 kg it predicts 16 mm, but the cable stretched 22. A model is a useful approximation, and this one works at lower loads but breaks down at higher ones, so it needs updating rather than throwing out.

hypothesis_hollow.q: Hypothesis: plants grow taller under red light than under blue light. Plants under red light averaged 21 cm and plants under blue light averaged 20 cm, but within each group heights varied by about 8 cm. The result:
opts: is too small a gap to count as clear support
strongly supports the hypothesis as stated
shows that blue light works better
proves that red light works best
hypothesis_hollow.why: The averages do match the prediction, which is the pull toward “supports”. But a 1 cm gap is tiny next to an 8 cm spread within each group; the difference could easily be chance. A difference smaller than the spread inside the groups is weak support.
